source: trans. for ScriptureBot from the Latin (ed. Morard, 1480/81 text)

1.1:
**“The word of the Lord, that came”**
• which “in the beginning was with God; and the Word was God”
• the Word which was “in the beginning” with the Father came, that is, spoke; or, it came to pass that he spoke to the prophet
**“to Osee”**
• the name means “saviour”
• This is as it were the title of the book.
• Jerome: that he might make him a prophet of the Lord, one “to whom the word of God was spoken”; and as God makes gods, and “enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world,” and says to the apostles, “You are the light of the world,” so the Saviour himself might make his prophet a saviour. For Osee means “saviour,” as does Josue the son of Nun. For he was not called Auses, as is read in some Greek and Latin copies, but Osee, that is, saviour; and “of the Lord” was added, that he might be called the saviour of the Lord.
*Jerome:* Osee means “saviour.” The word of the Lord came to the prophet so that, by inspiring his mind, it might make him a god, and the saviour of his people, by announcing to them the words of God and giving them examples of good living. The saints to whom the word of the Lord comes are gods and saviours by grace, while there is one God and Saviour by nature, who was prefigured by all of them. So Hosea signifies Christ, the son of that well who says of himself: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have digged to themselves cisterns that can hold no water.” For a well has waters flowing from a living spring; a cistern, waters brought in from outside, which it only keeps cool.
**“the son of Beeri”**
• the name means “of my well”
• Son of Beeri, “of my well”: that is, of the wells that Abraham and Isaac and Jacob dug, which the Philistines tried to stop up. A well has lasting waters flowing from a living spring; a cistern, waters brought in from outside, which it keeps cool. Hence: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have digged to themselves cisterns that can hold no water”; and hence: “With thee is the fountain of life.”
**“in the days of Ozias”**
• the name means “the strength of the Lord”
• The prophets so promise the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles that what they say fits the present time; lest they seem not to teach the assembly, called together for another purpose, about what it has in mind, but to play with things uncertain and to come. So here Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, whom Hosea marries and who bears a son named Jezreel, which means “seed of God,” in revenge for whose blood the kingdom of Jehu is overthrown, is to be referred to the calling of the Gentiles in a way that fits the time in which she is said to have borne the son. So these two women, Gomer the harlot, who bears three children, first Jezreel, second a girl called Without mercy, and third one called Not my people; and the other, who is hired for fifteen pieces of silver and a core and a half core of barley, and is called an adulteress, are referred to Israel and Judah. These are the two women who in Zechariah are said to have the wings of the hoopoe, the kite or the heron, and to go into the land of Shinar, where Babylon was built. Ezekiel signifies them under the names of two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah. These are the two sticks that Ezekiel joins into one stick.
• The Hebrews hold that all the fathers or grandfathers or kinsmen of the prophets whose names are set at the beginning of their books were prophets, though their prophecies are not read. So it is plain that Beeri, Hosea’s father, was a prophet.
**“In the days of Ozias”** — Jerome: These kings reigned over the people of God, whose name means “confession”; but in Israel, which had made idols for itself, reigned Jeroboam, whose name means chronismos, that is, temporality or delay, because he loved the world and strove to linger in the love of it, not seeking the world to come.
*Jerome:* Uzziah, also called Azariah, reigned in Jerusalem over the two tribes fifty-two years. His son Jotham succeeded him and reigned sixteen years; after him his son Ahaz, likewise sixteen years, in whose eleventh year the ten tribes were taken captive by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians (others say of the Chaldeans), and settled in the mountains of the Medes. After Ahaz reigned his son Hezekiah twenty-nine years. So it is plain that Hosea prophesied before the captivity, under Uzziah and Jotham; mourned it as it came on, under Ahaz; and told it over, when it was past, for the amendment of Judah, under King Hezekiah. At the time Uzziah began to reign over Judah, Jeroboam was in the twelfth year of his reign over Israel: the great-grandson of Jehu, to whom the Lord had promised that his sons would reign to the fourth generation, because he had killed Jezebel and two wicked kings, Joram king of Judah and Ahab king of Samaria, with his seventy brothers.
*Jerome:* “Hosea was of the tribe of Issachar, born in Belemoth. In his prophecy he gave a sign: ‘The Lord will come upon the earth like the oak that is in Shiloh,’ and so on. He was buried in his own land and sleeps in peaceful rest.” “He bears the figure of Christ, who out of the fornication of the Gentiles took the Church into his body.” He prophesied against the ten tribes, saying little of the two. He prophesied, as history, that the Jews would return to Christ in the last time. He also foretold the third day, of the Lord’s resurrection.
*Jerome:* By the surface of the story it seems strange that the Lord should command, or the prophet, commanded to take a harlot, should obey. But neither did the Lord command a shameful thing, nor did the prophet sin by obeying; rather he called the harlot back to chastity and, remaining in his own goodness, made her good from bad. What is done in him according to the flesh is done in God spiritually, who took the synagogue, forgetful of her husband and committing fornication with the many gods of the Gentiles. And note that in this prophet and in the others the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles are so foretold that the root of the history, as the letter sounds, is not wholly abandoned, but what the prophet says fits his own time; lest he seem not to teach the assembly he speaks to about what it has in mind, but to play with things uncertain and to come. So the two women Hosea took, Gomer the harlot, who bore three children, and the other, who is hired for fifteen pieces of silver and called an adulteress, are referred to Israel and Judah.
**“Joathan”** — the name means “the perfection of the Lord”
**“Achaz”** — the name means “strength”
**“Ezechias”** — the name means “the rule of the Lord”
**“kings of Juda”** — these reigned over the people of God
1.2:
**“The beginning of the Lord’s speaking by Osee”**
• or: the beginning of the Lord speaking in Osee
• Since other prophets too prophesied under Uzziah, Jotham and Ahaz and set those names in their titles, it can be said that he spoke first to Hosea and afterwards to the rest; or that to Hosea he spoke first the things that follow about the harlot, and afterwards the rest.
• Note that the Lord spoke to Hosea by inspiring prophecy in him, and spoke in Hosea, that is, through Hosea, setting teaching before others.
**“and the Lord said to Osee”** — the Father to the Son
**“Go, take thee a wife of fornications”** — Not only a harlot, but one who has committed many fornications; for the prophet is the more patient, the fouler the woman he marries.
**“Go, take thee”** — The Septuagint: “Take thee a wife of fornication and children of fornication.” He is commanded to take a harlot and to take her children, so that, where she had borne children of fornication, he might beget children of the harlot.
**“and have of her children of fornications”**
• or: of fornications
• because they are of a harlot
**“for … by fornication shall depart”** — as if to say: these things are said not so much in fact as in signification
**“the land”** — Judah; or properly Samaria and Israel, that is, the ten tribes, which had departed from the Lord when this was said
**“from the Lord”**
• departing
• not to him, but through him to others
**“the land … from the Lord”** — Since it does not add “all the land,” not Judah but the ten tribes can be understood.
1.3: **“So he went and took Gomer, the daughter of Debelaim: and she conceived, and bore him a son”** — Gomer means “consummated and perfect”; Diblaim, “cakes,” that is, a mass of fat figs, which they shape like bricks and tread and press together so that they keep a long time unspoiled; such were laid on Hezekiah’s boil. Or Diblaim means “pleasure.” So the promised Saviour, from the nation of the Jews, is commanded to take as wife that same nation of Israel, become abominable in fornication and pleasure, which seems sweet to those who enjoy it; and he calls the son born of her Jezreel, that is, “seed of God,” as a figure of himself, born of her according to the flesh.
1.4:
**“And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezrahel”**
• the name means “seed of God,” or “son of God”
• CALL HIS NAME, and so on. This is as if he had said: Call his name Naboth, whose blood was to be avenged. But Naboth is designated by the name of the place in which his blood was shed, to signify that he would be avenged in that same place; as if he had said: Call him the Jezreelite. And this is a figure of Christ, whose blood was to be avenged on those who crucified and mocked him.
**“Call his name”** — As to the letter, Jezreel is a chief city in the kingdom of the ten tribes, in which Naboth was killed; to avenge him Jehu was raised up, who destroyed Ahab and Jezebel. But because he and his sons afterwards turned to idolatry, his kingdom too is said to be overthrown. Under his great-grandson Jeroboam Hosea began to prophesy. When that Jeroboam died, his son Zechariah succeeded him, whom Shallum, born of another stock, killed in the sixth month of his reign; and at once the kings of Assyria took Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, which was beyond the Jordan, then Naphtali, and at last all the remaining tribes. From Zechariah, Jehu’s great-grandson, to Hoshea, under whom all the tribes were taken captive, were forty-nine years. But the figure of the seed of God and the vengeance for his blood are referred to the Lord’s passion, for which both the house of Judah and the kingdom of all Israel are said to be overthrown.
*Jerome:* Jezreel is a chief city in the kingdom of Samaria, near which are very wide plains and a vast valley stretching more than ten thousand paces. There, when battle was joined, Israel, that is, the ten tribes, was cut down by the Assyrians. They are called Ephraim because of Jeroboam, born of Ephraim, who first made the schism in the people. They are called Joseph too, because Joseph was Ephraim’s father. They are called Samaria too, which was itself another chief city of the ten tribes, afterwards called by Augustus Augusta, that is, Sebaste, in which the bones of John the Baptist are laid. After the division of the ten tribes from the two, because of the very great multitude that followed Jeroboam, the old name Israel remained with the ten tribes; and because of the tribe of Judah, which reigned in Jerusalem, the two tribes are called Judah.
**“for yet a little while, and I will visit the blood of Jezrahel”** — the slaughter of my people
**“upon the house of Jehu”**
• which then reigned
• Haimo: Jehu, on whom the blood of Naboth shed in Jezreel is said to be visited, signifies the Jews, of whom the blood of Christ is required, when they were killed by the Romans and taken captive through the whole world.
• In all the prophets the ten tribes signify the heretics, whose multitude is very great; but especially in Hosea the two tribes, in which is the king of David’s line, are referred to the person of the Church. So the bow, that is, the strength of the heretics, of whom it is said, “The sons of Ephraim, who shoot with the bow, have turned back in the day of battle,” will be broken in the valley of the seed of God, that is, of Christ, of whom they thought lowly and earthly things; for “the Father does not judge any man: but hath given all judgment to the Son.”
**“and”**
• so that it is no more
• no wonder, for I will even make it cease
1.5:
**“And in that day”** — when I avenge Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and destroy the kingdom of Israel by the Assyrian’s victory
**“I will break in pieces the bow”** — its strength
1.6:
**“And she conceived again, and bore a daughter”** — After Israel was broken and its kingdom destroyed, there is born no longer Jezreel, that is, the seed of God, nor a male, but a female, of the weaker sex, open to the assault of vices, with a woman’s mind, leaving God and worshipping idols. So she is also given over to forgetting, for to this day she serves the kings of the Persians.
**“Call her name, Without mercy”** — Allegorically: Those who, because of the blood of the seed of God, are called Without mercy are the Jews who said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” But the house of Judah, that is, those of the Jews who confessed Christ, are saved not by the strength of an army but by the preaching of the Gospel, while the people that disbelieved in him is condemned to perpetual slavery under the Romans.
**“and he said to him: Call her name, Without mercy: for I will not add any more to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them”** — What is said of Israel and Judah according to the history is referred to the gatherings of heretics and to the Church: for those are left without mercy and deprived of the kingdom, while the Church of God overcomes by God’s power.
1.7:
**“And I will have mercy on the house of Juda, and I will save them by the Lord, their God”** — in myself, or in my Son
**“And I will have mercy on the house of Juda”** — Jerome: When the ten tribes were taken captive by the Assyrians, Judah is saved from the hand of Sennacherib, not by human strength but by the might of God alone, who sent his angel and in one night struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the army.
**“and I will not save them by bow”** — by weapons of war
1.8:
**“And she weaned her that was called Without mercy”** — Others: Not beloved; but this is truer.
**“And she weaned”** — Jerome: He who was called the seed of God, turned into a woman, and led into captivity for the weakness of his strength and for offending God, because he did not have God’s mercy, is said to be weaned in the feminine, not the masculine, because he had now lost a man’s strength.
*Haimo:* One who is weaned no longer takes his mother’s milk but is fed on other food. So Israel, cast off by the Lord and taken captive in Babylon, is fed on the food of the Gentiles, eating things offered to idols, and no longer takes the milk of the law by which it lived in its own land. So she is said to be weaned without mercy, so that she does not understand even the surface of the law.
1.9: **“Not my people”** — Haimo: This can be referred to those who were then taken captive by the Assyrians, and most of all to those who after Christ’s coming, by denying and killing Christ himself, lost their place and nation, and are called not the people of God but children of the devil; for he who has not the Son has not the Father either. It can also be referred to the heretics, who, thinking ill of God, are driven back by him, so that God is not the portion of their inheritance.
1.10:
**“And”** — for
**“the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea”** — scattered everywhere, as they are now
**“And the number … shall be”** — Though the Jews were taken captive, then by the Assyrians or now by the Romans, yet they are innumerable to men, kept now for the good of believers, and so that at the last their fullness may come in.
**“that is without measure, and shall not be numbered”** — for their multitude
**“And it shall be in the place”** — Haimo: Among the Gentiles; for now among all the nations the Jews are called not servants of God but of the devil; but when they believe at the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, they will be called sons of God by all. Or the place is Jerusalem, where for a long time the Jews, worshipping idols, were called not the people of God; but at the time of Christ’s incarnation, when the apostles and other faithful were taken from there, “he gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
**“You are not my people: it shall be said to them: Ye are the sons of the living God”** — when they cast away their deaf and dumb idols
1.11:
**“And … shall be gathered together”**
• with the Gentiles into one faith
• those of the two tribes converted to the faith
**“the children of Juda, and the children of Israel”**
• of the ten tribes
• Hence Ezekiel: “And one prince in the midst of them, David my servant.”
**“And the children of Juda … shall be gathered together”** — Haimo: By Judah are signified the two tribes joined to it, namely Benjamin, and the priestly tribe, that is, Levi; by Israel the other ten. At the time of Christ’s incarnation those of both the two and the ten tribes who had returned from captivity were living in Judea, and many of them believed in Christ. Or by Israel the Gentiles, by Judah the Jews who would believe, are signified. Or by Israel the heretics, by Judah the catholic men; all of whom will set Christ as their head, and will come up from earthly senses, and from the lowliness of the letter that kills, to the spiritual understanding. For great is the day of Jezreel: for the time from the Lord’s incarnation to the end of the world is of great brightness, in which remission of sins is given and the entrance of the kingdom of heaven is opened.
**“together: and they shall appoint”** — all
**“themselves one head”** — Christ
**“and shall come up”** — Judah and Israel, as if from hell, because they were dead in unbelief
**“out of the land”** — in which Judah and Israel will have one prince
**“for”** — therefore
**“great is the day”** — “This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein.”
**“of Jezrahel”** — of the seed of God, who is Christ, in whom is truly fulfilled what is prefigured by the blood of Naboth the Jezreelite

2.1:
**“Say ye”** — O tribe of Judah
**“to your brethren”** — the ten tribes; lest you despair of their salvation
**“Say ye to your brethren”** — Jerome: Since there is such brightness and power in the day of Christ, let the men of the tribe of Judah not despair of the salvation of the ten tribes, but call them to repentance by word, by prayer and by letters; for he is called brother from being called My people, and sister from being called Hath obtained mercy. This can also be referred to all believers: so you who believe in Christ, Jews and Gentiles alike, say to the broken branches, that is, to the former people that was cast off: My people, for he is your brother; and Hath obtained mercy, for she is your sister. “For when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, then all Israel shall be saved.” This is said so that we may not wholly despair even of the heretics.
2.2:
**“Judge your mother, judge her”**
• for such is your mother; but you, her sons, reprove her
• because, made a wife from a harlot, she does not leave her former ways
**“Judge your mother”** — Haimo: Show the synagogue that she who cast me off is no longer a lawful wife, and I will cast her off, so as not to be her husband. But that I may join her to myself again, I who am the husband of the soul, let her repent, at least after my coming in the flesh, of the uncleanness and fornication she practised with idols. Let her remove, then, the worship of idols from her love and her presence, for she lay open to the lust of many, worshipping the gods of all the nations. Let her take away her adulteries too from between her breasts, that is, from the heart, in which an evil deed is first conceived. For the heart is between the breasts, and from it come forth the thoughts which afterwards go on to deeds. So he exhorts her not to be deprived, for her crimes, of the grace given her by God. After the warning he adds the threat: Lest I strip her naked. The garment by which that people was ruled is understood as God’s help, the teaching of the law and the prophets, and the protection of the angels; all of which he threatens to take away unless she repents of her crime, so that she goes back to the day of her birth, that is, is made like the heathen. After the coming of the truth, even the observance of the law is counted as idolatry.
**“because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband”**
• Note the patience and mercy of the husband to one already divorced, already cast off. He commands the sons to call her back to repentance as their mother, not to insult her as one sent away by their father.
• say this:
**“Let her put away her fornications”** — Jerome: A fornicatress is one who joins herself to many; an adulteress, one who leaves one husband and is joined to another. The synagogue sinned in both ways.
**“Let her put away her fornications from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts”** — All this fits the Jews who deny Christ, and the heretics who follow divers doctrines in heart and deed. Their fornication is between the breasts, that is, it dwells in the heart, in the crafting of idols and of divers doctrines; and unless they repent they are made like unbelievers, and stripped of the virtues they received in the Church, so that even what they falsely seemed to have is brought to nothing.
2.3:
**“Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born”** — when she was in Egypt without God and without a husband
**“and I will make her”** — if she will not be converted
**“as a wilderness”** — as he did in the wilderness: so that she is led into captivity, thirsting for all good things, and cannot return to her country. Hence: “Behold, your house shall be left to you, desolate.”
**“and I will make her as”** — Haimo: I will do even more than this. For “when I brought them out of Egypt,” the fathers were killed in the desert, but their sons entered the land of promise. But now the sons will be taken captive with their fathers and will die outside the land of their birth, because they are children of fornication: for they were begotten in the worship of idols; the faith the fathers had, they handed on to their sons. Hence there follows: For their mother hath committed fornication. Viper bred viper; and she grew so shameless towards God that she sought glory in her crime, saying: I will go after my lovers, who give me what I need for food and clothing. The Jews said this when they worshipped the gods of the Gentiles: that the gifts they had from God they had from demons. It can also be referred to those who, denying the Son of God, chose the author of sedition. So they were confounded, so as to condemn not only themselves but their descendants too, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” It can be referred to the heretics too, who are called mother because they beget others in error; and they are confounded with their followers when they are caught in error, because they had resolved to follow the divers doctrines of heresy.
**“and will set her as a land that none can pass through”** — “Invia”: that is, without a way.
2.5:
**“For their mother hath committed fornication … is covered with shame”** — she was stunned; she was turned to wonder at her crime
**“she that conceived them”** — she made them children of the devil
**“for she said: I will go after my lovers”**
• the demons, the idols
• I will follow the gods with faith and love; or, I will imitate the nations whose gods I worship
**“that give me my bread”** — Jerome: The bread of the heretics is everlasting mourning; their water, the muddy teaching with which they choke even the baptized; their wool and flax, feigned holiness and purity, for “they come in the clothing of sheep”; their oil, flattery. Hence it is said: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” Their drink is the holy Scripture, which they pervert.
2.6:
**“Wherefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and I will stop it up with a wall”** — so that you cannot go where you wanted
**“and she shall not find her paths”** — which you have often trodden with your foot
**“Therefore”** — By the thorns, the prick of sorrows; by the wall, an obstacle. So I will entangle your ways, that is, your actions, in hard labours, and set an obstacle, lest you reach what you want. And her paths: in the prophet’s manner he passes suddenly from one person to another, to frighten the hearers from imitating her.
2.7:
**“And she shall follow”** — with great eagerness
**“after her lovers”** — the Assyrians or the Chaldeans, seeking help from them in trouble
**“And she shall follow after her lovers”** — God’s providence often withdraws from us what we desire, and afflicts us besides, so that we are forced to return to him. Hence in the book of Judges the children of Israel, often weighed down by evils, cry to the Lord, who raises up a saviour for them. The heretics too follow lovers, and, often deserted by them, return to the bosom of mother Church; for scourges teach Israel in all things.
**“and shall not overtake them”** — so that they bring her help; but she will be taken captive by them
**“and she shall seek them, and shall not find”** — favourable to her
**“and she shall say”** — and, driven by this necessity
**“I will go”** — “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound with bread.”
**“and return to my first husband”** — God, who betrothed me to himself by the law
**“because it was better with me then”** — when I obeyed his commands
**“than now”** — when, wretched, I am afflicted for idolatry
2.8:
**“And she did not know”**
• as regards the part that does not return; or even the part that first returned and afterwards sins worse
• Haimo: This looks back to what he said above: that the people of Israel ascribed to idols the temporal goods it had received from God, and, because it did not know that God was their author, made from that gold and silver Baal, the idol of the Sidonians. Mystically, wine signifies spiritual gladness, which they ought to have had not in this world but in God; corn, the law by which they ought to have been fed; oil, the enlightening of the mind; silver, the brightness of speech; gold, the commandment of the love of God and of neighbour. In all these they venerated not God but demons.
**“that I gave her corn”** — which strengthens man’s heart
**“and wine”** — which gladdens
**“and oil”**
• which enlightens
• Oil, which “enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.” Because they referred all these to idolatry rather than to the worship of God, deceived and deceiving others, God takes them all away, so that those who did not feel it from plenty may feel it from want.
**“and … her silver”** — “tried by the fire, proved, purged from the earth”
**“and multiplied … and gold”** — wisdom
**“which”** — or: with which
**“they have used in the service of Baal”**
• the idol of the Babylonians
• Baal means “higher,” because they think their doctrines higher than the Church’s; or “devouring,” because in that knowledge of false opinion a man is devoured.
**“which they have used in the service of Baal”** — Jerome: The same idols are named Baal in the singular and Baalim in the masculine plural. For wherever we read the syllable -im at the end of a Hebrew word, it is plural and masculine, as cherubim, seraphim; but where -oth is read, it is plural and feminine, as sabaoth, which means “of hosts,” “of armies,” “of powers.” And because Baal was worshipped in many places, it is counted in the plural, Baalim.
2.9:
**“Therefore will I return, and take away my corn”** — from the harvest or the granary; for the sorrow will be greater when what is already under cover is, as it were, snatched from their hands
**“in its season”** — of the vintage, or of the winepress
**“I will set at liberty my wool”** — While they are slaves of the devil, they hold the wool and flax under that slavery; but God sets them free, so that they are not possessed by wicked masters.
**“which covered”** — Jerome: The disgrace that they covered is their idols, whose altars they adorned with divers garments. Spiritually, the garments are God’s help and the guard of the angels, which God the giver takes away from the ungrateful, so that, left in their iniquity, they are handed over to the devil for eternal punishment.
2.10:
**“And now”** — the wool and flax being set free
**“I will lay open her folly in the eyes of her lovers”** — so that those who loved her veiled may despise her laid bare
**“And now I will lay open”** — The lovers are the Chaldeans and the Assyrians, whose idols they worshipped, and with whom the Jews had long been at peace. In their eyes the folly of the Jews is laid open when, Jerusalem taken and the temple overthrown, the enemies saw the images of the cherubim and the idol Baal, and said: Because the Jews worshipped idols like other nations, they are made subject to us for their iniquity.
*Jerome:* Judea suffered this both historically and allegorically. Taken captive first by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and at last irreparably by the Romans, she does not celebrate her solemnities with gladness according to her rite; all of which, taken from them, are celebrated spiritually by the faithful in the Church. Hence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.” This is referred to the heretics, who, changing doctrine and knowledge, go out of the Church and are forsaken by God. Their shame lies open to the lovers whom they had deceived before; and, handed over to the beasts, that is, to the devils, they are left to their bites.
**“and no man shall deliver her out of my hand”** — no one’s strength will be able to snatch her from my power; but by just judgment I will have her taken captive by her enemies
2.11:
**“And I will cause all her mirth to cease”** — when she is in slavery in Babylon
**“her solemnities”** — of the Pasch, of Pentecost, of Tabernacles
**“her new moons”**
• the calends
• Neomenia: the new moon, the calends.
**“her sabbaths, and all her festival times”** — on which they gave themselves to feasting and idleness
2.12:
**“And I will destroy her vines, and her fig trees, of which she said”** — I will take them away because she said, that is, thought, that these were given not by God, as by a husband, but by the devil, because she worshipped him
**“And I will destroy”** — Historically, by hail, frost and drought, so that they have no fruit-bearing tree. Mystically, by the vine, gladness of heart; by the fig, the sweetness of temporal delight; which are taken from the ungrateful as from a harlot.
**“and I will make her”** — So that she has no fruit trees but is brought to a wilderness: which was fulfilled first by the Assyrians and Chaldeans and at last by the Romans. Hence there follows: and the beasts of the field shall devour her: the army of the Romans; or the beast is the devil, who devours them by drawing them to his worship, for which they are destroyed for ever.
2.13:
**“And I will visit”**
• Though “visit” is more often taken in a good sense, here it is put in a bad one, for affliction
• He keeps up the figure of the harlot, who to please her lovers decks herself with gold and gems, and seeks by art the beauty that nature has not given her.
• By the earrings, teaching, with which the ears are adorned; by the necklace, the preaching sent out to others. These she cast “before swine, and gave that which is holy to dogs,” according to that saying: “A golden ring in a swine’s snout, a woman fair and foolish.” The heretics too burn incense to Baalim, when they follow the doctrines they have feigned for themselves like idols; they adorn the ears with which words are heard, and the neck by which they are uttered, so as to please by the charm of their eloquence. For they do not stoop to the Church’s rustic simplicity, which casts off a harlot’s ornaments, but aim to please their lovers, men or demons, with an artful and elegant lie.
**“upon her the days of Baalim”** — that is, I will afflict her for the days on which she worshipped Baal
**“to whom”** — she will be afflicted with punishments on the very solemnities on which she sacrificed to demons
**“she burnt incense”** — not to God but to demons
**“and decked herself out with her earrings, and with her jewels, and went after her lovers”** — forgetting her lawful husband, so far as not even to remember him
2.14:
**“Therefore, behold I will allure her”** — as if to say: yet do not despair, though I threatened above
**“Therefore”** — Because I am merciful I will coax her, that she may turn to me; for the promise of good things softens evils. Hence: “Come to me all you that labour.” And as before I brought her out of Egypt and protected her from her enemies in the desert, so I will do when I bring them back from the land of captivity to their own soil. For at the coming of the Son he will open the hope of salvation, and give place for repentance, and coax her.
**“and I will speak to”** — Jerome: He speaks soft and comforting words, to temper sadness with joy. He speaks to the heart who satisfies a saddened heart with tidings of joy. This was fulfilled when Christ said to the disciples: “I will not now call you servants, but friends.” And again: “Little children, these many things I have spoken with you.”
2.15:
**“And I will give her vinedressers out of the same place”** — as at the going out of Egypt, Moses and Aaron
**“And I will give her”** — Jerome: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” To it were given leaders from the same people: first Moses and Aaron, afterwards Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah and Ezra, at last the apostles.
**“and the valley of Achor”**
• where Achor was killed
• understand: I will give
• When the children of Israel had taken Jericho, Achor stole from the accursed thing; for which sin Israel could not stand before its enemies. But when Achor was killed in the valley that takes its name from him, the grief of the Israelites was turned into joy and their despair into hope. And as, when he was punished, the Israelites had hope of victory, so, when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed by the Romans and those who sinned against Christ were punished, the figures being as it were destroyed, the apostles now have joy and hope that they will subject the whole world to Christ. Achor means “trouble,” because he troubled Israel and was afterwards troubled himself.
• Achor: the valley of tumult, or of crowds, because Israel was in tumult, or troubled, there.
**“for an opening of hope: and she shall sing there according to the days of her youth, and according to the days of her coming up out of the land of Egypt”** — for Jerusalem is in the mountains, Egypt in a low place; of which it is said spiritually: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help.”
**“and she shall sing there”** — When she came out of Egypt, at which time that people was growing in the faith of God, turned from the idolatry of the Egyptians and going up to better things; as now the Church, freed from the devil by baptism, sings and rejoices and says: “Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified.”
2.16:
**“And it shall be in that day, saith the Lord”** — after she has truly believed in me
**“And it shall be in that day”** — In memory of Belus was consecrated the idol called Bel, and by this name the prophets often call the idol of Babylon. The Sidonians often call him Baal or Baalim. Baal means “having,” Baalim “having me.” Hence women too call their husbands Baalim, that is, my husband, namely the one who has me in marriage. But in the Hebrew tongue a husband is called is, and a wife issa. So it is said here that the believing people, wishing to show me to be her husband, will call me is, that is, husband, not Baalim, which likewise means my husband: for though by its etymology it could be said, yet out of hatred of idols it ought not to be said, lest in the worship of God we recall the name of idols, and lest, while she names her husband, she think of the idol, as could happen through the ambiguity of the word. From this we learn that heresy can be incurred by words alone, carelessly uttered.
**“she shall call me: My husband, and she shall call me no more Baali”** — though it could rightly be said, yet because of its likeness to the name of the idol it ought to be avoided
2.18:
**“And in that day I will make a covenant with them, with the beasts of the field”** — When I have taken away the names of the idols. Hence in Isaiah: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb.” Peter was told to kill and eat all the beasts.
**“with the beasts”** — By the name of beasts and birds the Gentiles are signified, who worshipped these as God. So, once cleansed, they are called not by these names but rational. In them God has now “broken the powers of bows, the shield, the sword, and the battle”; and these weapons broken, believers now sleep securely under one shepherd, Christ.
**“and with the fowls of the air, and with the creeping things of the earth: and I will destroy the bow, and the sword, and war”** — all the rebellion that was between Jews and Gentiles; for Christ, coming, “hath made both one,” joining the two walls in the hope of the resurrection to come
**“out of the land”** — out of the Church
**“and I will make them sleep secure”**
• Or: now the souls of the saints rest in the hope of the resurrection to come.
• to rest securely in my faith and peace
• this seventh age, of those who rest, Christ made when he came in the flesh
2.19:
**“And I will espouse thee to me for ever”** — the circumcision given to Abraham was an everlasting sign between God and his seed
**“and I will espouse thee to me in justice”** — that you may live justly
**“And I will espouse”** — He puts “I will espouse” three times. First he betrothed her to himself in Abraham, or when he brought her out of Egypt, to have her as wife for ever. Second, on Mount Sinai, giving them as betrothal gifts the justice and judgment of the law, and mercy joined to the law, so that if she sinned she would be taken captive, and if she repented she would be called back. Third, at the coming of the Son, which is in the faith of the Trinity: believing in this faith, they know at once that he is God whom before they denied. So this harlot, who had been joined to the embraces of strange men, because she worshipped idols in Egypt, is taken again through the law; and because she transgressed it, killing the prophets as if they were the bridegroom’s companions, the Son came third; and when he had been crucified and had risen from the dead, she is espoused no longer in the justice of the law, but in faith, in the grace of the Gospel, and in the knowledge of the truth.
*Jerome:* Note the mercy of the husband, God: the harlot, after long fornication, returns to her husband, and is said not to be reconciled to her husband but to be espoused. And see the difference between the marriages of God and of men: men make a virgin no virgin; God, joined to harlots, makes them virgins again.
**“and judgment”** — discernment between good and evil
2.21:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”**
• when I espouse you to me in faith
• The Jews assert that these things are to be fulfilled in the time of their Messiah: that, so that all things run in their order, the creature will serve its Creator.
**“And it shall be in that day”** — Jerome: According to the letter it can be understood that at the coming of Christ temporal goods are promised to believers, so that, for his sake who is the seed of God, all things run in their order, as they were made from the beginning, and serve the good of men; and yet the Jews, after so many good things, still look in a carnal way for Antichrist. Spiritually, the heavens, which “shew forth the glory of God,” are heard when they ask for the Canaanite woman and for Peter’s mother-in-law; and the heavens hear the earth, that is, the men who are in the Church; and the earth hears the wheat, that is, it so gives the spiritual understanding of the Old and New Testament as to gladden the hearts of the hearers, measuring its teaching to their capacity. And all these, that is, heaven and earth, namely the apostles and the universal Church, will hear Jezreel, that is, they will bring the seed of the word of God to the fruit of works, so that one seed bears fruit a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold.
**“I will hear, saith the Lord, I will hear the heavens”** — the apostles
**“and they shall hear the earth”** — that they may water it with heavenly rain
2.22:
**“And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil, and these shall hear Jezrahel”** — the earth of which it is said: “Truth is sprung out of the earth”; in which the householder sows good seed
**“and these shall hear”** — Jerome: Spiritually this belongs to the apostles, who, beginning from Jerusalem, by their preaching and miracles make the hearts of their hearers bear fruit everywhere. They are the seed while they hear from the Lord, and sowers when “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth.”
2.23:
**“And I will sow her unto me in the earth”**
• good earth
• as a son of the synagogue that believes, which was without mercy while she worshipped idols
**“And I will sow her”** — The harlot who had been joined to God and had borne three children, first Jezreel, second Without mercy, third Not my people, now sees their names changed because of the faith of God and the seed of God. All this can be referred spiritually to the ten tribes, which are called Israel, which under the name of the harlot bore three children; and in general to all the Israelites who believed.
**“and I will have mercy on her that was without mercy”** — I will change the names, some being taken up
**“And I will say to that which is not my people: Thou art my people”** — Of this people it is said: “You are they who have continued with me in my temptations: and I dispose to you, as my Father hath disposed to me, a kingdom.”
**“and they”** — converted to the faith
**“shall say: Thou art my God”** — “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God.”

3.1:
**“And the Lord said to me: Go yet again, and love a woman beloved of her friend, and an adulteress”** — According to the letter: you love her, an adulteress, but she does not love you; despising you, she loves another more than you. And what this concerns he adds: as the Lord loveth the children of Israel much, but they, despising him, worship strange gods.
**“yet again”** — As by the harlot the ten tribes, so by this adulteress, whom the prophet is commanded to join to himself, we understand Judea especially. Yet by both the one and the other the Israelite people as a whole can be designated.
**“as the Lord loveth the children of Israel, and they look to strange gods, and love the husks of the grapes”** — the grape-skins
**“the husks of the grapes”** — By the husks, the demons, who were created in the great richness of the Holy Spirit, but, dried up by pride, were cast down from heaven; and the Jews worship them. Or the husks are the traditions of the Jews, empty of all truth, for which the Jews forsake the traditions of God. For this adulteress signifies the present time of the Jews, whom God loves, who looks for the salvation of all and opens the door to the penitent; but they, forsaking God, follow useless things.
3.2:
**“And I bought her to me”**
• the Latin reads “I dug her”: as a vineyard
• The Septuagint: I hired her to me for a price, as a woman; so that, having received her wage, she might cease committing adultery and sleep with the prophet.
**“for fifteen pieces of silver, and for a core of barley”** — thirty measures
**“and for half a core of barley”**
• fifteen measures
• which is the food of beasts, for she was like “the mule, which hath no understanding”
• A CORE OF BARLEY, that is, thirty measures, and a half, that is, fifteen, which make forty-five measures: for this wage she is hired. On the fifteenth day of the month Nisan, which is March, the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck down, and Israel was brought out of Egypt and by this wage hired into the service of God; and for the firstborn of Israel, who did not feel the plague, fifteen shekels of silver are offered for the temple. On the forty-fifth day the people came to Mount Sinai, and at once, the next day, they are commanded to abstain from women, and, sanctified for three days, to prepare themselves to receive the law; and on the fiftieth day Moses received the ten commandments. Fittingly, then, they are said to be hired for forty-five measures of barley, who after the coming of Christ sit and wait for the coming of their husband, “until the fulness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved”; who meanwhile neither has God nor serves idols, nor uses the food of men but the barley of beasts, because it has nothing spiritual in the law but follows the letter.
• Nisan is the name of the month in which the Pasch falls, whether March or April.
3.3:
**“And I said to her: … many days”** — for this wage
**“Thou shalt wait”** — The Septuagint: thou shalt sit
**“for me: thou shalt not play the harlot”** — with idols
**“and thou shalt be no man’s, and I also will wait for thee”** — nor will you be lawfully joined to me, by whom you were hired
**“I also will wait”** — Lest you think I do you wrong, I pay like for like. I, your husband, sit in mind and wait for the adulteress’s repentance, so that at least at the end Israel may believe, and “there shall be one shepherd and one fold.”
3.4:
**“For … many days”** — until the day of judgment
**“shall sit”** — huddled
**“the children of Israel”** — fed on barley
**“without king”** — Christ, who is appointed king over Sion
**“and without prince”** — of Jacob; that is, without Christ himself, saviour and priest; for Christ will not come until the prince fails from Judah and Herod, a foreigner, reigns
**“and without sacrifice, and without altar”** — because, the temple overthrown and Jerusalem burnt, they can exercise neither sacrifice nor priesthood
**“and without ephod”**
• the shoulder-garment
• Jerome: Ephod is properly the shoulder-garment, but here it is taken for every priestly vestment; it can be put for linen vestments too, as Samuel is read to have been girded with a linen ephod. All this the Jews refer to the seventy years of captivity; but it is better understood either of the present time or of the last conversion of the Jews. For now the Jews sit without all these things, having lost their place; but we have Christ the priest, and his body and blood, and the garment of innocence, and theraphim, that is, the sign and memory of the Lord pressed into our hearts.
**“and without theraphim”**
• And without theraphim. Theraphim are figures and images, by which here we understand the cherubim and seraphim, or any other ornaments of the temple.
• Theraphim: figures or images.
3.5:
**“And after this the children of Israel shall return”** — when the time of the blindness that has happened in part in Israel is ended, they will return by faith through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch
**“and shall seek the Lord, their God”** — the Father
**“and David, their king”** — Christ, of the stock of David, who with a mighty hand frees those of his people bound in captivity
**“and they shall fear the Lord”**
• converted
• They shall fear: they will stand in awe before the Lord the Father, and before his good, the Son: the Father’s good, when they see him reigning in his own majesty and the Father’s; or before the good things of which it is said: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”; or before the good, that is, the Holy Spirit, who with the Father and the Son is one God.
**“and his goodness, in the last days”** — we are they “upon whom the ends of the world are come”

4.1:
**“Hear the word”** — From the beginning of the prophecy up to this place, under the description of the harlot and of the adulteress, who after heavy punishments and long abandonment are afterwards restored to their former or a better state, the sins of the ten tribes, or of the two tribes, and of all in common, are numbered. Now the discourse turns to the ten tribes, showing that God is not angry for nothing when he threatens and inflicts such heavy punishments; lest it seem to anyone that the sentence was brought unjustly on those who had not sinned, not from the truth of judgment but from the power of God. All this is referred most of all to those who would not receive Christ in the flesh, and to their descendants. With the inhabitants, that is, with the Jews who love earthly things, the Lord enters into judgment, condemning them, because he is not in them who says, “I am the truth.” And there is no mercy: they have mercy neither on the orphan nor on the widow, nor on Christ himself; and in their minds dwells no knowledge, that is, faith and the knowledge of God, or the very Wisdom of the Father. Cursing belongs to those who said, “Thou hast a devil”; lying, to those who said, “He is guilty of death”; killing, because they killed him and the prophets; theft, because they steal themselves and their children from God, saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children”; adultery is referred to uncleanness or idolatry. Blood touches blood when sin is added to sin; for by the name of blood sin is signified.
**“Hear the word of the Lord, ye children of Israel”** — Those called to judgment are called the inhabitants of the land, that is, not strangers and pilgrims but dwellers in the land. But he who passes through the world as a stranger and pilgrim follows truth and mercy, and so the knowledge of God, so that he is not swept away by the flood of cursing and the other sins.
**“for the Lord shall enter into judgment with the inhabitants of the land”** — for the Lord wishes to plead with his people and lay open the causes of his indignation: namely, that there is no truth
**“for there is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land”** — Truth without mercy cannot stand; mercy without truth makes men neglect justice; and he who lacks these has no knowledge of God either, but on the contrary, for truth, lying, and for mercy, cursing and killing.
4.2:
**“Cursing, and lying, and killing, and theft, and adultery, have overflowed”** — are done in abundance
**“and blood hath touched blood”** — sin to sin: they add new sins to old
4.3:
**“Therefore shall the land mourn”**
• in the captivity of the ten tribes
• the land seems to mourn when it is left untilled
• The land shall mourn, that is, the lovers of the land, when they lose the things in which they gloried: the carnal Jews, who were weakened, caught by enemies who were also beasts, that is, fierce, and birds, that is, lifting themselves up on their merits; and fishes, sunk in the depths of vices and not seeing the free air.
**“and every one that dwelleth in it shall languish with the beasts of the field”** — it is natural that, when the inhabitant is taken away, the beasts too and the birds and the fishes should fail, and that even the dumb animals, which the Creator fed for men’s use, should feel the wrath of God
**“and with the fowls of the air”** — understand: shall languish
**“yea, the fishes of the sea also shall be gathered together”** — understand: to death. Hence another translation: the fishes of the sea shall fail.
4.4:
**“But yet let not any man”** — a just man
**“But yet”** — Jerome: I called them, as it were, to judgment, that they might know that they were handed over to their enemies not by the power of God but because of their sins. But because, neglecting correction, they remain shamelessly in their crimes, they are unworthy to be rebuked.
**“judge”** — the unjust man
**“and let not … be rebuked”** — by the godly
**“a man”**
• the ungodly man
• for
**“for thy people”** — whom I was calling to judgment
**“are as they that contradict the priest”** — As the common people do not obey the priest, so your people do not obey my mouth
4.5:
**“And”** — therefore
**“thou shalt fall”** — Before, he spoke to the prophet about the ten tribes; now he speaks to them
**“today”**
• in the present
• Not by fraud or ambush but in open daylight, so that all may know you were taken captive for your sins.
**“and the prophet also shall fall with thee: in the night I have made thy mother to be silent”** — and this evil will be so heavy that in this night, that is, in the darkness and distress of captivity, no one will dare to tell his trouble before the enemies; but the people, caught, will waste away in silence, not daring to resist the enemies; and this because they did not have the knowledge of God’s law so as to fulfil it. And rightly the mouth that was shut to the praise of God is shut to the bewailing of its own troubles.
**“and … also shall fall”** — And the prophet: whether the false prophet, or all grace of prophesying. For before the captivity the ten tribes had prophets, Elijah and Elisha and others who prophesied in Samaria; but after the captivity no prophet is read to have been among the ten tribes. Hence Amos, who was of the tribe of Judah, is made to go back to his own country, so as not to prophesy in Samaria, as in a foreign kingdom.
**“in the night … to be silent”** — All that is said of the ten tribes can be referred to the heretics, who leave the kingdom of David and Jerusalem, that is, Christ and the Church; and so, covered by night, they are silent from the praise of God. And because they have no knowledge, that is, the true faith of Christ, they are often driven from the priesthood by an untimely death, lest, unworthy, they handle the body and blood of the Lord, and lest by living long they corrupt others by teaching or example; and those whom such men beget will be crushed with them in eternal damnation.
**“thy mother”** — Judea in general is the mother; individuals are the sons.
4.6:
**“My people have been silent, because they had no knowledge”** — of the Lord
**“because thou … knowledge”** — of the Lord
**“hast rejected”** — by adoring idols, one in Dan, the other in Bethel
**“I will reject thee, that thou shalt not do the office of priesthood to me”** — namely; or, in the shrines of idols
**“and”** — because
**“thou hast forgotten the law of thy God”**
• which forbids idols to be adored
• therefore
**“I also will forget thy children”** — handing them over to everlasting captivity; nor will I have mercy, as once in the desert. He who ignores him will be ignored.
4.7:
**“According to the multitude of them”**
• as if to say: as many men as it had, so many altars it built to demons
• Or: the priests, flattering men in their sins, take their sins upon themselves. Hence Isaiah: “O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee.”
• These priests were not of the tribe of Levi but of any tribe whatever: by giving gifts to the kings of the ten tribes they were made priests in the temples of idols.
**“According to the multitude”** — Allegorically: The more numerous the heretics are, the more they offend God; and according to their number they enlarge the doctrines of errors. Their glory, that is, the dignity of being Christians, is changed into shame when, for past sins, they slip into greater ones, and from there into punishment. They eat the sins of the people while they deceive hearts with sweet words and “devour the houses of widows,” saying: God seeks nothing but the truth of the faith; if you keep that, he does not care what you do. And so they lift up their souls in their sins, so that they do not repent but rejoice in their crimes. So the people who are taught and the priest who so teaches will perish alike.
**“so have they sinned against me”** — against me
**“their glory”** — the idol in which they gloried
**“I will change into shame”**
• when for this crime priests and people were taken captive
• for
4.8:
**“the sins of my people”** — that is, the offerings for the sins of the people
**“They shall eat”**
• the priests, whose part it is to eat the sacrifices
• Jerome: The heretics are not filled with their error, nor do they cease from the foulness of their fornication; and by not keeping the law they forsake God, rave and are drunk, and with ruined minds adore the idols they have feigned in their heart, and are possessed by the spirit of fornication.
**“and shall lift up their souls to their iniquity”**
• for they not only do not correct them but even praise them and promise them impunity; so they are lifted up to sin
• Pleasure is insatiable: once had, it breeds hunger, not fullness. Against this: “Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice: for they shall have their fill”; for justice is a substance that fills, but iniquity has no substance, and so leaves empty the bellies of those who devour it.
4.9:
**“And there shall be like people like priest”** — since they sin equally, they will be punished equally
**“and I will visit”** — I will punish
**“upon them”** — the priest, or the people
**“their ways”** — their evil deeds
**“and I will repay them their devices”** — they will be punished not only for their deeds but for their thoughts too
4.10:
**“And they shall eat and shall not be filled”** — that is, they will do evil deeds
**“they have committed fornication”**
• the strength of fornicators fails, but their desire burns
• that is, the ten tribes, with the idols of Jeroboam
**“and have not ceased”** — understand: to commit fornication
**“because they have forsaken the Lord”** — not being able to serve two masters
**“in not observing the law”**
• him who says: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore
• his commandments
4.11: **“and wine”** — As drunkenness with wine perverts the drinker’s mind, so fornication, bodily or spiritual, makes a rational man as it were a brute beast, so that men frequent brothels and adore wood and stones as God. So the prophet, as if wondering, adds: My people, which was once called by my name, in their stocks.
4.12:
**“have consulted their stocks”** — There was a kind of divination done with wood and a staff, by which omens of the future were sought. Hence in Ezekiel it is read that Nebuchadnezzar, marching against Ammon and Jerusalem, shuffled arrows among his other divinations, and the rod came out against Jerusalem. Perhaps these too asked in this way whether it were better to worship God or the idol; and so, by the just judgment of God, they were led astray by the devil through the staff’s answer. Hence there follows: For the spirit of fornication hath deceived them.
**“for the spirit of fornication hath deceived them”** — that is, the devil, who has himself adored in images. The beginning of fornication is the devising of idols.
**“and they have committed fornication against their God”** — they departed from him by idolatry
4.13:
**“upon the tops of the mountains”**
• in pleasant places
• The heretics promise themselves loftiness of doctrines, and sacrifice under the oak and the poplar and the terebinth, trees, that is, that bear no fruit; for they have not the fig and the vine, under which the saint is said to rest.
**“upon the tops”** — The law commands that he sacrifice to the Lord in the place the Lord shall choose, and that no grove or trees be planted beside the temple, lest pleasant places soften religion. Israel, on the contrary, leaving the most high God, loved to sacrifice in high places, and, having lost the truth, sought the shade. Hence it is read in the books of Kings: “But yet he took not away the high places: for the people still sacrificed in the high places.”
**“They offered sacrifice … and burnt incense upon the hills: under the oak, and the poplar, and the turpentine tree”** — understand: they offered sacrifice
**“because the shadow thereof was good”** — that is, it pleased them for following their pleasures
**“therefore”** — because you have committed fornication against God
**“therefore shall … commit fornication”** — The daughters and spouses of the heretics are the souls they have begotten in error and betrothed to their doctrines. Such are unworthy of God’s correction, since all their worship is fornication, and the foul mix with the foul. So they will be beaten, that at some time, through the blows, they may understand that they have forsaken God.
4.14:
**“I will not visit upon your daughters, when they shall commit fornication”**
• because you, my sons, have committed fornication; and what you have done to me, your father and husband, you will suffer in your wives and daughters
• They worshipped Beelphegor, whom we may call Priapus, because of the size of his obscene member. Hence it is said that “Asa did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and took away the effeminate, and removed his mother Maacha from being the princess in the sacrifices of Priapus.”

• The Hebrews dream of salvation for themselves after a cycle of a thousand years; but salvation is promised on the third day, on which Christ rose from the dead. They refer the second day to the coming of their Christ, and the third day to the judgment, in which they are to be saved. But let them answer what the first day is, that is, the Saviour’s first coming. And since they cannot answer, let us say that the first day is the Saviour’s lowly coming; the second, when he will be seen by all in glory; the third, when, the judgment done, he will show his elect the greater glory of his brightness. The Jews, who accept the second and third, confess that they have lost the first; for a second and a third cannot be so called except with respect to a first. Or the first day is the first age of the world; the second, at the coming of Christ, in which we are given life by faith, or already by hope sit together with Christ in the heavenly places; the third, the day of resurrection, in which, through Christ rising, we shall rise with him. Or for us the first day is when we are reborn by baptism; the second, in the rest of souls; the third, in the general resurrection.

**“Galaad is a city of workers of idols, supplanted with blood”**
• The Septuagint: There the city of Galaad despised me, working vain things and troubling the water; and thy strength is as of a man that is a pirate.
• this city was the beginning of idolatry for those beyond the Jordan
• Allegorically: Gilead means “the passing over of testimony.” These are the heretics, who despise God by perverting the testimonies of the Scriptures; whose works are vain; who trouble the waters of the Church and make filthy streams out of pure springs; whose strength is like a pirate’s, that is, the devil’s, in the sea of this world, through which the ships of the world pass.
**“Galaad”** — Gilead was a city of priests beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Gad, and a city of refuge. In it the idol was first consecrated; and the more famous it had been before, the more it became afterwards, through idolatry, the beginning of all evils; and so these were the first to be taken captive by the Assyrians. And it is supplanted, that is, humbled, with blood: the blood that Jehu shed, anointed in Ramoth-gilead, when at God’s command he destroyed all the house of Ahab. Or supplanted with blood, because vengeance came on it for the blood it shed. And like the jaws of robbers: the jaws of robbers are the caves in which, hidden, they rob and kill passers-by. So the priests of Gilead lay in wait for the simple people, robbed them of faith and killed them in mind; and those they could not deceive they stripped of their clothes and killed in body. Hence he adds: they conspire with the priests. For the way through Shechem was the road for those of Israel who wished to sacrifice in the temple at Jerusalem; on this road the priests of the idols laid ambushes, to draw passers-by to worship the idols in Dan or Bethel. With these priests the priests of Gilead had conspired, and in like manner they had killed those who wished to go up at the Pasch or Pentecost or Tabernacles to sacrifice in Jerusalem according to the commandment.
6.9:
**“And like the jaws of highway robbers”**
• of the priests
• All false priests hide the way and kill men by evil works, so that they do not reach Jerusalem.
**“they conspire with the priests”** — of the idolaters
**“who murder in the way those that pass out of Sichem”**
• to Jerusalem, where alone it is lawful to sacrifice
• SHECHEM means “shoulders,” by which work is understood. Hence: “Put thy heart to thy shoulder,” that is, do what you understand. But the heretics shut the way, so that we do not go from Shechem, that is, from good works, to Jerusalem. These are like the jaws of robbers, that is, of those who kill those who wish to go by the way of this world to the truth.
**“for they have wrought wickedness”** — so I liken Gilead to those priests, because they have wrought like wickedness, whether in killing men or in idolatry
6.10:
**“in the house of Israel”** — of the ten tribes
**“in the house”** — Jerome: In the house of the heretics a horrible thing is seen, when, the teachers committing fornication, the people they have led astray are defiled with them. Judah too, that is, the Church, is commanded to prepare a harvest of cutting, that is, of reaping according to sins on the day of judgment. This is said not as a wish but as a prophecy; for if they repented they would obtain pardon from the merciful judge, who rebukes them here so that they may not perish there. Hence he adds: When I would have healed.
**“I have seen a horrible thing”**
• the worship of idols
• Hence Jeremiah: “The heavens are astonished at this, and the earth hath trembled.”
• for
**“the fornications of Ephraim there: Israel is defiled”** — Jeroboam, under whose lead the people of Samaria was defiled; and so the discourse turns to Judah too
6.11:
**“And thou also, O Juda”** — Do not think yourself safe: set yourself a harvest, that is, beget sons to be cut down; for the time is near when you too will be led captive to Babylon by the Chaldeans, and the time of your harvest, that is, of your slaughter, will come.
**“And thou also, O Juda, set thee a harvest, when I shall bring back the captivity of my people”** — As if to say: The Chaldeans will reap you, but I will bring you back from there, which will be under Cyrus and Artaxerxes. And when I shall bring back: understand, you shall see it; for many who were led captive saw the return, and with those who had been born in Babylon went back to their own land. Of this return no promise is made to the ten tribes, which are held in perpetual captivity.

7.1:
**“When I would have healed Israel”** — to forgive the sins of idolatry it practised in Egypt or in the desert
**“When I would have healed”** — Allegorically: When the Saviour, after the shedding of his blood and the gathering of the Church from the Gentiles and the peoples, wished to heal the people’s sins by repentance, suddenly Ephraim, that is, the heretics, who promise the fruitfulness of false doctrines, and the people of Samaria, which says it keeps the commandments of God, made the idol of false doctrines; and through them the thief and the robber came in, that is, the devil, or the false teaching of the heretics itself, into the Church. The thief deceives secretly by ambush; the robber seizes boldly. So he puts it pointedly: the thief has come in secretly, the robber strips outside; for they can strip no one of the garment of Christ unless they have first drawn him outside the Church to their own doctrines.
**“the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria”** — idolatry was practised openly by Jeroboam and by the people of Samaria, which followed its king; this wickedness stood against God when he wished to pardon that people’s former sins
**“for they have committed”** — the king and the people
**“falsehood”** — the idol, or those lying words: These are thy gods, O Israel
**“and the thief is come in to steal, the robber is without”** — Jeroboam, who came in secretly to deceive the house of Israel, and, like a robber forcing the people of God into idolatry by violence, stripped it of God’s protection
7.2:
**“And lest they may say in their hearts”** — And when they are so punished, let them not think that I punish them for the old sins of their fathers; for now, that is, at present, for the wickedness they have devised, their sins have beset them about; and their evils cannot, as they think, be hidden from me, but rather their very devices are open before my face, which sees all things clearly
**“And lest they may say”** — Allegorically: The heretics cannot plead old sins against God, since they add new ungodliness to the old works and are bound by their own sins; and when they think they are hiding from God, they cannot escape his eye, for “the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things.”
**“that I remember all their wickedness: now have beset them about”** — their present sins
**“their own devices … they have been done before my face”** — they do not reverence my face
7.3:
**“They have made the king glad with their wickedness”** — He sets out what they did before the face of God, who, consenting to Jeroboam’s will, worshipped idols.
**“with their wickedness”** — Allegorically: He who does evil, or thinks ill of Christ, makes glad the king, that is, the devil, and, by the lies of wicked teaching, the princes of this world, whose wisdom God destroys; for the princes of darkness rejoice in our sins. Or the king is he who first invented the heresy; the princes, those who, set over the peoples of the heretics, claim a false priesthood for themselves.
**“and with their lies”** — when they said: These are thy gods, O Israel
**“the princes”** — who were over the people under Jeroboam
7.4:
**“They are all adulterers”** — because they made him glad, they are all adulterers, departing from God
**“like an oven heated by the baker”** — as an oven is heated to bake bread, so they were heated by Jeroboam with the fire of idolatry, to bake the bread of ungodliness
**“like an oven”** — Allegorically: The hearts of the heretics are heated by the devil’s fire, so that in them the bread of Antichrist may be baked. At first they speak secretly in the Church and promise to make peace in all things; and the leaven of their teaching, of which it is said, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” creeps on little by little like a cancer; and when it has swelled in the hearts of those deceived, then they break out into open madness. Of them it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”
**“rested”** — Jerome: When the idols had been made, Jeroboam did not at once force the people to worship them, lest, if some resisted, their worship should come to nothing. So the city rested a little, because the people were left to their own will, until the whole lie was leavened: so that first the princes, then the attendants, at last all the people, consenting to the king of their own will, were corrupted. For what is done by compulsion is soon undone; what is done by will endures.
7.5:
**“The day of our king, the princes began to be mad with wine”**
• to suffer the madness of luxury, or of idolatry
• Allegorically: The peoples, led astray by the king, the devil, and by his princes, or by the prince of a heresy and its leaders, leave the Church and keep other solemnities, and cry: This is the day of our king, Valentinus, Arius, Marcion. And those who hear that they are set over them are not made drunk with wine, lest the sin be thought light, but are mad with wine; of which Moses says: “Their wine is the gall of dragons, and the venom of asps, which is incurable.” So, when the peoples and their leaders have been deceived, the prince stretches out his hand with the scorners, whose hearts are heated. For all the day long the heretics will not see “the sun of justice,” because their understanding is weighed down; their hearts are heated with divers passions, such as anger and avarice; and they devour their judges, that is, those who have something of virtue and discernment by which to tell evil from good. Or the judges of the heretics are devoured by their own peoples, so that those whose houses they devour for the sake of filthy gain devour them in turn by agreeing with them.
**“The day of our king”** — When the mass of the people had been heated in the veneration of the idol, they began to say at Jeroboam’s doors: This is the day of our king, which our emperor has made a feast for us; on it we rejoice and play and adore the calves. And while the people cried out so, the princes, who had been set to govern the city and the people, losing with the people the understanding of the mind, began to forget God, to dash themselves against the wooden idols, and, like men possessed, not to know what they were doing.
**“he stretched out his hand with scorners”** — The king, seeing the people crying out and the princes raving, stretched out his hand, that is, gave his assent to those who flattered him with divers praises. These scorners, while their king was laying snares for them and leading them away from their God, gave him their heart like an oven, so that he might make them burn with the flames of idolatry. For he gave his assent to the people because he saw it turned to error with its whole mind.
7.6:
**“Because they have applied their heart like an oven, when he laid snares for them: he slept all the night baking them, in the morning he himself was heated as a flaming fire”**
• Busy in the darkness of sins, and having put fire into the oven, he was at ease, for he saw no one resist his will, but all baking the bread of ungodliness. But in the morning, heated with the flame of crime, he openly and shamelessly withdrew from the worship of God and came before all to sacrifice.
• what more?
• WHEN HE LAID SNARES: Jeroboam made the calves by guile, lest the people of Israel, going to the temple of God in Jerusalem, should take the occasion to be reconciled to the king of Judah. So he laid snares for them, that they might not go up to the temple of the Lord but might adore the calves he had made.
7.7:
**“They were all heated like an oven”** — for they now withdraw from the worship of God, no longer by snares but shamelessly
**“and have devoured their judges”**
• they killed those who would not consent
• or: they corrupt those who understand rightly by their wicked example
**“all their kings have fallen”** — In short, all the kings after Jeroboam withdrew from the religion of God and walked in the ways of Jeroboam, “who made Israel to sin.”
**“all their kings”** — All the princes of the heretics fall; for though they cry to God, they do not call on his name worthily; for “every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
**“there is none amongst them that calleth unto me”**
• so as to leave the idols and return
• There is none amongst them: as if to say: they have suffered all this so that they may seek God, whom they would not seek.
7.8:
**“Ephraim”** — the kingdom of the ten tribes
**“himself is mixed among the nations”** — of the nations, like them, withdrawing from the worship of God
**“Ephraim is become as bread baked under the ashes, that is not turned”** — bread that is not turned is full of dirt on every side; so Ephraim, by not doing penance, is covered round with the ashes of sins
**“Ephraim is become”** — Allegorically: The heretics differ in nothing from the error of the Gentiles; and he who was a prince in the Church has become bread baked under the ashes, covered on every side with unclean ashes and the heat of the fires, so that he does not return to God but remains in error. His strength the demons devour, who are strangers and enemies; but they do not notice that they are enemies.
7.9:
**“have devoured”** — by killing them and seizing their goods
**“Strangers”** — the Assyrians, the Chaldeans
**“his strength”** — the strong men of that people, or the treasures in which they trusted
**“and he knew it not”** — his God, or the cause why he was handed over
**“yea, grey hairs also are spread about upon him, and he is ignorant of it”**
• understand: that the end of the kingdom was at hand
• they do not know
• Grey hairs: they are spread upon the heretic when the folly of his heart persists in him to the end of his life. For as in the just man grey hairs are taken for wisdom, so in the ungodly for folly. And when the heretic is so brought low, he does not know the oldness of his wickedness, of which it is said that what grows old and decays is near its end; and he will not return to the Lord by repentance.
• Allegorically: The heretics who withdraw from the Church are compared to a dove without a heart, because, desiring earthly things, they are handed over to the Assyrians. And when they have gone out from the Church, God will spread over them a net, woven of the testimonies of the Scriptures and the skilful speech of wisdom, so as to drag down to lowly things those who lift themselves up against the Lord’s wisdom, threatening them with punishment, so that, corrected in this way, they may not perish for ever.
**“yea, grey hairs also”** — He was in this wickedness no short time, but remained in error up to old age and the final overthrow of the kingdom.
7.10:
**“And the pride of Israel shall be humbled before his face”** — he who lifted himself up, trusting not in God but in the multitude of his army, is humbled by him who “resisteth the proud”: the captains of the army in whom he gloried will be killed by the Assyrians, and that before his face, that is, in the present
**“and they have not returned”** — he explains what he had said obscurely: Ephraim is become as bread baked under the ashes
**“to the Lord their God”** — who would soon have returned to them, if they had returned. Hence Jeremiah: “Return to me, and I will return to you.”
**“nor have they sought him”** — so as to believe perfectly or to work well
**“in all these”** — adversities
7.11:
**“And Ephraim is become as a dove”** — As it is said in the Gospel: “Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and simple as doves”: simple, that we may harm no one; wise, that we may not be caught by the snares of others. Prudence without simplicity is cunning; simplicity without prudence is folly. So here the dove signifies the folly of the people, which calls not on God but on Egypt.
**“that is decoyed”** — by the devil
**“not having a heart”** — understanding: the dove, which cannot defend its young
**“they called upon Egypt, they went to the Assyrians”**
• for help, by worshipping their gods
• and therefore
• not willingly, but as captives
7.12:
**“And when they shall go”** — into captivity
**“I will spread … upon them”** — there they will not be able to hide from my power, but I will show it over them, so that they cannot return to their land until I will it
**“my net”** — by which they will be caught
**“I will bring them down as the fowl of the air”** — I will bring them down from the height of their pride
7.13:
**“Woe to them”**
• that is, eternal damnation after the present tribulation
• To the heretics belongs eternal woe: they withdraw from the Creator who redeemed them with his blood, and speak lies against God, false doctrines; and they howl in their gatherings, which are called beds, as if the dens of wild beasts, in which they give themselves to lust and debauchery; and whatever they say they think they say in praise of God. It is the howling of wolves and the noise of raving dogs. Rarely does a heretic love chastity; and he who pretends to love it, like the Cataphrygians, promises honey with a poisoned mouth; but it is shameful even to speak of what he does in secret.
