**“for they have departed from me”**
• by worshipping idols
• therefore
**“they shall be wasted”**
• by their enemies, and they will be wretched
• All together, from the king to the beggar, will be wasted, as by common counsel the idols were made. These words can be referred to the time of Christ’s passion: for as by common counsel they plotted his death, so together, at the feast of the Pasch, they were slain by their enemies.
**“because they have transgressed against me”** — by adoring the calves and transgressing my commandment, in which I said: Thou shalt not have strange gods
**“and”** — yet
**“I redeemed them”** — from the slavery of Egypt
**“and they have spoken lies against me”** — “These are thy gods, O Israel.”
7.14:
**“And they have not cried to me with their heart”** — though they did with the mouth
**“but they howled”** — he calls the song of idolatry howling, because, having lost the sense of reason, they were like wolves or dogs
**“in … beds”** — giving themselves to luxury
**“their: they have thought upon wheat and wine”**
• with false mysteries of the body and blood of Christ
• UPON, that is, upon the body and blood of Christ: he pretends to ruminate and meditate on the law of God, and withdraws from God, who taught him in the Church and gave him strength to resist his adversaries; and he imagines evil against God by setting up a heresy.
• They did not eat as men, but chewed the cud like beasts; that is, they called back again and again, as it were to the throat, for pleasure, the abundance of things they had, so as to feed on it more delightfully, seeking nothing but food and luxury.
• The heretics return to the rites of the Gentiles, so as to be without the yoke of Christ and the knowledge of God. They have become like a deceitful bow; a deceitful bow wounds the one who aims it: so the heretics, attacking the author of the Scriptures by the authority of the Scriptures, bring death upon themselves. So their princes, that is, the heresiarchs, will be struck by the sentence of God the judge for the madness of the tongue with which they blaspheme God; doing in a church falsely so called the same thing they did before in Egypt, that is, while they lived in the darkness of heathenism. For the heretics and the Gentiles have the same questions against the Church, because they follow not the authority of the Scriptures but human reason.
**“they are departed from me”** — by giving themselves to the idol
7.15:
**“And I have chastised them”** — through Moses and the other prophets
**“and strengthened their arms”** — I gave them strength to fight, as in the time of Joshua or of the Maccabees
**“and”** — yet
**“against me”** — who have done such things for them
**“they have imagined evil”** — since they could not harm me by thought alone, they transferred my power to idols
7.16:
**“They returned, that they might be without yoke”** — to what they were before I called them through Abraham and Moses: so as to fall headlong, without the yoke of the law and of the knowledge of God
**“they became like a deceitful bow”**
• God bends them against their adversaries; they are turned against God and shoot the arrows of blasphemy
• therefore
**“shall fall by the sword”** — the material sword or the spiritual
**“their princes”** — those who deceived others are the first to fall
**“for the rage of their tongue”** — who dared to call the calves gods
**“This is their derision in the land of Egypt”** — In the land of promise they make the mockery against God that they learned in Egypt, by worshipping Apis and the other monsters of the Egyptians.

8.1:
therefore
**“in thy throat”**
• in the mind, not only in the mouth
• So lift up your voice, that it may be like a trumpet, so that many may hear; because many have sinned, cry this: So will Nebuchadnezzar come against Jerusalem and the temple of God, with such swiftness and greed as the eagle hastens to its prey.
**“Let there be”** — O Hosea
**“a trumpet”** — the voice of God to the prophet
**“like an eagle”**
• open preaching
• By the eagle, the devil, who longs to set his nest above the stars of heaven. Hence: “Though thou be exalted as an eagle… thence will I bring thee down, saith the Lord.” Hence too the law commands us not to eat the eagle. This eagle comes upon the gatherings of the heretics, which were once the house of God; and this because they have transgressed the law, and say without cause: Thou art my God; and: We who are called Israel and are counted by the Christian name know thee. But the Lord says they say this in vain, since they have set up kings for themselves, and have as princes my adversaries, whom I have not known, because they do not deserve to be known by me; and their silver and their gold, whatever they had of speech or spiritual understanding, they turned by their nature into the idols they feigned in their heart; and so they perished.
**“upon the house of the Lord: because they have transgressed my covenant”** — to destroy Jerusalem; he will not come to another place, and I will command it for no other cause than this, that they have transgressed my covenant by making idols
**“and have violated my law”** — in which I said: “You shall not make gods of silver, nor … gods of gold.”
8.2:
**“They shall call upon me”**
• when tribulation is at hand
• O
• saying, pressed by distress:
**“O my God, we, Israel, know thee”** — We know: we who are called Israel, keeping the name of Jacob, who pleased thee, while the other nations did not know thee.
8.3:
**“Israel hath cast off the thing that is good”**
• God’s answer: How are you called Israel, you who have cast off the good, that is, God, from whom you were named Israel?
• therefore
**“the enemy”** — the Assyrian, or the devil
8.4:
**“They have reigned”**
• leaving me, their king, they asked for themselves King Saul, or Jeroboam
• Against my will they asked for themselves a king, such as the other nations have. To call them back from this folly Samuel set out to them the law of the kingdom, and foretold that their sons and daughters would serve the kings, so that they might return to God, their most merciful king.
• This can be understood of Jeroboam and the kings who succeeded him. For though God, angry with Solomon, willed his kingdom to be divided, Israel ought not therefore to have set up a king for itself, but according to the commandment of the law should have asked God what king he wished to be appointed. For what God wills to be done for good is sometimes fulfilled through men who do not know it and resist it, to their own damnation. Hence: “The Son of man must be delivered,” but “woe to that man by whom he shall be betrayed.”
**“but not by me”** — not by my will but by the people’s
**“they have been princes, and I knew not”** — because I did not choose them, I rejected them
**“of their silver and their gold they have made idols to themselves, that they might perish”** — Because of the abundance of riches I gave them for plenty and adornment, neglecting me, they made themselves idols, which are the cause of their ruin.
8.5:
**“Thy calf … is cast off”**
• as if to say: of gold and of silver they made the calf; and so he is angry
• Jerome: The calves were not set up in the city called Samaria, but in Dan and Bethel. So by Samaria all the cities of the ten tribes are designated; and the calf, put in the singular for the plural, is to be understood of the two calves. And he sets out their ruin: it is cast off, that is, by the Assyrians the temple of the idols was destroyed, and the calves themselves melted down and carried into captivity; for my wrath took vengeance on them, the calves or their worshippers.
• Allegorically: The heretics are calves, who, leaving heavenly things, are bent to the earth, and yet say they keep the precepts of the law. These calves God casts off, and is angry with them, and wonders that there is such perversity that they worship the idols they have made. These calves Israel did not receive from others, Israel which fancies itself apart from the other nations as seeing God; but out of the holy Scriptures it cast a perverse understanding, and is the maker of its own god, which will soon perish, like a spider’s web that is broken by a light breath.
• These things can be read in common, both of the heretics and of those who made the calves in Samaria.
**“O Samaria”** — because Samaria does not hear the voice of the Lord, he turns to others, as to a third person
**“my wrath is kindled against them. How long will they be incapable of being cleansed?”** — As if to say: What madness is this? I gave them room for repentance, and they would not be converted. And he sets out what the calf is, from whose filth they cannot be cleansed: they did not receive it from others, as Baal from the Sidonians, but Israel and the people of Jeroboam invented it.
8.6:
**“For itself also is the invention of Israel: a workman made it”** — the thing made is weak
**“and it is no god”** — which the hand of a workman shapes
**“for the calf of Samaria shall be turned to spiders’ webs”** — As a spider’s web is broken up by the wind, so that calf is brought to nothing, however fine it looks because it is golden.
8.7:
**“For they shall sow wind”** — that is, they do vain works; for “an idol is nothing”
**“For … wind”** — He sows wind who scatters seed spoiled by the wind and without kernel, from which no fruit springs up; so in them there is no hope of good work.
**“and”** — therefore
**“and reap a whirlwind”**
• the storm of captivity
• He is “carried about with every wind of doctrine,” and “of the flesh shall reap corruption.”
**“there is no standing stalk in it”** — there is neither stalk nor hope of fruit in them
**“standing stalk”** — Gregory: The stalk has no bud when life lacks merits. The stalk makes no meal when he who prospers in this present world understands nothing fine, and renders no fruit of good work; but if ever hypocrites show good works, the desires of the evil spirits are satisfied with them.
**“the bud shall yield no meal”** — into which the woman of the Gospel puts the leaven
**“shall yield no”** — The heretic makes no meal, that is, does not come to the fruit of good work. And if they sometimes do good works, strangers eat them; for, puffed up by the favour of men, they will lack reward, and are devoured by enemies, that is, by demons. For they are like pagans, so as to lose the name of Christians. They are vessels unto dishonour who ought to have been unto honour. For what is more unclean than the doctrines of the heretics?
**“and if it should yield”** — If ever they have done some good, the Assyrians or the demons will take it away; for the birds of the air will eat the seed that is sown.
8.8:
**“Israel is swallowed up”** — killed by enemies, or by the demons, who take away good things
**“now is he become among the nations like an unclean vessel”** — Israel has become like the Gentiles who worship idols; or, having lost the Christian name
**“like a … vessel”** — An unclean vessel is one we use for throwing out dung; to its uncleanness the heretic is compared; or because he is stained with the filth of those idols.
8.9:
**“For they are gone up to Assyria”** — not of their own accord, but by unwilling captivity
**“they are gone up”** — Assur means “great understanding.” To this the heretic goes up when he thinks he understands something great beyond the rest; so he seems to himself to be as it were solitary; he gives gifts to the devil; and as the Gentiles adore bodily images, so these adore the idols they have fashioned in their heart.
**“a wild ass alone by himself”**
• not the sheep of God’s pasture
• A WILD ASS: to the wild ass, which does not keep to the pastures of home but wanders of its own accord through divers pastures and loves a solitary dwelling, he compares those who withdraw from God and make divers idols; and so they are deserted by God.
**“Ephraim … gifts”** — for help
**“hath given … to his lovers”** — to the Assyrians, with whom they were once joined in friendship in the time of Menahem
8.10:
**“But even though they shall have hired the nations”** — for help; hence above: “Ephraim went to the Assyrian, and sent to the avenging king.”
**“now will I gather them together”**
• Together for battle, so that you may fight together and, conquered together, be taken captive.
• Now will I gather them together into the Church, namely those who had before been scattered; and they shall rest a while from the burden of the king (hence the Apostle: “You reign without us: and I would to God you did reign”) and of the princes they have, set up in the synagogues of the devil.
**“now will I gather”** — Jerome: Those who until now loved to give gifts to the adversaries they loved, I will now make to cease, so that they pay no tribute to their princes, until in captivity they offer, not tribute, but themselves to bear every insult.
**“and they shall rest a while from the burden of the king, and the princes”** — so that they give no gifts or tribute, until they come to the Assyrians, where they will give no gifts as free men, but will be weighed down by heavy slavery
8.11:
**“Because Ephraim hath made many altars to sin”**
• not only in Dan or Bethel did king and people worship idols, but on the mountains and in divers places, adding sin to sin
• therefore they will be led into captivity, so that they cease giving gifts to kings
**“Because … hath made many”** — Allegorically: Though there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism,” the heretics multiply altars, that is, divers doctrines, not to appease God but to multiply sin. So they do not deserve to receive the laws of God, since they despise them when received; and if they say anything from the Scriptures, it is to be compared not to the divine words but to the notions of the Gentiles. These, leaving the one victim, Christ, sacrifice many and eat them all; and so whatever sacrifices or virtues or alms they have done are not received by God.
**“altars are become to him unto sin”** — according to the measure of the altars, the measure of the sin
8.12:
**“I shall write to him my manifold laws”** — In those I have already given: that is, from those given before and neglected it is plain that they would neglect these too.
**“I shall write”** — I had given a law that there should be one altar, in Jerusalem; but since they made many altars and despised the law given through Moses, with what medicine shall I be able to correct them? It might seem that if I wrote other laws for them they would be corrected; but these too they would neglect out of their wickedness; so it seems they are not to be added.
**“which have been accounted as foreign”** — it might seem that the altars were multiplied for the worship of God; this he rules out
8.13:
**“They shall offer victims”** — they offer divers sacrifices, not to please God but to fill their belly; and so God does not receive them
**“they shall sacrifice flesh, and shall eat it, and the Lord will not receive them: now”**
• in the present
• and because they remain in their sins
**“will he remember”** — for vengeance
**“now will he remember”** — Allegorically: Iniquity is that before baptism, which is forgiven in baptism; sin, that after baptism. Hence it is said: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.” All these will be charged to the heretics, so that they are punished for the old and the new; for those who went out of Egypt by confessing Christ return to Egypt by unbelief, and, forgetting their God, make many shrines for themselves. And Judah, that is, the churchman, by evil works or by a perverse interpretation of the Scriptures has built himself fenced cities, not with God’s help but by artful falsehood; and these errors God will set on fire and destroy with the fire of the Holy Spirit.
**“their iniquity”** — before the law
**“and will visit”** — by the scourges of captivity
**“their sins”** — after the law
**“they shall return to Egypt”**
• by worshipping their gods or seeking help from them, distrusting God’s protection; or even in body, against God’s prohibition, they turned back and went away into Egypt
• and this because
8.14:
**“And Israel hath forgotten”** — the ten tribes
**“his Maker, and hath built temples”** — to idols on the high places
**“and Juda hath built many fenced cities: and I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the houses thereof”** — Though the two tribes had seen the ten punished for departing from God, they were not converted to God, but built cities by which to be protected from their enemies; but it did them no good, for in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah Sennacherib destroyed those fenced cities, burning, like fire, houses public and private alike.

9.1:
**“Rejoice not, O Israel”**
• one who does not know God is punished in one way, one who departs from God in another; for the servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it “shall be beaten with many stripes”
• Let the heretics not rejoice, nor think themselves like the other nations. For those never believed in God; these, which is graver, have apostatized from God. They multiply floors and winepresses, and eat the wheat from which the bread of mourning is made, and drink the wine of Sodom, which is trodden with the gall of asps. And because they prepare many floors and winepresses for themselves, they do not use the floor and the winepress that Christ trod; but whatever they think they have is corrupted by falsehood.
• As if to say: You thought the abundance of things, which is signified by the floors and the wine, was being paid you as the reward of fornication. But because you thought what I had given was paid you for worshipping the idol, I will send on you the want of famine, so that there is no wheat on the floor nor wine in the press. And this was done in the time of Elijah and Elisha, when mothers in Samaria, driven by famine, fed on the bodies of their sons.
**“Rejoice not”** — The Gentiles, not having the knowledge of God, rejoiced in the worship of their gods. So too Israel, departing from God, rejoiced in the worship of idols, thinking it would have peace by it. So he says: Rejoice not; for you will not have the peace you expect, but will be punished in captivity, because you have made yourself like those who do not know God.
**“rejoice not as the nations do”** — the nations that do not know God
**“for thou hast committed fornication against thy God”** — and therefore justly to be punished
9.2:
**“The floor and the winepress shall not feed them, and the wine”** — with which they drank themselves drunk
**“shall deceive them”**
• shall fail
• they will not only be worn down by famine in the land they received from God, but will also be taken captive from it, the land they have defiled by their crimes
9.3:
**“shall deceive them”** — for
**“They shall not dwell”** — Jerome: The heretics, who withdraw from the Church and eat the sacrifices of the Assyrians, that is, of the demons, do not dwell in the Church of the faithful, nor offer wine to the Lord, for they do not rejoice in him spiritually. So neither they nor what they offer will please him, but will be counted unclean; and their sacrifices will be like the bread of mourning; for whatever they have done to please their hearers, receiving temporal things from them, will be turned into mourning for them, and those who have received their teaching will be defiled. The gatherings of the heretics too are called not the house of God but a den of thieves.
**“is returned”** — in heart, or by worshipping their idols
**“Ephraim … to Egypt, and hath eaten unclean things among the Assyrians”** — For as they ate things offered to idols in their own land, so, taken captive by the Assyrians, they used their sacrifices, which are defiled by being offered to idols.
9.4:
**“They shall not offer wine to the Lord”** — but to demons
**“They shall not offer wine”** — Placed in Chaldea, they will be without the temple and the altar on which offering is wont to be made to God; and those who offer wine to strange gods will not please him.
**“their sacrifices”** — Among the Jews, when a sacrifice was offered for the dead, the offering was called the bread of mourners, because it was offered by mourners; and if anyone ate of it, he himself and the sacrifice were called unclean. Otherwise: the bodies of the dead were lamented for seven days, and within that time, if anyone ate anything of the dead man’s house, he became unclean. So both he who offers and he who eats, and the things offered to idols, are called unclean.
**“all that shall eat it shall be defiled: for … bread”** — for bread is taken for any food offered
**“their … is life for their soul”** — understand: is prepared; for they offer so as to satisfy their gluttony
**“it shall not enter”** — the defiled do not please God
**“into the house of the Lord”** — which was burnt with the fire of the Babylonians
9.5:
**“What will you do”** — When the day of captivity comes, which will be a solemn day to me, and as it were a pleasing victim; for on it I will take vengeance on my enemies, and put an end to their insults, and scourge my ungrateful sons.
**“What will you do in the solemn day, in the day of the feast of the Lord?”** — O heretics, what will you do when the day of judgment comes, when he will render life to his own and death to his enemies? For behold, you have been laid waste by the demons, who have stripped you of the virtues, and you have imitated the works of the unbelievers. For this, Memphis shall bury you; for you will be condemned according to the opinions and blasphemies of your mouth, and what you have spoken you will feel in torments. And whatever silver you had in the brightness of eloquence and false doctrine, the nettle shall possess, which will consume you with eternal burning; and in your tabernacles, that is, in your consciences, the bur, that is, the memory of your past evil life, will torment you.
9.6:
**“For behold they are gone”** — that is, they will go
**“they are gone”** — They will go: for, when the Chaldeans press on them, they will flee to Egypt so as to escape.
**“because of destruction”** — when they do not answer, he answers himself; or rather he sees with divine eyes what they will do, and foretells it: for behold, when the Chaldeans press on them they will flee into Egypt so as to escape
**“Memphis”** — Memphis was the chief city of the Egyptians before Alexandria was raised up. When Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had set over the land, had been killed by Ishmael, the remnant of the two tribes, fleeing the Chaldeans, went into Egypt with the prophet Jeremiah against the Lord’s command; and there afterwards, when the Chaldeans pursued them, they were either taken or buried in that city.
**“their beloved silver”** — By silver are signified all things that are bought with silver, such as estates. It signifies a long desolation: for where there were pleasant dwellings, burs and nettles will grow.
**“nettles shall inherit … the bur”** — The bur is so called because it has a huge stalk spread over the ground. The Greeks call this plant philanthropos, because it clings to men’s clothes by its roughness.
**“shall be in their tabernacles”** — of which above: What will you do?
9.7:
**“The days of visitation are come”** — of affliction
**“the days of repaying are come”** — that they may receive such things as they have done
**“are come”** — Jerome: The day of judgment will come upon the wicked, on which Israel will be afflicted: that is, he who boasts that he knows God and is not ruled by the Holy Spirit, but is carried about in divers directions by a demon, not knowing what he says: calling the Son of God a creature, denying the Holy Spirit to be God, and saying that the good God is one and the creator of the world another. Their madness is manifold, because their iniquities are many. And once for all it must be known that whatever is said in this prophet of Israel and Ephraim is referred to the heretics, who, truly mad, speak lies against God.
**“know ye”** — Now recognize your own words, which you used to say of my prophets
**“O Israel”**
• that … was
• O
**“know ye, O Israel”** — Or: O Israel, who promised yourself peace, know that in this you were a foolish and mad prophet, who thought yourself spiritual; but peace did not come as you expected.
**“was foolish”**
• without understanding
• towards me
**“that the prophet”** — Know also that the prophet whom I sent you to announce the truth, whom you called mad, was a man full of the Holy Spirit and prophesying true things.
**“the spiritual man was mad, for the multitude of thy iniquity, and”** — is
**“the multitude of thy madness”** — So, because of your countless sins, you have fallen into great madness, so that you did not know of yourself what you were doing, and would not hear those who prophesied true things to you by the Holy Spirit, but called them mad.
9.8:
**“The watchman”**
• is
• God set up kings and priests and prophets to provide for the people. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel.” So the prophet says: Ephraim, that is, Jeroboam, was set up with my God, that is, according to my God’s will, as watchman, so that he and the kings who followed him might provide what was good for the people of God, and, like the prophets, raise them up to good things. But in all his ways, that is, his actions, he became a snare, for by persuading and by forcing them with his power he led them into idolatry. Hence it is said: Madness is in the house of his God.
**“of Ephraim was with my God”** — and he is
**“the prophet is become a snare of ruin”** — but he himself is the snare in which the people is caught
**“upon all his ways, madness”** — the golden calf
**“madness”** — The prelates of the Churches sometimes devise madness in the Church of God, either by interpreting the Scriptures wrongly, or by begetting error in each of the believers, who is rightly called the house of God; so that whoever follows them is snared to his fall.
**“is in the house of his God”** — in Bethel, where the house of God was before
9.9:
**“They have sinned deeply”** — down to the abyss of ungodliness
**“as in the days of Gabaa”**
• therefore
• AS IN THE DAYS OF GABAA: he recalls the crime of the children of Israel when the wife of the Levite returning from Bethlehem was killed by an abominable outrage; or when, forsaking God, they made themselves a king from the city of Gabaa, that is, Saul. And now they sinned much worse by choosing Jeroboam and adoring idols: for then the people remained in the worship of God, but now, after the schism, idolatry followed. This can also be referred to the prelates of the Church, who by wicked teaching harm those whom they ought to profit.
**“he will remember”**
• God, who, because he bears with them, is thought to have forgotten
• first, by separating them from the Church
**“their iniquity”** — he will kill them in captivity
**“and will visit”** — at last, by condemning them
**“their sin”** — which are in them
9.10:
**“I found Israel like grapes in the desert”** — in Abraham
**“like the firstfruits of the fig tree”** — which are delightful and gathered with love because they ripen so early
**“in the top”** — at the beginning of that people I chose by grace Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who clung to me
**“his”** — of the fig tree
**“I saw their fathers”** — but, though born of good men and brought out of Egypt, they served lust
**“but they went in to Beelphegor”** — the idol of the Moabites, and the god of lewdness
**“and alienated themselves”** — from God
**“to that confusion”** — they withdrew to their own confusion, deserving the reproach of all
**“and became abominable, as those things were, which they loved”**
• hence: “Let them that make them become like unto them”; so that they are called, not idolaters, but idols themselves
• and therefore
9.11:
**“Ephraim”** — the ten tribes
**“As for Ephraim”** — The ten tribes gloried, and set themselves above their brother Judah, because they had many sons and armies; but all these were either taken captive or killed. So their glorying quickly left them. Or their glory, that is, the help of God, quickly left them and flew away, even from the birth and from the womb and from the conception; for God’s help forsook even their sons and descendants. Hence it is added: And though they should.
*Jerome:* The heretics, unstable and wanton, withdraw from the Church and glory if they beget many by their wicked doctrine; and even if these are brought up, the Lord threatens that they are to be punished in their fornication with their teachers, and there will be everlasting woe to them. He repeats too what Ephraim was like: When, he says, he was in the Church amid the waves of this world, he stood firm, founded on Christ; but now he leads his sons out of the Church to the devil, to death. In the moral sense, by the sons are understood evil thoughts or wicked doctrines; all of which “the Lord shall kill with the spirit of his mouth,” and “in that day all their thoughts” and doctrines “shall perish.”
**“hath flown away like bird”** — he went swiftly from his place into captivity
**“their glory”**
• because they gave birth easily
• which was
**“from the birth, and from the womb”** — because they easily carried in the womb
**“and from the conception”**
• because they easily conceived
• understand: hath flown away
9.12:
**“And though they should bring up their children”** — If they have leave to bring up many sons, it will not profit them, for they are to be handed over to death or captivity
**“I will make them without children among men: yea, and woe to them, when I shall depart from them”** — and not only this temporal punishment, but there will be everlasting woe to them, deprived of my help
9.13:
**“Ephraim, as I saw”**
• he sets out what Ephraim was before, so that his downfall may be the plainer
• who is now deserted, was once
**“was a Tyre, founded in beauty”**
• Tyre, in the midst of the sea, abounding in all riches: to this Tyre the ten tribes thought themselves like in the multitude of their riches; and as Tyre does not fear the waves that beat round it, so that people, girt about with God’s help, made nothing of the anger of the hostile peoples.
• So fair and strong, walled about by God’s help as Tyre by the sea; or, according to the Septuagint: like a very hard rock, which despises all the storms that beat round it.
**“Ephraim shall bring out”** — This murderer is understood as Hazael king of Syria, who so afflicted Samaria with famine in a long siege that its inhabitants understood it was better to go out to him and perish quickly by the sword than by long starvation. And because the prophet sees that they had grown proud in the abundance of God’s gifts, he prays that the cause of pride be taken away, calling on God to take it away: Give them, O Lord; and at once he answers himself: Give them a womb without children, that they may not glory in the multitude of their sons.
**“and Ephraim shall bring out his children to the murderer”** — If we use what God gives as a blessing for the contrary, it is sometimes justly taken away; according to that saying: “Let deceitful lips be made dumb”; and elsewhere: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.”
9.14:
**“Give them, O Lord. What wilt thou give them? Give them a womb”** — the voice of the prophet
**“without children, and dry breasts”** — so that, even if they bear children, they have nothing to suckle them with
9.15:
**“All their wickedness is in Galgal”**
• where Saul was anointed king; there Samuel announced the wrath of God to the people
• God hates them there because, choosing a man as king, they withdrew from the rule of God. Or in Galgal, where the people had been circumcised the second time, they afterwards worshipped idols on the pretext of religion, and in their worship they committed every crime.
**“in Galgal”** — Galgal means “revelation” or “wallowing-place.” So he says that all the wickedness of the heretics is to be revealed when their womb is made barren; for they will see their shame, and those who boasted that they climbed to high things will be thrust down into hell. God hates them for this reason, that they speak lies against him. Hence there follows: For the wickedness of their devices I will cast them forth out of my house; so the heretics are cast out of the house of God.
**“for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their devices”** — the worship of idols that they devised
**“I will cast them forth out of my house”** — Since the ten tribes had withdrawn from the house of God, how are they said to be cast out of it? But the house of God can be called the land of promise, or Bethel, or Jerusalem, from which they were led captive; or surely the house of God is heaven, from which, when they die in the body, they are to be driven back.
**“I will love them no more”** — while they remain in error
**“I will … no more”** — That he does not love them is plain, and that all the kings of Israel were departing from God; for to this day they remain in captivity.
**“all their princes”**
• the heresiarchs, or the demons
• The kings of the ten tribes all withdrew from God through idolatry. It can be said of the coming of Christ, at which both Judah and Israel were cast out of the house of God, so as not to be saved with those who believe.
**“are revolters”** — like Arius and the others
9.16:
**“Ephraim is struck”** — by God, who handed them over to their enemies
**“their root is dried up”** — God, in whom he was founded; or the good fathers, who will not be able to help those who go astray; nor will God protect them; so they will bear no fruit, for they will neither beget sons nor have good works
**“they shall yield no fruit”**
• A metaphor from a tree: if its root dries up, it bears no fruit; and if it bears a little, it at once dries up in the very flower.
• This can be said of all the Jews who cried out for his death; so God rejected them and dried them up, so that they cannot bear fruit. And though they should bring forth, and should appear to meditate on the law of God, and bring forth from their heart, like their best-loved sons, something of knowledge and teaching, they will be cut down by God and will be wanderers among the nations, having neither temple nor altar nor city.
• The heretics cannot bear the fruit of virtues, for they have lost God, in whom they ought to have been rooted; and if they beget any, they will die, God being against them. Or their fruit is all that they feign and beget from their heart, which will dry up and perish. They are cast off by God, and so are wanderers among the nations, passing now to these opinions, now to those, and imitating the errors of the Gentiles.
**“And if they should have issue”** — as above: and though they should bring up their children, I will make them without children
9.17:
**“will cast them away”** — he will make them go as captives
**“My God … because they hearkened not to him”**
• the Lord of the prophets
• so as to worship him alone
**“and they shall be wanderers among the nations”** — Following divers worships in divers places.

10.1:
**“Israel a vine full of branches”**
• understand: once it was so in the fathers, having good shoots, who did good works
• The heretics, while they are in the house of God, are called the Lord’s vineyard and bring forth rich fruit; but withdrawing from the one altar, that is, the unity of the faith, they build many altars of error, and according to the plenty of their land, that is, according to the sharpness of the mind God gave them, they abound with idols: for the sharper they are by nature, the deeper and more unheard-of the doctrines they bring forth.
**“a vine full of branches”** — Another translation: Israel is a watery vine, which is taken in a bad sense; for as a watery vine runs riot more in putting out leaves than fruit, so Israel grew in the multitude of its peoples; but when its husbandmen should have brought forth grapes, it brought forth wild grapes.
**“the fruit is agreeable to it”**
• for among the patriarchs there was none who did not bear the fruit of good works
• but
**“according to the multitude of his fruit, he hath multiplied altars, according to the plenty of his land he hath abounded with idols”** — he turned the multitude or abundance of his fruits into a multitude of idolatry, so that the more peoples he had, the more altars he built, and outdid the abundance of the land with the number of his idols
10.2:
**“Their heart is divided: now they shall perish”** — the hearts of the heretics are sometimes divided, and fight among themselves with contrary opinions; hence they shall perish, and the Lord shall break the idols they have fashioned
**“is divided”** — The Hebrews hand down that as long as kings and people worshipped the calves with one consent, the captivity did not come, because the people could in some way be excused, as being drawn into idolatry by the violence of the kings. But after Hoshea, who was the last king of the ten tribes, allowed the people to go, if they wished, to the temple of God at Jerusalem and sacrifice there, their heart was divided: for the people did not agree with the king in this, that they should be called back from idolatry. And so, left without any excuse, in the ninth year of this Hoshea they were taken captive by Sennacherib and carried away to the Assyrians, dwelling in the cities of the Medes by the river Gozan. Hence he says: now they shall perish; now that every pretext is taken away, they shall at once perish in an everlasting captivity. Shalmaneser is the same as Sennacherib.
**“he”** — almighty God
**“shall break down”** — by the Assyrians, as by his servants
**“their idols, he shall destroy their altars”** — he will destroy the opinions of the heretics, divided among themselves, and condemn them for ever
10.3:
**“For now”** — Allegorically: When their lies have been crushed, the disciples of contrary doctrines will say too late: We have no king, that is, no masters, who once commanded us, and deceived by whom we did not fear God. And what shall a king do? As if to say: What good was it to us to follow those whose help we do not feel in our need? They say this seeking some pretext, so that they may seem to have erred not of themselves but through their teachers. Hence both the words and the visions of the heretics will be unprofitable, and they will make a covenant not with God but with bitterness, so that in the day of judgment it may spring up on the furrows of the field, that is, of their heart; so that what they sowed in joy they may reap in tears.
**“For now they shall say: We have no king: because we fear not the Lord: and what shall a king do to us?”** — When in the ninth year Hoshea is taken by Sennacherib, and when the Lord has broken the idols, they will say: We have no king to defend us, for all our princes are taken and slain. And why this is so, he adds the cause: we are without a man to rule us because we did not fear the true king, God, without whose help what is a man king worth?
10.4:
**“You speak”**
• The voice of the prophet, speaking for God, who mocks those who promised themselves peace and prosperity.
• You speak: we read in the book of Kings that Menahem king of Israel sent Phul king of the Assyrians a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him; among which gifts the golden calves are believed to have been sent.
**“words of an unprofitable vision, and you shall make a covenant: and judgment shall spring up as bitterness in the furrows of the field”** — You promise yourselves prosperity, as you have done till now, but everything will turn out the contrary for you. Hence he adds: and you shall make a covenant, not with God but with a lie, saying: We shall have peace. And so this covenant of lying will not spring up in good fruits to fill you, but in the judgment of bitterness, that is, of captivity and slaughter; and this on the furrows of the field, that is, on earthly hearts, from which the evil seed came forth.
10.5:
**“The inhabitants of Samaria have worshipped the kine of Bethaven”** — The ten tribes were so overthrown, away from God, that they worshipped not only calves as gods but even kine in Bethel.
**“the kine”** — Jerome: The heretics, who say they dwell in Samaria, that is, in the keeping of God’s commandments, worship kine, that is, wanton sects. But in the day of judgment, when they are bitterly punished, the peoples will mourn over the calf, that is, over the perverse doctrine that they held as a god. But of the wardens he did not say they shall rejoice, but they rejoiced over its glory, because they once fashioned glorious things, since the people had gone over away from God, or the glory of God had gone from the people by whom it had been forsaken. And whatever the heretics speak in fair words, they send as presents to their king, that is, the devil, to whom all things are referred; hence they will be confounded for ever.
**“for … have mourned over it”**
• note that by the kine is signified the one calf that was in Bethel; hence he puts it in the singular: over it
• When the fraud was found out, that the calves were of brass, the king of the Assyrians thought the king of Israel had wished to mock him; and the gifts that had been given to appease him made him the angrier. Hence afterwards he made war on them and conquered them. So he says: shame, that is, ruin, shall fall upon Ephraim, and Israel shall be confounded in his own will, that is, in the counsel by which he had sought help from a foreigner.
**“for … have mourned”** — Jerome: It is strange that the priests rejoice while the people mourn. But the Hebrews hand down that the golden calves were stolen away by the priests, and in the same place were put others of brass, gilded. So while the people mourned because the king of Israel had sent the golden calves, among other gifts, to Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, the wardens rejoiced, because their fraud could not be found out.
**“the people”** — who worshipped it
**“his”** — of the calf
**“and the wardens of its temple”** — the priests
**“that rejoiced over it in its glory”** — that is, in the calf, which was the glory of its people, because they had golden gods
**“because it is departed from it”**
• it was carried over to the Assyrians
• so the people mourn and the priests rejoice
10.6:
**“For itself also is carried into Assyria”** — which was dearer to the people
**“a present to the avenging king”** — Sennacherib, because he avenged the wrong done to God on the idolaters
**“shame … upon Ephraim”** — accusative
10.7:
**“Samaria hath made her king to pass as froth upon the face of the water”** — As froth and a bubble of water is quickly dissolved, so the kingdom of the ten tribes will quickly be ended; for they would not hear King Hoshea, so as to return to Jerusalem, but made him perish with them.
**“to pass”** — Allegorically: Samaria, that is, the spiritual wickedness that had divided itself from the people of God, makes its king, that is, the teaching of the heretics, pass quickly, like froth, which is dissolved while it is still being seen. For the heretics swell with foaming words, but they will quickly be destroyed, the things in which Israel sinned; and so great will be the desolation of the wicked teaching that the thorns and thistles which grow in untilled places will grow up over their altars; and, all being overthrown in the day of judgment, they will say to the mountains, that is, to the masters whom they thought high: Cover us.
10.8:
**“And the high places of the idol … shall be destroyed”** — on which they sacrificed to idols
**“the sin of Israel”** — which high places were the sin of Israel
**“the bur”** — a sign of utter desolation
**“and the thistle shall grow up over their altars”** — so that not even a trace remains
**“and they shall say”**
• wishing rather to die than to see what brings death
• These things can be referred not only to the captivity of the ten tribes, but also generally to all the Jews in the time of the Romans. Hence the Lord in the Gospel: “Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me, but weep for yourselves.” Or in the day of judgment they will say to the saints, who are mountains by the height of their virtues: Cover our sins with your prayers; and to the hills, which have no height of their own nature but were thought to have some loftiness. The mountains will cover, the hills will fall. Or, according to the letter, as judgment draws near they will be shaken with such fear that, if it could be done, they would wish to escape the presence of the judge, and to be punished for a time rather than for ever.
**“to the mountains”** — to the saints, who are truly high
**“Cover us”** — “Blessed are they … whose sins are covered.”
**“and”** — they shall say
10.9:
**“From the days of Gabaa, Israel hath sinned”** — when by unlawful intercourse they cruelly killed the Levite’s wife, or when, forsaking God, they chose Saul as king
**“From the days”** — From the time when Benjamin shamefully killed the Levite’s wife, Israel sinned, who rose up against the children of iniquity more from a kind of natural impulse than to please God; and, taking vengeance for a man, it did not avenge the wrong done to God, nor overthrow the idol in Micah’s house. For it ought first to have avenged the wrong done to God, and afterwards that done to man. But because it disdained to avenge the sacrilege against God, the battle in Gabaa overtook them; that is, they were justly taken captive for this, and not, as they themselves think, because they took vengeance on the sons of Benjamin in the battle of Gabaa. For there they did well, since they avenged the crime with blood, though they did more from natural grief than from love of justice.
**“From the days of Gabaa”** — Gabaa means “hill.” The heretic thinks himself more learned than the Church, and to have found something loftier. So Israel sins from the days of the hills, that is, from the time when, forsaking the mountains of the Church, it went down to these hills; and in these hills the battle will not overtake them. As if to say: having left the mountains of the Church, they beget children of iniquity on these hills; when persecution comes, the devil spares his own. Otherwise it is read as a question: Israel hath sinned from the days of the hills, and there they stood. But ought not a battle to be fought against them by churchmen, and their error destroyed, upon the children of iniquity? And if they are overcome, God promises that he will chastise and teach them, and the disciples who were deceived before will be gathered against their masters, and they will see their correction for their two iniquities: because they both forsook the Church and invented false teachings.
**“there they stood”**
• they persevered in those very sins
• because the idol was not overthrown in Micah’s house, the people persevered in idolatry, so as not to return to the Lord
10.10:
**“According to my desire”** — will
**“I will chastise them”**
• I will hand them over to their enemies
• and
**“the nations shall be gathered together against them, when they shall be chastised for their two iniquities”** — The multitude of the Assyrians, by whom he will be chastised and corrected for his two iniquities: namely, that he avenged the wrong done to man and not to God. Or that he sinned first in Micah’s idols, secondly in the calves. Or that he sinned in the two calves in Dan and in Bethel. Or also that he forsook God and worshipped idols.
10.11:
**“Ephraim is a heifer taught to love to tread out corn”** — Septuagint: strife.
**“Ephraim is a heifer”** — Allegorically: Ephraim, that is, someone learned in the law of God, so that he might tread the floor of the Scriptures and meditate on it day and night, began to cast off the yoke of the law, and to strive against churchmen to the overthrow of those who hear him. So the Lord will press down with the yoke the neck that is raised up and promises itself high things, and he himself, passing over, will tread on it with his feet and climb upon it, so that it may know it has a Lord. But Judah, that is, the churchman, will plough the ground of his heart, going forward in good; and Jacob, that is, the supplanter of vices, will break the clods, that is, the hardness of the history, and divide it spiritually into parts, so that they may yield spiritual fruits. The divine word has this custom: to express the truth of the history by the moral sense and by metaphor. So Ephraim is like a heifer that from her youth has learned on the threshing floor to separate the grain from the chaff, and that sometimes, worn out with work, leaps off the floor, but soon, from love of her accustomed work and food, comes back to the floor. So Israel, often afflicted for idolatry, yet by its own will and the greed of its belly returns to idolatry.
**“and”** — therefore
**“I passed over”** — I tamed her
**“upon the beauty of her neck: I will ride upon Ephraim”** — because Ephraim will not receive the law, I passed over upon her beauty, the swelling bulls, and tamed her by putting a yoke on her neck; and I will ride upon Ephraim, I will crush her with a heavy yoke laid on her, so that the wanton heifer may learn to labour, which she will not. Or by the yoke is meant the rule of the Gentiles, which he promises to remove from her neck, so that so at least she may return to him.
**“Juda shall plough”** — When the ten tribes had been taken captive for idolatry, the two tribes and Jacob, that is, those who were left of the other tribes, began to plough their hearts and break their hardness, so that they might yield good fruit in the worship of God.
10.12:
**“Sow for yourselves in justice, and reap in the mouth of mercy, break up”**
• make yourselves a new heart
• Those who are separated from the Church and are called false Christians are commanded to do penance, and to sow the justice of the Old Testament so as to reap mercy in the New, and to break up the fallow ground of good works, and to seek God, who may teach them the way of justice.
**“Sow for yourselves”** — He still keeps to the words of the metaphor, and bids them sow in justice, that is, in the keeping of the law, and reap in the grace of the Gospel; hence it is said: “Do penance,” and: “Do good to them that hate you.”
**“your fallow ground”**
• fallow ground is a field then first broken
• Fallow ground: land newly tilled.
**“the time”** — the reason for all these things
**“but … to seek”** — understand: will be then
**“the Lord is, when he shall come that shall teach you justice”** — Through the Incarnation, when all the things that were hoped for in the law will be made plain; “for the end of the law is Christ.”
10.13:
**“You have ploughed wickedness, you have reaped iniquity, you have eaten the fruit of lying”**
• You have received your recompense: you dreamed of good things for yourselves, and adversity came.
• The heretics plough wickedness by teaching evil, and will be condemned for the desert of their iniquity and lying. “For what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap.”
**“You have ploughed wickedness”** — When I urged you to good, you on the contrary thought to withdraw from me and worship idols. Hence you reaped death, and brought captivity upon yourselves.
**“because thou hast trusted”**
• O Ephraim
• The heretic trusts in his false opinions and in those whom false knowledge has made strong. And so a tumult will arise among the people, for whatever he speaks is not reason but clamour and tumult. And all thy fortresses shall be destroyed: for he trusts not in the testimonies of the Scriptures but in the craft of the devil and the arguments of the philosophers.
**“in thy ways”** — of idolatry
**“in the multitude of thy strong ones”**
• in the strength of the army, and not in God
• In this are marked the leaders of the heretics, who have tried to claim the altar of God for themselves. Hence those who said: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God for an inheritance,” preaching false things to the deceived peoples, so that they do not seek the true bread “which came down from heaven.” So hath Bethel done to you because of the evil of your iniquities: this fits the heretics properly. So will your church do to you, which you call the house of God. But since it is held by you, it is to be called not the house of God but Bethaven, that is, the house of an idol, because of your wickedness.
10.14:
**“shall arise”** — therefore
**“A tumult”** — that is, the sound of the howling Assyrians will come
**“among thy people: and all thy fortresses shall be destroyed”** — In Isaiah it is written that “Sennacherib … came up against all the fenced cities of Juda, and took them.”
**“as Salmana was destroyed”** — a prince of the Midianites
**“by the house of him”** — by Gideon’s household
**“that judged Baal”** — that is, he condemned his altar by destroying it and cutting down the grove
**“in the day of battle, the mother being dashed in pieces upon her children”** — the mother is dashed upon her sons, that is, she is wrung with excessive grief at her sons’ death
**“the mother … upon her children”** — That as Zalmunna killed sons before their mothers, and the mothers too were killed upon their sons, so your sons too, O Ephraim, will be killed with you. Hence Gideon too said to the prince of Midian: “As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.”
10.15:
**“So hath … done to you”** — O Israel
**“Bethel”** — in which you worshipped the calf and venerated the gods of Egypt
**“As the morning”**
• the rising of the dawn
• He had said above: “Samaria hath made her king to pass … upon the face of the water”; he sets out the same thing under another likeness. For the morning is the rising of the dawn and the beginning of the day, from the end of the night to the rising of the sun.
• The heretics will pass away like the dawn, and their king too, that is, the devil or the heresiarch. God loved them in their infancy, when they believed and were little ones and were called Christians, and through the teachers of the Church he called them out of the darkness of Egypt; but when they were called they went away from before their face, and worshipped Beelphegor, that is, they served their vices and lust, and afterwards sacrificed to the idols they had fashioned for themselves. For the heretics have each their own gods, and whatever they fashion they worship as a graven and molten thing.
**“passeth”** — so swiftly
**“so hath the king of Israel passed away”**
• Hoshea, taken by the enemy
• of the ten tribes

11.1:
**“Because Israel was a child”**
• he sets out the benefits God conferred on them in the patriarchs
• was in Egypt, worshipping idols
**“and I loved him: and I called … out of Egypt”**
• through Moses
• Matthew uses this testimony when, at the angel’s command, Jesus returns with his mother from Egypt to the land of Israel; for these things are referred figuratively to Christ, yet those who bore the figure of the Saviour did not signify him in all their works. For a figure points to a part; if the whole goes before in the figure, it is no longer a figure, but must be called the truth of history. Spiritually, God called his Son out of Egypt when at the Ascension he set him at his right hand.
**“my son”** — “Israel is my son, my first-born.”
11.2:
**“As they called them”** — Moses and Aaron, that they should go out of Egypt
**“they went away from before their face”** — but, when they were called, they turned their backs in the desert, worshipping idols
**“they offered victims to Baalim”** — Moreover, in the time of Ahab, in the land of promise, they sacrificed to divers idols.
11.3:
**“And I was like a foster father to Ephraim”** — because I was their father, by day I hid them with a cloud, lest they be scorched; by night I gave them light, lest they be frightened by the darkness
**“And I was like”** — Allegorically: I loved them so much, and was so merciful a shepherd of my own, that I carried the sick sheep on my shoulders. But they did not know that I healed them by my Passion, and that I, the lover of all, drew them with the bands of love to believe. Hence: “No man can come to me, except the Father … draw him”; and they thought “my yoke,” which “is sweet,” to be most heavy. And I came down to him, leaving heaven so as to dwell with them, and, having taken the form of man, I gave them my body as food.
**“I carried them in my arms: and they knew not that I healed them”**
• lest they be harmed in the wilderness; hence: “he spread his wings, and hath taken him”
• When they had made the calf’s head, I gave them room for penance, and they did not know that I wished to cleanse them from their idols.
11.4:
**“I will draw them with the cords of Adam”** — That is, with the same love with which I made Adam holy, I wished these to be made holy; which he explains by adding: with the bands of love, in the affection of love.
**“with the cords”** — Another translation: With the cords of men; that is, with the same love with which I bound Abraham and Isaac and the rest to me, I will join these to me too.
**“with the bands of love: and I will be to them as one that taketh off”** — taking from them the yoke of the other nations
**“the yoke”** — that is, my law, which they carried as the very heaviest weight of a yoke
**“on their jaws: and I put his meat to him that he might eat”** — I gave them manna in the desert; not that God bent down to him, but he made the manna come down.
11.5:
**“He shall not return into the land of Egypt”**
• the words of one who threatens
• The heretics say they have the holy land and the Church of the Saviour, but by their perverse faith they are always in Egypt. So because Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, the great thought, that is, the Assyrian, shall be his king. For Ephraim would not return to the Church, and, having lost strength, that is, Christ, he lives always in sickness, subject to demons and to disturbances. Therefore the sword, that is, the spiritual judgment, or the word of the churchman that fights them down, will always be at work in his cities, which he wickedly built against God; and the deceived people will hang in their worship, uncertain what to do.
• And when he can find no remedy, then, repenting too late, he will long for my return when the enemy is already laying everything waste, and then it will not profit him.
**“He shall not return”** — Septuagint: Ephraim dwelt in Egypt.
*Jerome:* Under Menahem, king of the ten tribes, he wanted to flee into Egypt from before Sennacherib, but was taken by him, who also ruled over him by right of conquest. Or he is said to have returned when in the holy land he worshipped the gods of Egypt in place of God.
**“but the Assyrian shall be”** — Sennacherib
**“his king: because”** — and this is so because
**“they would not”** — trusting rather in man than in God
**“be converted”** — by penance
11.6:
**“hath begun”**
• therefore
• understand: to kill
**“The sword”** — of the enemy
**“in his cities”** — not only in the fields and estates
**“and it shall consume his chosen men”** — the princes and the strength of the army
**“and shall devour their heads”** — the princes themselves, who rule the others by the right of a head; or the heads are their counsels
11.7:
**“but a yoke”** — When the others have been killed by the sword, a yoke of the heaviest servitude will be put on those who remain, for the greatness of their sin; for to this day they are in the mountains of the Persians.
**“And my people shall long for my return: but a yoke shall be put upon them together, which shall not be taken off”** — This can be referred to the times of the Romans, when the Jews were condemned to their last captivity.
11.8:
**“How shall I deal with thee, O Ephraim?”**
• how can I, without grief, hand thee over to captivity?
• how
**“shall I protect thee, O Israel?”** — If I wish to protect thee as a father, I will not find thee worthy of protection.
**“how shall I make thee as Adama, shall I set thee as Seboim?”**
• although not without grief, I will reduce thee to a wilderness, and to ashes, like Adama and Seboim and the other cities of the Sodomites
• How etc.: Since from the threat above God’s sentence seemed hard, leaving no room for penance, he now speaks with the affection of a loving father, who to an incorrigible son adds blows after words.
• Among the five cities overthrown, Sodom and Gomorrah were the greatest in crime and in punishment; and to these two are compared the two tribes when they sin. Hence in Isaiah: “Hear the word of the Lord, ye rulers of Sodom, give ear to the law of our God, ye people of Gomorrha.” And Ezekiel: “Sodom is justified by thee.” So because the two tribes had the temple and worshipped idols there, sinning more, they are worthy of a greater punishment than the ten tribes, which were far from the temple and from Jerusalem. So the two tribes are justly compared to Sodom and Gomorrah, and the ten to Adama and Seboim, which, being lesser and subject to the greater, were corrupted by their example, and so are less to be punished. Likewise churchmen too, if they are defiled by the same crimes as the heretics, are compared not to Adama and Seboim, which are lesser, but to Sodom and Gomorrah, which are greater. But to the heretics and to the deceived people the Lord says, because they do not repent: They shall be set like Adama and Seboim, and shall have no hope of salvation. But again the loving father changes his sentence, and repents of having spoken such things. In this he calls them to conversion and penance: I will not scatter, as far as lies in me. I am God, understand: to the fallen. I stretch out my hand, I call back the wanderers; and because I am holy, I will not enter into the city, that is, the gatherings of the heretics, but I will receive those who come out from them. Or: I will not enter into the city that was built with blood and crime, as Cain, the first murderer of his kin, built a city in the name of his son Enoch; but I will abide in the city that began from Abel.
**“my heart is turned within me”** — the severity of the judge is overcome by mercy, the father’s love softens it; the bowels of mercy cannot bear that the people be blotted out
**“together”** — as I said this
**“my repentance is stirred up”** — I repent of blotting out my people
11.9:
**“not”** — therefore
**“I will … execute”**
• so as to blot out
• according to
**“the fierceness of my wrath: I will not return”** — from my mercy
**“to destroy Ephraim”**
• I will not destroy, as far as lies in me
• I will not strike so as to destroy for ever, but so as to amend. My severity is an occasion of penance and of love. This is so because I am God: man punishes to destroy, God to amend. If thou wilt repent, I will be in the midst of thee, sanctifying and saving thee.
**“because I am God, and not man: the holy one in the midst of thee, and I will not enter into the city”** — of another nation; understand: so as to forsake thee
11.10:
**“because I am God, and not man: the holy one in the midst of thee, and I will not enter into the city”** — the voice of the prophet
**“They shall walk after the Lord”** — because the Lord in his mercy promises pardon and prosperity if, converted, they follow him
**“he shall roar as a lion: because he shall roar, and”**
• then
• When the lion roars, the birds and beasts, rooted to the spot by the terror of his voice, cannot move. So, when the Lord threatens, the children of the sea, that is, of this stormy world, are afraid and go to their nests, that is, the Churches, in which he will dwell with them. This the Jews refer to the coming of the Christ, whom they still await. But we see it already accomplished: that both from Egypt and from the Assyrians, that is, from the east and the west, from the north and the south, there come every day those who sit down with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Otherwise: when the truer lion has roared, the false lion, who is our adversary, will tremble and will not be able to open his mouth for wicked doctrine; and those whom he had taken, set free by the roar, that is, by the threat of the true lion, will follow their God; and the children of the sea, who were begotten in the bitterness and false waters of the heretics, will be afraid and will fly back from them to God, so that those who toiled under the heretics may rest in the Churches from which they had strayed. Egypt means “tribulation” or “straitness”; Assyria, “directing” or “reproving.” From these the heretics will be set free when they dwell in their own houses and say to their evil fathers: Your house shall be left to you desolate.
**“as a lion”** — Hence Amos: “The Lord will roar from Sion.” The Lord roared in threatening, when he said: I will set thee like Adama; and again: “Every tree that yieldeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire.” He will roar when he says: “Depart from me, you that work iniquity.”
**“the children of the sea shall fear”** — because they will be caught from the sea of this world by the Lord’s net
11.11:
**“And they shall fly away like a bird out of Egypt”** — making from the world for heaven
**“and like a dove”**
• imitating the simplicity of the dove
• “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?”
**“out of the land of the Assyrians”** — of the demons
**“and I will place them in their own houses, saith the Lord”** — in the Churches, or in the heavenly mansions
11.12:
**“Ephraim hath compassed me about with denials”**
• Jeroboam denied me by worshipping idols and attributing nothing divine to me; the ten tribes too wanted to mock me by worshipping idols as though there were something divine in them.
• Jeroboam and the kings after him
**“hath compassed me about”** — Allegorically: The heretics compass the Lord about with their denial. For whatever they say is denial and lying, and in deceit, because whatever they feign they put together in crafty speech. But Judah, that is, the churchman, is not proud, is not puffed up like the heretics, but is humbled with God, and is faithful with the choir of the saints.
**“and the house of Israel with deceit”** — the people serving the kings
**“but Juda”**
• the two tribes
• The Hebrews hand down that at the going out from Egypt, when there was a high mountain on one side, the Red Sea on another, and the enemy on another, and the other tribes despaired, wishing either to go back to Egypt or to fight, Judah alone, at God’s command, went boldly into the sea with the faithful saints Moses and Aaron; and so this tribe earned the kingdom. Otherwise: while the ten tribes worshipped idols, Judah, that is, the two tribes that had the temple and the law, believing God and serving him, went down, humbling themselves, following in the footsteps of God, like the holy patriarchs and the other faithful.
**“as a witness”** — of the truth and power of God
**“went down … with God, and … with the saints”** — angels, patriarchs, prophets
**“is faithful”** — to God

12.1:
**“Ephraim”** — therefore
**“feedeth on the wind, and followeth the burning heat”**
• wavering between two nations
• Allegorically: The heretics gladden the unclean spirit with evil works, and follow the burning heat that shakes down the flowers and buds; and they multiply lies, that is, false teaching by which they deceive many, and from it desolation, that is, destruction, for themselves and their own. They make a covenant with the Assyrians, because they are at peace with the demons, whose will they follow, whose prince is the great thought, so that whatever they have fashioned may seem to have been wisely devised. They carry oil into Egypt, because, though they are in darkness, they falsely claim to have the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. But though they try to mix the truth with a lie, oil does not mix with water and other liquids: the truth always stays on top, the lie below.
**“Ephraim feedeth”** — The history relates that Menahem king of Israel, having made peace with Assyria, sought help from the Egyptians. That is what it is to feed on the winds, that is, to deceive oneself with vain hope by putting one’s hope in man; and to follow the burning heat, that is, to go to the southern region; and all the day, that is, all the time, to do nothing but make sport of oneself and, by worshipping a lie, that is, idols, to prepare desolation for one’s cities while running hither and thither; and he carried oil into Egypt. When Menahem saw Sennacherib turned from an ally into his enemy, he sought help from Pharaoh, sending him among other gifts the finest oil, in which Samaria abounds, and none such is found in Egypt.
12.2:
**“Therefore there is a judgment of the Lord with Juda, and a visitation for Jacob”**
• as he has done, so shall he receive
• Therefore there is a judgment of captivity and miseries; for when the ten tribes had been taken captive for their sin, Judah did not repent, but, as Ezekiel says, outdid her sisters in crimes; and a visitation, that is, scourges, upon the two tribes that sprang from Jacob.
**“according to his ways, and according to his devices”** — for not by chance but on purpose he devised the things in which to sin
**“he will render to him”** — for
12.3:
**“In the womb”** — of Rebecca
**“he supplanted”**
• not by his own strength but by the disposition of God, who foresaw that he would be a faithful patriarch to him
• Allegorically: These same things can be said to the churchman who is rebuked by God because, unmindful of God’s benefits, he does not cease to add sin to sin. When the Church was bringing thee forth in faith at thy birth, thou didst supplant thy brother, the Jew or the Gentile, and receive his birthright. And by thy strength thou hadst success with the angel, or by overcoming the evil spirits; or, strengthened by the blessings of the angel, that is, of God. Thou didst prevail over the angel by thy prayers, making him thy helper, so that thou mightest prevail against men; and when thou hadst overcome, thou didst weep, and pray to the angel of the Lord, and, remembering thy sins, thou didst find him in Bethel, that is, in the house of God, which is the Church. And so that it may be known who this Judah was, he adds: there, that is, in the Church, he spoke with us Christians; and from that name we are reckoned by the name of Christ to this day. So, O man who confessest God, turn daily to God by penance, and if thou hast sinned, say with the prophet: “I have laboured in my groanings, every night I will wash my bed.” Show mercy, that thou mayest obtain mercy; judge as thou wouldst be judged, and hope in God.
**“In the womb he supplanted”** — He sets out the benefits God conferred on Jacob, and in him on Judah his son, for in the father the son too is named; so that both God’s mercy towards Jacob, that is, Judah, and Judah’s hardness towards God may be known.
**“his brother”** — Esau
**“and by his strength he had success with an angel”** — when he wrestled all night with the angel so as to be blessed; hence he is called Israel, that is, “made straight” or “upright.”
12.4:
**“And he prevailed over”**
• against
• The prophet turns to address Judah: O Judah, since these things are so, imitate thy father: weep, pray, believe. This was fulfilled when five thousand believed on one day and three thousand on another.
**“he prevailed over”** — Obtaining the blessing by prayers.
**“the angel”** — having received a blessing from the one he overcame
**“and was strengthened”** — so as not to fear his brother
**“he wept, and made supplication to him”** — But first, weeping, he prayed: “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.”
**“he found … in Bethel”** — When, by the counsel of his father and mother, he fled into Mesopotamia.
**“him”** — the same angel
**“and there he spoke with us”** — in the father he spoke with us, his sons, saying: “The land, wherein thou sleepest, I will give to thee and to thy seed.”
12.5: **“Even the Lord God of hosts, the Lord is his memorial”** — Even the Lord: that is, he gave him this memorial of his name, that he should be called Israel, that is, “seeing God”; a name his sons keep to this day, and by this name he is always reminded of the name of God, by whom he is so called.
12.6: **“mercy and”** — Have mercy on thy own soul, then on thy brethren; then discern between good and evil; and so, always going forward to greater things by good works, hope in God always, for all praise is sung at the end.
12.7:
**“He is like Chanaan, … in his hand”**
• that is, Ephraim, in whose hand is a deceitful balance, against what the Lord says: “Let … the bushel [be] just, and the sextary equal.”
• Allegorically: In the hand of the heretics is a deceitful balance, because they deceive whomever they can, and slander the innocent; and when they have deceived them, they are wont to say: We are become rich, a crowd of disciples; we have found an idol. All the inventions of the heretics are idols, and differ nothing from the images of the Gentiles. They are wont also to say: Whatever I do cannot be laid to my charge, for I have riches, the arguments of the philosophers, a multitude of people; since whoever sees me sin will not think it so.
**“Chanaan”** — Having admonished Judah, the word turns to the ten tribes, which are called Chanaan, not by nature but by imitating its wickedness. Hence it is said to Jerusalem: “Thy father was an Amorrhite, and thy mother a Cethite.”
**“there is a deceitful balance …, he hath loved oppression”** — he says oppression because he not only has an unjust measure, but also oppresses the poor by his power
12.8:
**“And Ephraim said”** — He makes plain whom he called Chanaan: that is, the ten tribes.
**“I am become rich”** — As if to say: I do not care where I get this from. It is enough for me to have what I may possess; nor do I care to give to others.
**“I have found me an idol”** — As the belly is a god to the glutton, so gold to the miser.
**“all my labours”** — As if to say: Those who need my money will not accuse me of having got it by sin, but will rather praise me; for he who does wicked things is blessed, and the rich have many friends.
12.9:
**“And I”** — as if to say: Thou rejoicest in crime and riches, but I
**“that am the Lord thy God from the land”** — where thou didst serve in clay
**“And I that am the Lord”** — Allegorically: It is said to those who have been led astray by the heretics, that they should return to God, who brought them out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness and error of the Gentiles. And lest, remembering their sin, they be slow to return, he says: I will yet cause you to dwell in tabernacles; so that what baptism did, penance may do, and they may dwell in tabernacles, that is, in the Churches. And lest they think the heresiarchs spoke by the Spirit of God, he says: It is I who have spoken to the prophets, not to your masters.
**“of Egypt”** — I brought thee out
**“will yet cause thee to dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of the feast”**
• I still grant room for penance, and invite thee with promises to believe.
• Of the feast, that is, of Tabernacles, which is kept in the seventh month in memory of the going out from Egypt. As, he says, I set thee free from Egypt, and thou didst dwell forty years in tabernacles, hastening to the holy land, so now I will bring thee out of the captivity that threatens, so that thou mayest keep the solemnities in the manner of the fathers; if only thou doest what I command. For I have spoken by the prophets.
12.10:
**“And I have spoken by”** — that is, by
**“the prophets”** — Moses and Isaiah and the others
**“and I have multiplied visions, and … by the ministry”**
• work
• We read of visions multiplied in the prophets when Isaiah saw “the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and elevated,” and when Moses stretched out his hands in the form of a cross so that Amalek might be overcome, when Jonah was three days and three nights in the deep, and in many others.
**“and I have multiplied visions”** — All prophecy is called a vision; hence prophets were also called seers, because they understood spiritually what they spoke. To them God showed things to come, not in one way but in many kinds of prophecy.
**“I have used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets”** — as Adam bore the figure of him who, sleeping, formed the Church from his side; so Jonah, who was three days in the belly of the whale; so David, who struck down Goliath
12.11:
**“If”** — although
**“Galaad”**
• understand: worships
• Allegorically: Galaad means “the passing over of testimony,” and Galgal “wallowing-place.” So it can be said that the princes of the heretics pass the testimonies of the truth over into a lie, and whatever they worship is an idol, and their sacrifices are like heaps of stones. For as heaps of stones, or of gravel, are gathered here and there, so the heretics build images out of worldly wisdom, fraud and lying; and while they sacrifice to their errors, worshipping the works of their own hands, they do everything for earthly gain, like oxen.
**“If Galaad”** — Galaad is a city beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Gad; hence above: “Galaad is a city of workers of idols.” Galgal is a city in the tribe of Judah, near Bethel, of which above: “All their wickedness is in Galgal.” So he says: If Galaad, that is, the ten tribes, which lack the temple and the priests and the religion of God, worship an idol, yet thou, O Judah, worshippest idols in Galgal in vain, since thou hast the temple, the priesthood, etc.
**“be an idol, then”** — or: yet
**“in vain were they in Galgal”** — the men of the two tribes
**“with bullocks”** — with calves
**“offering sacrifices”**
• imitating the error of Samaria
• truly in vain
**“for their altars also”**
• understand: will be left
• when both have been taken captive, their altars, or their worship, will be like mounds gathered of stones or sand
12.12:
**“Jacob fled”**
• to Laban
• hence above: In the womb he supplanted his brother
• Allegorically: Jacob, “supplanter” or “seeing God,” is Christ. Rachel, at first barren but beautiful, whom Jacob loves, is the Church; Lia, blear-eyed but fruitful, is the synagogue. Moses is Christ, who brings the people out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of the world, and leads them to the Jordan, that is, to the waters of baptism.
**“into the country of Syria, and … served”** — seven years
**“Israel”** — Jacob himself, Israel
**“for a wife”** — for Rachel
**“and … for a wife”** — for Lia
**“was a keeper”** — another seven years
12.13:
**“But the Lord by a prophet brought”** — by Moses, or by the prophet Christ, God the Father brought the people out of darkness
**“But … by a prophet”** — He refers to the history in Genesis, in which he again recalls God’s benefits to the people and the people’s hardness towards God.
**“Israel”** — the twelve tribes
**“out of Egypt: and he was preserved by a prophet”** — and yet
**“he was preserved by a prophet”** — By Moses: when the wrath of God was stirred against that people for the sin of the calf, then Moses, lying prostrate, said: Either forgive them, or strike me out of the book of life; and so by his prayer the people was preserved.
12.14:
**“me to wrath”** — their loving leader
**“to wrath”** — Allegorically: The heretics provoke God to wrath, and by the hardness of their heart drive him who wishes them to repent to punish them before death; and the blood of those who have shed their own blood and that of many will come upon their heads; and the reproaches with which they blasphemed God their Lord will render to them; not that he is their Lord now, but that he once was.
**“Ephraim hath provoked … with his bitterness, and his blood shall come upon him”** — he himself is the cause of his death
