The prelate puts the boy in the stews and sells the girl for wine who sees men entangled in lust and other vices and does not rebuke them, for the sake of shameful gain.
**“and I will plead”** — that is, I will judge
**“with them there for my people, and for my inheritance, Israel”** — Convincing them, not by the might of my majesty, but by the truth of reason; them who have divided my inheritance by divers errors.
**“whom they have scattered among the nations”** — where, after the manner of the Gentiles, some worshipped Jupiter, others Juno, and the like
**“and have parted my land”** — so that one part of the land served one god, another another: Crete Jupiter, Thrace Mars
3.3:
**“And they have cast lots upon my people”** — how many of them the king should take as menservants and maidservants, and how many each prince
**“and the boy they have put in the stews”** — so that against nature they worked shame upon males
**“and the girl they have sold for wine, that they might drink”** — putting gluttony and the greed of the belly before lust, abusing boys in place of women
3.4:
**“But what have you to do with me, O Tyre, and Sidon”**
• understand: is there in common, that you always attack me in my inheritance
• But what etc.: The Jews think this is said against Tyre and Sidon and the Philistines, because in the time of the Jewish captivity, when the Jews were conquered by the Romans, they persecuted the people of God, or rather God in his people. So they maintain that the vengeance for the blood of Christ, and the overthrow of Jerusalem, which happened by God’s judgment, came upon Tyre and Sidon on their behalf.
• Tyre and Sidon, cities of the Gentiles, joining with the Philistines who lived in Palestine, often afflicted the people of God; so the Lord will rebuke them. Tyre means “straitness,” and they straitened the people of God; Sidon “hunting,” and they hunted the people to death.
• By Tyre and Sidon can be understood the Gentiles, and above all the Romans, who persecuted the apostles and martyrs of Christ; hence they will be condemned on the day of judgment. By those who took the silver and gold are signified the heretics, who take from the Church the silver of the divine word and the gold of spiritual understanding and turn them to their errors, and sell the sons of the Church to the devil and make them heathens, so that they are far from the number of the elect.
**“and all the coast of the Philistines?”** — who drank the blood of my people, otherwise of God
**“will you revenge yourselves”**
• that is, will you always fight against me?
• As God is said to be clothed, fed and refreshed in his own, so he is said to be afflicted and to suffer persecution in them.
**“on me?”** — or: on yourselves
**“and if you revenge yourselves on me”** — understand: for a time
**“I will very soon return you a recompense upon your own head”**
• as you have done, so I will render to you: you have killed, you will be killed; you have persecuted, you will suffer persecution from your enemies
• all these things can also be referred to the day of judgment, the vengeance not differing, though in time they seem to differ from what went before
3.5:
**“For … my silver”**
• the words of Scripture
• That he says the Tyrians and Sidonians took away the vessels of the house of God, the history tells that the Chaldeans did this; and when Belshazzar, the great-grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, afterwards drank from those vessels, at once his kingdom was transferred from the Babylonians to the Medes. But since these things are said to be after the great and dreadful day of the Lord, which the apostles interpret of the Lord’s resurrection, and the Hebrews put off to the time of judgment to come, it is rather to be understood of the Romans. For Titus and Vespasian, having taken the Jews captive, built at Rome the Temple of Peace, in which they dedicated the vessels of the temple and all its offerings. At that time too the children of Judah and Jerusalem (not the children of the ten tribes, which are held among the Medes to this day) were sold to the children of the Greeks and driven out of their borders, and the whole world was filled with the Jewish captivity.
**“and my gold you have taken away”** — the understanding of the Scriptures
**“and my desirable”** — which are in the Church
**“and most beautiful things”** — understand: the vessels or ornaments of the temple
**“you have carried”** — you have made them slaves to your errors
**“into your temples”** — into the temples of the gods
3.6: **“And the children of Juda, and the children of Jerusalem, you have sold to the children of the Greeks, that you might remove them far off from their own country”** — but
3.7:
**“Behold I”** — The Jews rave that in the last time they are to be gathered by the Lord and brought back to Jerusalem, and that the Lord will hand over to them the sons and daughters of the Romans, so that the Jews may sell them, not to their neighbours, but to the Sabeans, a nation far off.
**“I will raise them up out of the place”** — out of heresy
**“wherein you have sold”** — O heretics
**“them”** — when they had been led astray
**“and I will return your recompense upon your own heads”** — After his coming the Lord daily raises up to penance those who lie in error, who once stood in the Church, and gives them back to the teachers of the Church. In this he repays the heretics, handing over the sons whom they had taught in mystical things and in carnal, into the hands of the princes of the Church, so that, when they have taken them, they may sell them to the Sabeans and make them captives, and, converted to better things, they may serve the institutions of the Church.
3.8: **“And I will sell your sons”** — This was fulfilled in part in the time of Cyrus, when the Jews, returning from captivity, brought many of the Chaldeans with them: both those who joined them of their own accord and those they had bought, and whom they afterwards sold. Saba is a region beyond the borders of Ethiopia, from which came the queen of Saba.
3.9:
**“Proclaim ye”** — O saints, who are to judge the nations
**“this among the nations”** — what I am about to say
**“Proclaim ye this”** — The literalist Jews say that when their Christ comes, and the golden Jerusalem comes down from heaven, the savage nations, Gog and Magog, will come to war against the Jews; and that the divine word urges these to give up their farming and prepare themselves for war against the Jews, and to bring with them the help of all the nations; whom the Lord challenges to this ironically, because there not the Jews but they themselves are to be killed. Hence he says: there will the Lord cause thy strong ones to fall down, O Gog and Magog. But it is better to refer these things to the day of judgment, in the moral sense: God warns his own to prepare themselves to avenge and to fight against the enemy.
**“prepare war”** — prepare yourselves for war at the judgment
**“rouse up the strong”** — to battle
3.10:
**“Cut your plough-shares into swords”** — let the perfect turn all the effort with which they tilled their own souls to fighting for others
**“and your spades into spears”**
• with which you dug the ground
• Spade: an iron tool for digging; spades (ligones) are so called because they lift the earth, as if “lifters.”
**“Let the weak say”** — I do not warn the greater only, but let the weak and simple, that is, the meek, grow strong too
**“I am strong”** — to judge
3.11:
**“Break forth”** — out of the tombs
**“and come”** — to the judgment of God
**“all ye nations from round about, and gather yourselves together”** — you who have persecuted the people of God
**“there”** — at that judgment
**“will the Lord cause … to fall down”** — O evil generation
**“all thy strong ones”** — the demons, who by their strength drive men to depart from the law of God
3.12:
**“Let them arise”** — out of the tombs
**“Let them arise, and”** — Others say that the nations to be condemned are warned to rise to the judgment of their condemnation, and are ironically warned to prepare themselves for the war in which they are to be killed, because their wickedness is complete.
**“and let the nations come up into the valley of Josaphat”** — The wicked always go down.
**“for there I will sit to judge all nations round about”**
• Which have transgressed my laws.
• Some interpret this in a good sense, and say that the nations go up into the valley of Josaphat, which means “the judgment of the Lord,” and that the Lord sits there to reward the good, who will be gathered from round about against the adversaries of God; and they will cut down the harvest of the enemy and tread them down, because their wickedness is complete; and the new wine, that is, their wickedness, so overflows that the presses cannot hold it. And so that we may know of what vintage he speaks, he adds: their wickedness is multiplied, namely of those who have gathered against God.
• The Jews interpret this of Gog and Magog, who they think will come against the people of God into the valley of Josaphat after a thousand years, when Jerusalem has been restored, and be gathered there like a vintage.
3.13:
**“Put ye in the sickles, for the harvest is ripe”** — The sentence of judgment
**“come”** — O saints
**“and go down”** — to judge your persecutors
**“for the press is full, the fats run over: for their wickedness is multiplied”**
• by the ripe harvest and the overflowing presses the fullness of sins and the end of the world is shown
• And therefore
3.14:
**“Nations”** — O
**“nations in the valley of destruction”** — gather together for your damnation
**“for the day of the Lord is near”** — of vengeance
**“in the valley of destruction”**
• the sentence of the Lord’s judgment
• The valley of destruction is the name for God’s sentence, by which he will cut off and separate the elect from the reprobate.
• The valley of destruction, that is, of judgment.
3.15:
**“The sun and the moon”** — On that day the sun and the other stars will not be able to look on the torments of the perishing, but will withdraw their shining and will not dare to look on the severity of him who punishes; not that they are to be condemned by God’s judgment, but because every creature, at the torments of others, will be greatly afraid of its own judgment; hence nature and the powers of the heavens will be moved.
**“the sun and moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their shining”**
• For when the sun comes, all the lights will seem to lose their brightness.
• Hence the Lord: “the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven.” Or even to the reprobate everything will seem darkened.
3.16: **“And the Lord … out of”** — When everything has been darkened, the Lord, like a lion out of Sion, that is, out of the Church made up of angels and men, will cry against the reprobate with so lofty and terrible a voice that the hinges of the heavens and the foundations of the earth will be shaken; and he, severe to the wicked, will be the hope of his own, setting them free, and will give strength to those who are the children of Israel, that is, of the one who sees God.
3.17:
**“And you shall know”** — O elect
**“And you shall know that”** — At the judgment both those who are punished and those who are taken up will know that the Lord dwells in Sion, and in Christ his mountain, or in him who has prepared himself as a dwelling worthy of God.
**“dwelling in Sion, my holy mountain”** — in the midst of the elect, in the minds of those who contemplate heavenly things and are set on the summit of the virtues
**“and Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall pass through it no more”** — This the Jews refer to the fable of the thousand years, when they think Christ will dwell in Sion and in a golden Jerusalem, and the peoples of the saints will be gathered, so that those who were oppressed by others in this world may rule over all nations in that one.
**“and Jerusalem shall be”** — And after the day of judgment Jerusalem, made up of angels and men, will be without any of the defilement it contracted before from mingling with the wicked; and the stranger, that is, the devil, or any wicked thought, will find no way into the just, who have the peace of God.
3.18:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”** — When the Lord dwells in Sion after the Ascension into heaven, or after the day of judgment, the mountains, that is, the apostles and the lofty preachers, will abound in the sweetness of wisdom and of the divine word, and spiritual graces will drop from them; and the hills, that is, those who have not so great a fullness of understanding, will give forth milk, by which the infancy of the Church is fed; and through all the rivers of Judah, that is, over the believers and the sons of the Church, waters, that is, spiritual graces, will abound, for nothing in them will be dry.
**“and a fountain shall come forth of the house of the Lord, and shall water the torrent of thorns”** — Out of the house of the Lord, that is, the first Church, comes forth the fountain of baptism and of teaching, which waters the hearts of the Gentiles, which were pricked with the thorns of vices and the stings of evil thoughts; so that the flowers of the virtues may spring up there, where before the prickings of the vices sprang up.
3.19: **“Egypt shall be a desolation”** — These things too the Jews refer to the time when they await their Messiah; but they are better referred to the day of judgment or of the resurrection. Egypt means “grief,” or “darkness,” or “persecuting”; Edom “earthly” or “bloody.” So those who shed the blood of the martyrs and gave themselves to earthly works will be crushed by everlasting damnation; for daily they work evil against the sons of the Church and shed their blood by deceiving them.
3.20: **“And Judea”** — The province of confession and glory, and the city in which the glory of God is seen, will be the everlasting dwelling of God, not for one or several generations only, but to generation and generation: in the two generations of those who have believed from among the Jews and from among the Gentiles.
3.21:
**“And I will cleanse”**
• by avenging it
• The Lord cleanses in the Gospel the blood of sinners, which before in the law he had not cleansed, there leaving sinners and the unclean. For he hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all.
**“their blood”** — the martyrdom of Christ
**“which I had not cleansed”** — which I long let pass until the day of judgment, but there it will be avenged. When it is avenged, the Lord will dwell in the multitude of the saints.

1.1:
**“The words of Amos, who was among herdsmen”**
• understand: places
• The words of Amos. Jerome: Amos prophesies, not to Jerusalem, but to Israel in Samaria, as appears from what is written: “And Amasias the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos hath rebelled against thee in the midst of the house of Israel.” And a little after, Amaziah said to Amos: “Thou seer, go, flee away into the land of Juda: … and prophesy there. But prophesy not again any more in Bethel: because it is the king's sanctuary, and it is the house of the kingdom.” To whom Amos answered: “I am not a prophet, nor am I the son of a prophet: but I am a herdsman plucking wild figs. And the Lord took me when I followed the flock, and the Lord said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel.”
**“of Thecua: which he saw”** — With that sight by which prophets are called seers, who understood by the Holy Spirit what they prophesied.
**“concerning Israel”** — the ten tribes
**“in the days of Ozias, king of Juda, and in the days of Jeroboam, the son of Joas, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake”**
• Before Uzziah was struck with leprosy.
• That is, before the captivity shook everything; which, in the two years, shows the twofold distress of the ten tribes and of the two; so that, if they would do penance, they would not feel the earthquake afterwards.
• Uzziah is the same as Azariah, who, claiming for himself a priesthood not his due, was struck with leprosy on his forehead; and there was also a great earthquake through all Jerusalem. Jeroboam was the great-grandson of Jehu, to whom the Lord had promised that kings of his seed would be over Israel until the fourth generation; and in this Jeroboam that promise was fulfilled.
*Jerome:* Uzziah means “the rule” or “the strength of the Lord.” Jeroboam “pointing out,” or “the cause of the people,” or “the division of the people,” or “delay,” or “temporal.” Tekoa “sounding the trumpet”; Amos “torn away.” So at the time when the people was torn away from the Lord, or from the kingdom of David, Amos, like one sounding the trumpet, sang over Israel, which was once most upright before God, while Uzziah reigned in Judea, in whom, because of the temple and the holy of holies, the strength of the Lord remained, and he ruled a people that confessed him. But Jeroboam, who was the cause of the division of the people, reigns in Israel, which serves idols.
1.2:
**“And he said”** — Amos
**“The Lord … from”** — It is natural that all who wish to compare one thing with another should take their comparisons from the things they have experienced and been brought up among. For example, sailors liken their enemies to winds, loss to shipwreck, sorrow to a storm, and joy and prosperity to the calmest breeze, the sea to the plains. So shepherds liken their fear to the roaring of a lion, and call their enemies lions, bears or wolves. So this man, who was a shepherd of flocks, compares the fear of God to the roaring of a lion: he will roar from Sion and utter his voice from Jerusalem, where the temple and the religion of God were, not from Bethel or Dan, where the golden calves were. He will roar, that is, he will strike fear into the ten tribes, threatening captivity; and so the beautiful places of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall be withered. By these is signified the land of the ten tribes, which was most fertile, and which was soon to be taken captive by the Assyrians under Hoshea, their last king, who is signified by the top of Carmel. When he was carried off, the beautiful places of the shepherds, the princes of the world and the mighty of the ten tribes, mourned, because their land was emptied when the king was carried off.
**“and the beautiful places of the shepherds have mourned”**
• The greater ones in the people will weep, because Hoshea king of Israel will be crushed and taken captive.
• Allegorically: When God, from the watchtower of the Church, in which is the vision of peace, has uttered his voice through the teachers of the Old and New Testaments, then the beautiful places of the shepherds, namely the teaching of the heretics, which seemed fair and promised the knowledge of the true circumcision, will mourn and be dried up; and the peoples, who for their simplicity are called flocks, will wither in a sudden drought.
**“the beautiful places of the shepherds”** — They are the level plains, the green of the pastures, places abounding in divers grasses. There are two mountains called Carmel: one from which came Nabal the Carmelite, the other on which Elijah prayed; and both are very rich in pasture.
**“and the top of Carmel is withered”** — The knowledge of circumcision.
1.3:
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four”**
• If Hazael and his people had persecuted my people only once and twice, perhaps I would spare him; but because I waited long for his penance, so that, converted, he might recover his health, and he on the contrary abused my patience and afflicted them a third and a fourth time, I am forced to change my sentence, so as to chastise the offenders with blows
• He begins with Damascus because at the time when Amos prophesied, Hazael was grievously afflicting the ten tribes.
**“For three crimes of Damascus”** — Damascus is the chief city of Syria, which Eliezer, the servant of Abraham, founded in the field where Abel was killed. Gilead is a city and region beyond the Jordan, in the lot of the half tribe of Manasseh. At the time when Amos began to prophesy, Hazael king of Damascus so laid waste that region that, having overcome Ahab king of Israel at Ramoth-gilead, he crushed that whole region like the threshing-sledges that thresh the corn on the floors.
**“I will not convert it”** — from madness to mercy
**“because they have thrashed Galaad with iron wains”**
• that is, he crushed Gilead as the corn is beaten out on the floors by wheels shod beneath with iron and teeth, and the straw is crushed for the cattle’s food, for want of hay
• Allegorically: The first sin is to think evil; the second to consent; the third to fulfil it in deed; the fourth not to repent. He who sins in the first three, if he repents, God turns him to the face of his mercy; but if he does not repent, the face of his mercy is turned away from him.
• Allegorically: Gilead means “the passing over” or “the removal of testimony,” and signifies those who, having passed over from the Church into heresy, carry the testimonies of God they had received before into strange territory. Such as these the heretics crush with wains and iron wheels with teeth; of whom it is said: “The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows.” For the heretics not only think and do evil, but deceive the simple with wicked teaching and drink their blood: for Damascus means “a drinking of blood.” From such sins the Lord turns away his face, so that those who do not see the truth of the divine teaching, the divine face being turned away, may be overwhelmed with darkness. And when they try to deceive others, the Lord sends a fire into the house which they call Hazael, that is, “the vision of God,” and it devours in them the wood and the stubble, and also the whole house, that is, the structure of their fraud, and besides the bars, that is, the strongest arguments of their art of dialectic. When these are broken, the inhabitants of the plain of the idol are destroyed, that is, idolatry is destroyed; and when it is destroyed, those who seemed to hold the sceptre in it are made of no account; and the lofty and sublime people, which is raised up in pride and promises itself heavenly things, will be led away captive, so that it may be taken and carried over to its own salvation.
• The father of Hazael was called Benadab, with b as the last letter; the son of Hazael was called Benadat, with t. When Hazael died in Syria, while Uzziah and Jeroboam reigned, he succeeded his father in the kingdom; and from him all the kings of Aram, that is, of Syria and Damascus, were afterwards called Ben-hadad, as the Pharaohs from the first Pharaoh and the Caesars from Caesar. So he threatens that he will crush the royal house of Hazael, and his son Ben-hadad. For we read that Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, having overcome Egypt, came and plundered the ten tribes, and afterwards turned to Syria and killed Rezin king of Syria, of whom we read in Isaiah, and carried the people of Syria captive to Cyrene, which is at the furthest borders of Egypt.
**“because they have thrashed”** — Jerome: Another translation: because they have threshed the women with child of Gilead with iron saws. The women with child are the souls that have lately been made fruitful by the word of God, whom the heretics draw away from the Church and grind with iron teeth like food. For it belongs to the little ones to be scandalized, not to the perfect.
1.4:
**“And I will send”** — therefore
**“a fire”** — of captivity
**“into the house of Azael”** — upon his royal stock
**“and it shall devour the houses of Benadad”** — that captivity shall devour Ben-hadad, the son of Hazael, with his house
1.5:
**“And I will break the bar of Damascus”** — All the strength of the Syrians, with which once, as with a door and bars, they kept off the onset of their adversaries
**“and I will cut off the inhabitants from the plain of the idol”** — That is, from Damascus, which lies in a plain and is full of idols.
**“and him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of pleasure”** — understand: I will break
**“and … shall be carried away”** — by Tiglath-pileser
**“the people of Syria … to Cyrene”** — that is, the lofty
1.6:
**“For three crimes of Gaza”** — Gaza is the chief city of the Philistines, who are now called Palestinians, with Ashdod and Ashkelon and Ekron, and Gath, which is not mentioned here. He says a perfect, that is, an entire captivity was carried away by them into Edom, because whomever of the ten tribes they could catch, they sold to the Edomites as menservants and maidservants. So he threatens them with the fire of captivity, which will devour everything.
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza”**
• Because we read of five cities of the Philistines that were struck with plagues for the wrong done to the ark, after Gaza he passes on to Ashdod and Ashkelon.
• Ashkelon was anciently called Philistiim; hence the region was afterwards called Philistia and its inhabitants Philistines. So by Ashkelon the whole kingdom of the Philistines can be understood.
*Jerome:* Allegorically: Gaza means “strength” or “rule,” Edom “bloody” or “earthly,” Ashdod “fire of the breast,” Ashkelon “murderous fire,” or “hung up,” or “weighed,” Ekron “barrenness” or “rooting out.” Gaza is accused, which promises itself the strength of its knowledge and rule, because it shuts up captives in Edom. These are the masters of the Jews, who follow not the spirit but the letter, and interpret everything in an earthly way. So a fire is sent into the walls of Gaza, by which all the arguments by which they defend their lies are destroyed. It also consumes the houses, that is, whatever seems built by the art of dialectic; and from Ashdod is cut off the inhabitant who, following the letter, has breasts full not of milk but of fire; and the sceptre is taken from Ashkelon, where is the murderous fire of the devil, which kills whomever it breathes upon, as the fire of God refreshes those it enters. The hand is also turned against Ekron, where is barrenness: for to him who does not receive the spiritual understanding is given “a womb without children, and dry breasts.” Besides, all the rest of the Philistines are destroyed: either the city of Gath, where is the winepress of the devil, or all who fall by the cup. For when they are drunk, they will fall and wallow in their vomit.
**“and for four, I will not convert it, because they have carried away a perfect captivity to shut them up in Edom”** — Because it was not enough for you to persecute my people once and twice, but you have done it often, I will not turn the face of mercy towards you; but, when the Assyrians or Nebuchadnezzar come, I will send the fire of captivity on the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its houses.
1.8:
**“And I will cut off the inhabitant from Azotus”** — which is another chief city
**“and him that holdeth the sceptre”** — the royal dignity
**“from Ascalon”** — that city, or the whole kingdom of the Philistines
**“and I will turn my hand”** — my power
**“against Accaron”** — that other city
**“and the rest … shall perish”** — Bethel, namely all the villages that are subject to the cities named above
**“of the Philistines”** — of those who fall by drink
1.9:
**“For three crimes of Tyre”** — Tyre is a city of the Phoenicians, next to the Sidonians, whose citizens were merchants; and whomever of Israel they could plunder, they sold to the Edomites and other nations.
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre”** — We read in Ezekiel that Nebuchadnezzar made his army carry a mound round Tyre, so as to make the island part of the mainland, but he could not catch them, because they escaped by ship. Afterwards Alexander of Macedon cut down trees and brought them whole, and threw them into the sea together with earth and stones, and made it level with the land; and so took it and destroyed it.
**“and for four, I will not convert it: because they have shut up an entire captivity in Edom, and have not remembered the covenant of brethren”**
• That is, of the friendship that Hiram king of Tyre had with David and Solomon.
• Allegorically: Tyre means “tribulation” or “straitening.” Whoever would shut up the truth in earthly senses, and does not remember the brethren whom he ought to call from the letter to the spirit and instruct from the divine Scripture in its three senses, upon all his fortifications and buildings the Lord will send the fire of destruction.
• Men are called brothers in four ways: by nature, like Esau and Jacob; by kinship, like Abraham and Lot; by nation, as all Jews are called brothers; by friendship, like Solomon and Hiram. Hence Hiram, when he refused to accept the twenty cities that Solomon had given him in Bethshemesh, said to him: “Are these the cities which thou hast given me, brother?” For they were full of grass.
1.10: **“And I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour the houses thereof”** — by Nebuchadnezzar, or by Alexander the Great
1.11:
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not convert him: because he hath pursued his brother with the sword, and hath cast off all pity, and hath carried on”** — than he ought
**“For three crimes of Edom”** — Edom is the same as Esau and Seir; hence the mountains of Seir are named, and the region of Edom. He persecuted Jacob, so that for fear of him he fled into Mesopotamia; and he did not keep towards him the bowels of mercy, so as to understand that he was bound to him by the bond of brotherhood. And the hatred that was in the father the Edomites, born of him, kept against the sons of Jacob, so that when they came out of Egypt they would not even grant them passage into the holy land; in this casting off pity, so as not to know that they were brothers.
**“his fury, and hath kept his wrath to the end”**
• For as long as Israel remained in the land given it by God, he always persecuted it.
• Allegorically: The Jews, earthly and bloody, persecute the Christian people, plundering its substance, and do not keep towards it the rights of nature, and hold their ancient fury in their synagogues to this day, wishing the Christian name to be destroyed. But the Lord sends a fire into Teman, which means “south,” that is, Judea, dry and not watered by the rains of the prophets; by this fire its fortifications are destroyed, so that, as the sense of the letter falls, the Church of God may be built up on it.
1.12:
**“I will send”**
• therefore
• by the Assyrians
**“a fire”** — of captivity
**“into Theman”** — which is the chief city of Edom
**“and it shall devour the houses of Bosra”** — another city
*Jerome:* Bozrah: not, as some think, “another city,” but of Edom, according to that saying: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?”
1.13:
**“For three crimes of the children of Ammon”** — The children of Ammon, born of the stock of Lot, live in Arabia. Their prince, Nahash the Ammonite, in the times of Saul fought against Gilead, which is a city of the two tribes and of Manasseh, and so oppressed it that he even ripped up the women with child.
**“and for four, I will not convert him: because he hath ript up the women with child, of Galaad, to enlarge his border”** — so as to subject all the land of Gilead to his rule
*Jerome:* Jerome: This is the difference between the cruelty of the Damascenes and that of the children of Ammon: those crush with iron wains, these rip up the women with child of Gilead to enlarge their border. The Damascenes, who drink blood, signify the heretics, who not only tear new believers from the Church but crush and grind the people of God with iron teeth like bread. Ammon, which means “people of grief” or “my people,” signifies the schismatics, who separate from the Church the untaught souls that had lately conceived the word of God. Yet they do not butcher those they have cut off so cruelly as the heretics; but, remaining in the same rule of faith, they wish to spread the name of their own glory among those who come after. So God threatens that he will burn their fortifications, and that the author of the schism will go captive, and that the princes of the Church will bow their necks to the yoke.
1.14:
**“And”** — therefore
**“I will kindle a fire”** — by the Assyrians and Nebuchadnezzar
**“in the wall of Rabba”** — which is the chief city of the children of Ammon
**“and it shall devour the houses thereof with shouting”** — of the conquering army
**“in the day of battle, and with a whirlwind”** — of captivity and weeping
**“and with a whirlwind”** — So Nebuchadnezzar came upon them, and so moved them from their dwellings, as a storm and whirlwind snatch up straw.
**“in the day of trouble”** — of the deportation
1.15:
**“And Melchom shall go”**
• the idol
• Milcom, their idol, that is, their king, will be carried to the Assyrians, and his princes, that is, his priests, will be carried with him; or the king of the city and his princes will be taken captive with him.

2.1:
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not convert him: because he hath burnt the bones of the king of Edom even to ashes”**
• so that he would not allow even death to be the end of all evils
• Allegorically: The bones of the king of Edom are the most solid and firm spiritual understanding that lies within the letter. But the Jews turn it into flesh and reduce it to ashes, when, leaving aside the spiritual strength, they cling to the letter alone: for example, thinking of nothing in Hosea’s taking a harlot but the shamefulness of the story; and so in other things. He burns the bones of the king of Edom who, thinking ill of the majesty of God, thinks of God after the manner of a human body, as though he were stretched out in limbs, and saw and heard like a man.
**“because he hath burnt”**
• The Hebrews hand down that the Edomites were subject to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and the Moabites to Joram king of Israel. But a little after, when the king of the Moabites had revolted from Joram, Joram asked help from Jehoshaphat king of Judah. He came and brought with him the king of the Edomites to besiege the city where the king of Moab was shut up; and when the king of Moab tried to flee from the city by the side that the king of the Edomites was besieging, he was not allowed to by him. Then, going up on the wall, he sacrificed his son to his god; and for the monstrousness of this crime the children of Israel withdrew from the city. Afterwards, when the king of the Edomites had died and been buried, the Moabites, remembering what he had done against them in the siege, dragged him out of the tomb and burnt him with fire and reduced him to ashes, so that what they could not do to him living, they might avenge on him dead.
• To show that all the souls he has created belong to his rule, God threatens to avenge on the Moabites the crime they committed against the king of the Edomites, in that they did not end their cruelty even at his death. And if God so takes vengeance on those who did not know him, what will he do to those who worship him?
2.2:
**“And I will send a fire into Moab”** — which is the chief city of the Moabites, from which the whole province is so called; or into the whole province
**“and it shall devour the houses of Carioth”**
• of that city; it means “towns,” hence Kiriath-jearim is called “town of the woods”
• which means “from the father,” because he was born of God, but forsook him
**“and Moab shall die with a noise, with the sound of the trumpet”** — of the victors
**“shall die with a noise”** — Moab, that is, the heretics, will die no otherwise than with the sound of the trumpet, so that they may be overwhelmed by the lofty senses which in the divine books are compared to the sounding of the trumpet; and then the divine word kills all who are given over to earthly works, commanding the teachers of the Church: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion.”
2.3:
**“And”** — then
**“I will cut off the judge from the midst thereof, and will slay all his princes with him, saith the Lord”** — When the cities and the captains are burnt, the judgment of the princes and the counsel of the judges will be in vain.
2.4:
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Juda, and for four, I will not convert him: because he hath cast away the law of the Lord”**
• given by Moses
• Allegorically: Whatever is said of Judah is referred to the Church, in which is the confession and peace of God and the vision of the truth. She is reproved because, despising the law of God, each worships his own vices: as the miser gold, the glutton his belly; for “by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave.” Hence the Lord also condemns the wicked houses and the vicious foundations that destroyed the glory of Jerusalem.
• He who thinks he confesses God and sees him, if he remains in sin without doing penance, God turns the face of his mercy away from him.
**“For three crimes of Juda”** — He does not reproach the nations named before with having cast away the written law, but only the natural law; hence he says they cast off the bowels of mercy, or blazed into excessive rage. But he charges Judah with not keeping the law it had received, so that for transgressing both the natural and the written law it is to suffer misery. The other nations, which “have sinned without the law, shall perish without the law.”
**“and hath not kept his commandments: for their idols have caused them to err”** — Unless it had rejected the law, it could not be deceived by idols.
**“after which their fathers have walked”** — in Egypt they fashioned for themselves the images of Egypt, worshipping Beelphegor and Astaroth and Baalim
2.5:
**“And”** — therefore
**“I will send”** — by Nebuchadnezzar
**“a fire”** — captivity
**“into Juda”** — into the region of the two tribes
**“and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem”** — of the earthly Jerusalem, not of that in which is the vision of peace
2.6:
**“Thus saith the Lord: For three crimes of Israel”** — He puts the ten tribes last, because nearly all that follows refers to them.
**“and for four, I will not convert him: because he hath sold … for silver”** — To the neighbouring nations, not out of need of food or drink, but for the sake of avarice.
**“because he hath sold”** — The simple and just man is the churchman who has no knowledge of the Scriptures, but does what he is commanded. The heretic sells him for money, when he does the works of the just for mortal things, which are signified by the shoes. For he cannot stand on the holy ground with bare feet like Joshua, because something mortal clings to his works. This is the dust the apostles shake off their feet, which they have gathered from living among mortals.
**“the just man … and the poor man”** — any simple man
**“for a pair of shoes”**
• with which they tread the earth and smoke
• Selling the precious soul of man, not for a great thing but for a worthless one.
• Nor does poverty hold him back from iniquity.
**“and the poor man for a pair of shoes”** — Septuagint: and they strike the poor on the head, who have turned aside from the way of the humble; for they will not follow him who said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” and: “Come to me, all you that labour.”
2.7:
**“They bruise the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth”** — the precious soul of man
**“They bruise”** — The princes of the Jews had such customs as these: if a poor man joined them on the road, they flogged him and threw him on the dust of the earth, disdaining to walk with the simple. It also often happened among them that a son defiled his father’s wife, or again that a father defiled his son’s wife. Those too who would not go to worship the calves they killed or stripped, and, laying out pieces of their garments beside the altars of their gods, they reclined on them, and gave a part for wine, which they drank before the altars of the gods. This spoil is called a pledge, that is, a surety, because it was given for the killing of the body and the setting free of the soul. In all these things the name of the Lord is profaned. Whatever is done shamefully by them is turned to God’s dishonour, who says: “the name of God, through you, is blasphemed among the Gentiles.”
*Jerome:* Allegorically: The princes of the heretics swell with pride, turning aside from him who “resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.”
**“and turn aside the way of the humble”** — the way, which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”; “Come to me, all you that labour”
**“and the son”** — the Christian
**“and his father have gone to the same young woman, to profane my holy name”**
• the people of the Jews; hence: “our fathers were all under the cloud”
• He who enters the Church so as to keep the law together with the Gospel goes in with his Jewish father to the young woman, that is, to circumcision and the other observances of the law. So both the Jewish father and the Christian who imitates him are defiled by one fornication, thinking Christ not enough; of whom the Apostle: “if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.”
2.8:
**“And they sat down upon garments laid to pledge by every altar: and … the wine”** — the drunkenness of the Sodomites
**“of the condemned”** — those they thought gods, they defiled with shame and lewdness
**“drank … in the house of their God”**
• whom they had oppressed by force
• The heretics, committing fornication under the Christian name, spread the testimonies of the Scriptures over their errors, not laying them under the Saviour’s footsteps, so that they may bear him witness, but covering their sins with them. The apostles, on the contrary, spread their garments on the ass’s colt, so that the Lord may sit more softly, and climb the way paved from the law and the prophets. The heretics also drink the wine of the condemned, who are condemned from the fact that they have gone out of the Church; and they delight in the wine of the Sodomites and in “the gall of dragons, and the venom of asps, which is incurable” to whoever drinks it. And they drink it, not in the house of the Lord, as the temple and Jerusalem, but of their own god, whom they have fashioned for themselves by crafty speech.
• According to the Septuagint, so great was their contempt of God that they stretched with cords beside the altar the garments in which they slept or committed fornication, so that the fornicators could not be seen. And the heretics hold up before the eyes of onlookers their garments, which they have bound with the cords of sins, so that they may not see their crimes; and because they see them before the altar of God, they do not suspect lewdness.
2.9:
**“Yet I cast out”**
• against their evils he recalls the benefits he had done them
• Where God’s praises are concerned, the order of the history need not be minded. Mystically, before God leads us out of the iron furnace of Egypt, he destroys the Amorrhite, which means “bitter,” or “speaking,” or “famous,” one much talked of; who is Sihon, that is, “a fruitless” or “barren tree”: not because he never bears fruit, but because he bears evil fruit, and so he is cut down by the Lord.
**“the Amorrhite before their face”** — Sihon, king of the Amorrhites, who was lofty and strong, like the cedar and the oak
**“whose height”**
• pride
• his bed is said to have been nine cubits long and four wide
**“was like the height of cedars”** — “I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Libanus.”
**“and who was strong as an oak”**
• “When a strong man, armed, keepeth his court”
• He who passes over from the world must shun pride, which is signified by the cedar, and the desires of the flesh, which are signified by the oak.
• The oak is the hardest and strongest tree; from its name Philo thinks Esau is called “oaken” and “of oak,” though Esau can be understood as “made,” in that he was made for evil works.
**“and I destroyed”** — that is, I cast his pride to the ground, and crushed his root, that is, his stock, so that no sons should be begotten of him
**“his fruit from above, and his roots beneath”** — lest anyone, thinking it good, should eat and perish
2.10:
**“It is I”** — and no other
**“that brought … up”** — out of the vale of tears
**“you”** — ungrateful as you are
**“out of the land of Egypt”** — which is level, while the land of promise is mountainous
**“and I led you”** — by a long way round
**“through the wilderness”** — the dark world
**“forty years”**
• this number fits affliction and fasting and sorrow, for by these one comes to the holy land
• through penance
**“that you might possess”** — first his region should become your possession
**“the land of the Amorrhite”** — which Moses divided to the children of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh
2.11:
**“And”** — afterwards
**“I raised up of your sons for prophets”** — Such as Moses and Aaron and others who received the grace of prophecy
**“for Nazarites”** — That is, the sanctified, who offer their souls to God, and do not touch the wine that can make drunk and overturn the state of the mind, so that they may have long hair like Samson, in whose head is strength and victory; for “the head of every man is Christ.”
**“Is it not so, O ye children of Israel?”** — can you deny that I did so?
2.12:
**“And you”** — you on the contrary
**“will present wine to the Nazarites”** — who were commanded not to drink anything that can make drunk
**“And you will present”** — From this place, and because by the law it is said that the Nazarites are not to drink wine, Tatian asserts that wine is not to be drunk. But it is to be understood that both here and in the law it is drunkenness and the cares of the world that are forbidden, which overwhelm the strength of the mind.
**“and … the prophets”**
• the learned men I sent
• Amaziah the priest of Bethel forbade Amos. Zedekiah king of Judah forbade Jeremiah to speak in the name of the Lord, and burnt his book with fire.
**“command …, saying”** — overcome by envy
**“Prophesy not”** — the word of the Lord, which was given for the good of the hearers
2.13:
**“Behold”** — therefore
**“I will screek under you”** — threatening punishment
**“Behold, I will screek”** — No longer bearing the sins by which I have long been weighed down, like a wain with straw or hay, I will hand you over to burning like straw, and condemn you, saying: Flight shall perish from the swift.
**“as a wain screeketh”** — with a long sound and wailing
**“that is laden with hay”** — not with corn, to be stored in the barn, but with hay, which withers before it is plucked up
2.14:
**“And flight shall perish from the swift”** — The Hebrews say it is Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had first fled into Egypt and was swift to make idols
**“And flight shall perish”** — Mystically: Flight shall perish from the swift, for, as the Apostle says, not all “who run in the race” obtain “the prize,” because sins hinder his course; and the valiant in his own opinion, who trusts in himself and not in God’s mercy; and the strong, trusting not in the armour of God that the Apostle lists but in the strength of the world; and he that holdeth the bow, some heretic, who vainly bends his bow and cannot withstand the arrows of God; and the swift of foot, who for the sharpness of his wit runs about through the testimonies of the Scriptures and strives to overwhelm the truth, but falls, because he trusts not in God but in his own feet; and the rider of the horse, of which it is said: “Vain is the horse for safety,” does not save his life, but perishing will hear: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will call upon the name of the Lord, our God.” And the stout of heart among the valiant shall flee away naked, “stripping” himself “of the old man with his deeds,” and, weighed down by no burden of sins, naked and strong he escapes death. Or, on the contrary, he who is naked, having lost the garment of Christ, is not saved by his strength in the day of battle, but turns his back before the enemy.
**“and the valiant shall not possess his strength, neither shall the strong”**
• Omri
• The valiant, that is, Baasha, who was most ready for war: when the Assyrians come, he will not be able to resist being taken. And note that all who are counted here had long been dead; but by them their sons and their whole stock, who were to be taken captive, are understood.
**“save”**
• when the Assyrians come
• We can say that when the Assyrians come, no one stout, no one valiant, no one swift will be able to be saved by his own strength.
**“his life”** — his life
2.15:
**“And he that holdeth the bow shall not stand”** — Jehu, who killed Joram king of Israel with an arrow
**“and the swift of foot shall not escape”** — Menahem, who fled into Egypt and sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians so as to be protected by them; but afterwards he is taken captive by the same.
**“neither shall the rider of the horse save his life”** — Pekah the son of Remaliah, who, joined to the Assyrians, laid waste much in Judea under King Ahaz, but afterwards with his people is taken captive by the Assyrians.
2.16: **“the stout of heart”** — Hoshea, who was the last of the kings of the ten tribes, who was valiant in this, that he wished to call the people back to the worship of God; but because he would not persevere in it, he afterwards went out naked from God’s burning: naked, because under him the ten tribes were taken captive.

3.1:
**“Hear the word that the Lord hath spoken concerning you”** — with the ears of understanding
**“the children of Israel”** — who see God, to whom properly the word of God is spoken
**“concerning the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt”** — where you served in clay and straw
**“concerning the whole”** — Lest the word seem to be directed to the ten tribes alone, he makes clear that it is directed to all who were called out of Egypt, that is, to the twelve tribes.
3.2:
**“You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore will I visit upon you all your iniquities”** — So that nothing goes unpunished
**“You only”** — Though I am the creator of all, I chose you alone as a peculiar people, that you might have knowledge of me; and therefore, because I have held you alone as mine, I will still visit, that is, correct, the iniquities of your idolatry, so that you may cease; or, if you do not cease, you may be punished the more heavily, for “the mighty shall be mightily tormented.”
3.3:
**“Shall two walk together except they be agreed?”** — The lion does not roam in the sown fields, or vineyards, or fruit trees, which praise God, but in the woods and untilled ground
**“Shall … walk”** — Jerome: As to the letter, two enemies will not go the same way. Mystically, the Jews and the Gentiles cannot walk through Christ, who is the way, unless they first agree to be made one in the corner stone himself, so that, united, they may ask the Father and obtain whatever they ask, and in this life fear no onset of the adversary. But if they are separated by discord, at once the roaring lion attacks them; and not only are they open to the lion’s bites, but the lion’s whelp will seize them and carry them to his dark den: for “every one that doth evil” loves the darkness. The third punishment of those in discord is that they lose the wings by which they were borne aloft, and, falling of their own accord into earthly things, are deservedly held by the fowler, the devil. The fourth punishment is that those in discord are caught in the snare that is set, not in heaven but on the earth; delivered from which they say: “Our soul hath been delivered, as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers”; of which the Apostle: “may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet.” The fifth punishment is that those set in the city of God are terrified by the sound of the trumpet, that is, of the divine Scripture, which threatens sinners with punishment in a great voice. The sixth punishment is that those in discord are afflicted by God.
3.4: **“Will a lion roar in the forest, if he have no prey? will the lion's whelp cry out of his den, if he have taken nothing?”** — When the lion is hungry and sees its prey, it roars; and when the wild beasts hear that voice, they stand rooted to the spot, stunned.
3.5:
**“Will”** — not
**“the bird fall into the snare upon the earth, if there be no fowler?”** — unless the fowler sets the snare, the bird is not snared
**“Shall the snare be taken up from the earth, before it hath taken somewhat?”** — not
3.6:
**“Shall there be evil in a city”** — That is, affliction, which is not unjust, but seems grievous and evil to the one who suffers it; hence: “Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof,” and: “I make peace, and create evil.”
**“Shall there be evil”** — As the things recalled above do not happen unless there is a definite cause, so there will be no tribulation unless it comes from the Lord, who also reveals it.
3.7:
**“For the Lord God doth nothing without revealing his secret”**
• or his correction
• speaking
**“For … doth nothing”** — Not that he reveals to the prophets everything he does or has done in heaven; but what he was about to do on earth he revealed to Noah, Abraham and Lot, so that those who heard of the punishments to come might be corrected, or be punished the more heavily. So now through Amos he announces in mercy their punishments to the Hebrews, so that they may not be punished.
*Jerome:* God does not reveal to the prophets all that he does in heaven, or what he did before, but what he is about to do on earth. He revealed the flood to Noah, the overthrow of Sodom to Abraham, the seven years’ famine to Joseph; so now he revealed to Amos what he was about to do to the ten tribes, so that, turned to penance, they might be set free from danger. In this God’s mercy is shown: for he who foretells a punishment does not wish to punish sinners.
3.8:
**“The lion shall roar”**
• And since God reveals it to the prophets, who would dare to keep silent what the Lord reveals? As no animal dares to make light of the lion’s roar.
• Jerome: This shepherd, who was used to fearing the lion, compares the fear of the Almighty to the lion’s roar. Some interpret the roaring lion as the devil and the Lord who speaks as the Saviour: so that as the one is heard for evil by those who are to perish, so the other is heard for good by those who are to be saved.
**“who will not fear?”** — Rare is he who does not fear.
**“The Lord God hath spoken, who shall not prophesy?”** — There are few men who would dare not to prophesy when the Lord commands.
3.9:
**“Publish it”**
• O prophets, what I am about to say
• Amos, sent specially to prophesy to the ten tribes, is now also bidden to make it known to Ashdod and to Egypt.
**“in the houses of Azotus”** — in the cities of the Philistines, which have no knowledge of God, so that they may judge for themselves whether I shall justly do what I threaten; let them first see the crimes, and afterwards judge of my sentence
**“and in the houses of the land of Egypt, and say: Assemble yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria”** — the city so called, which is set on a mountain, or the whole land of the ten tribes, which is all mountainous, and is so called from its chief city. Samaria is named from Shemer, the owner of the mountain on which it was founded.
**“Assemble yourselves”** — For each one fashions for himself and worships what he will. So the heretics fashion divers errors for themselves, who falsely claim to be keepers of God’s commandments and are on the mountain of pride; to look on whose madness the nations are called, which have no knowledge of God. For they slander the simple believers, while under the name of truth they worship a lie; and because they are outside the bounds of truth, they have not known to do the right thing, and store up for themselves the doctrines of iniquity, and shut up the deceived in their houses.
**“and behold the many follies in the midst thereof”** — In place of God they worship calves, and sacrifice their sons.
**“and them that suffer oppression in the inner rooms thereof”** — Not content with this crime, they slander the poor and the simple.
3.10:
**“And they have not known to do the right thing, saith the Lord”** — that is, they would not worship God
**“storing up”**
• Not gold or money, which is sometimes got by labour.
• Gathering iniquity, that is, sin, in their hearts from idolatry and the slandering of the wretched, and gathering the plunder of the poor by violence in their houses: for because they forsook the worship of God, “God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient.”
**“iniquity”** — false doctrines
**“and robberies in their houses”** — of those deceived by false error
3.11:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord God”** — because they have done this
**“shall be in tribulation”**
• by the Assyrians
• at the judgment, or daily by churchmen with the testimonies of the Scriptures
**“and shall be compassed about”** — the inhabitants of the land of the ten tribes will be surrounded by the enemy
**“The land”** — of the heretics
**“and … shall be taken away from thee”** — O Samaria
**“thy strength”** — of syllogisms and verbal subtlety, with which they made their doctrine firm
**“shall be spoiled”** — those who had strayed from the Church will be brought back
**“and thy houses”** — which thou hast gathered in thy houses from the tears of the wretched
3.12:
**“Thus saith the Lord: As if a shepherd should get out of the lion's mouth”** — who “goeth about, seeking whom he may devour”
**“As if”** — The prophet still takes his comparisons from the shepherd’s work. As small remnants of a sheep or ram are left by the lion, so of the inhabitants of Samaria few will remain who are not taken captive by the Assyrians.
**“two legs, or the tip of the ear”**
• he who has ears to hear
• in the ear, the mysteries of what is said
**“so shall … be taken out”** — almost consumed
**“the children of Israel”** — the ten tribes
**“that dwell in Samaria, in a place of a bed”** — resting on the help of the Syrians
**“and in the couch of Damascus”**
• Promising themselves victory
• Mystically: While the devil mangles the sheep of the Church, often two legs or the tip of an ear are snatched from his mouth, when we can follow God both with sure foot and with safe ears. For by the legs is signified the way of teaching, by the ears the mysteries of what is said; hence the apostles walk without shoes or any skin of a dead animal, and it is said to believers: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” This way the heretic and the devil block, so that we may fall in the way, which is Christ. But if a churchman and man of God comes, and, like Samson, kills the lion, we can walk to God with sure foot and safe ears.
• We read in the history and in Isaiah that Pekah the son of Remaliah hired Rezin king of Damascus to fight with him against Judah, and put all his hope in him. So as a man tired with labour rests on his bed, so the ten tribes rested on the help of the Syrians, and had hope of victory in the security of the inhabitants of Damascus, and strengthened their broken forces with the help of a neighbouring nation; but in vain, for both were taken captive by the Assyrians.
3.13:
**“Hear ye”**
• the things that are to come upon this people
• understand, O prophets
**“and testify”**
• announce it with solemn witness
• so that they may be without excuse
**“in the house of Jacob”** — of the ten tribes
3.14:
**“That in the day”** — when the captivity has come
**“when … to visit”** — to avenge
**“I shall begin … the transgressions of Israel”** — or wickednesses
**“I will visit upon him”** — rendering what he has deserved
**“and upon the altars of Bethel: and the horns of the altars shall be cut off”**
• I will avenge by destroying
• The altar of the Church is one; the altars of the heretics are as many as their schisms; yet they boast that they have one. The horns of their pride, that is, their arrogance, will be cut off.
**“the altars of Bethel”** — Which Jeroboam made for the golden calf; where, while he offered, a prophet came who said: “O altar, altar, thus saith the Lord” etc.; then the altar was split into two parts, and Jeroboam’s hand withered.
**“and shall fall to the ground”** — Broken as the Assyrian lays waste.
3.15:
**“And I will strike the winter house”** — of the heretics, who toil in abstinence and fasting
**“And I will strike”** — The princes of the ten tribes were so rich that they had two houses: one for winter, facing south, the other for summer, facing north, in which they lived luxuriously as the seasons changed. Ahab too is read to have built two houses of ivory.
**“with the summer house”** — who, for the greed of the belly, take in every pleasure
**“and the houses of ivory shall perish”** — which are built with the splendour of art and rhetoric
**“and many houses shall be destroyed”** — When the one truth comes, many lies will be destroyed throughout the whole world.
**“saith the Lord”** — Mystically, the winter house is the kingdom of Israel, in which is the cold of religion and of the worship of God, and divers whirlwinds, and a cruel storm; the summer house is the kingdom of Judea, in which is the warmth of religion, and the temple, and the holocaust morning and evening.

4.1:
**“Hear this word, ye fat kine”** — the heretics, who serve the belly and gluttony
**“Hear this word”** — He speaks to all the nobles of the ten tribes, that they should hear the words of the Lord; and he calls them, not bulls that love the herd, but mockingly fat kine, because, staying at home, they served the belly and gluttony, oppressing the needy and crushing the poor in judgment, so as to turn their goods to their own use.
**“that are in the mountains of Samaria”** — in pride, from which you crush the humble
**“you that oppress”** — because they say they keep God’s commandments, and promise themselves lofty things
**“the needy, and crush the poor”** — the simple of the Church, who do not seek the eloquence of the heretics and the riches of their arguments
**“that say to your masters”**
• your shepherds, that is, kings
• the princes of perverse doctrines
• Only give us leave and command us, and we will plunder the houses of the poor, so as to turn their goods to our own use. He does not say “we will eat,” but “we will drink,” by which he marks them as given to drunkenness, which overturns the mind and breeds errors and lust.
**“Bring”** — Unless the greater give them power, the lesser will have nothing to devour. The same is to be understood of the heretics: for the lesser are made drunk by the teaching of the greater.
4.2:
**“The Lord God hath sworn”** — Every word of God, who does not lie, ought to be taken as an oath.
**“by his holiness”** — by himself, or by his Son, or by some chosen angel or man
**“that lo”** — as if in the present
**“the days shall come upon”**
• of captivity and distress
• of judgment, or of punishments
**“you”**
• stripped of the things for which you sinned
• O fat kine
**“when they shall lift … up”** — the Assyrians, or the demons
**“they shall lift you up”** — He keeps to the metaphor of the kine, whose flesh is wont to be lifted on poles. It signifies that when the Assyrians come, they will be taken in battle and carried off by right of victory.
**“on pikes, and what shall remain of you in boiling pots”**
• that you may be boiled down in the fire of tribulation
• that you may be burnt in the fires of Gehenna
**“in … pots”** — Those overcome in battle they will drive into the fortified cities, which are compared to boiling pots, because famine and pestilence will force the peoples shut up in them to come out and go into captivity.
4.3:
**“And you shall go out at the breaches one”**
• understand: kine
• Through the openings of the pots, that is, of the cities, because, when the cities are destroyed, they will go into captivity. Or openings, as though the ways were already prepared by which you will be led captive into Armenia, which is a region beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians.
**“over against the other”** — kine
**“one over against”** — According to the idiom of the Hebrews, “one over against the other” is put for what we call “mutually” or “in turn.”
**“and you shall be cast forth into Armon”** — which is called Armenia
4.4:
**“Come ye to Bethel”**
• Where the golden calf is.
• The wicked go into Bethel, that is, the house of God, which is the Church, and there they act wickedly against God by trampling on his commandments; and into Galgal, which means “revelation,” because they claim for themselves the knowledge of the Scriptures, and, proud of it, flow into every vice. They also bring in their victims in the morning, and their tithes on the third day, transformed into an angel of light; and they squeeze the threefold understanding of the Scriptures into the sense of a single day. For Scripture ought first to be understood according to the letter, so that moral precepts may be drawn from it; secondly according to allegory, that is, the spiritual understanding; thirdly according to the blessedness of things to come. But the heretics, despising the first and second day, put together for themselves certain spiritual fictions, laying a roof on top without foundation or walls; and, withdrawing from the Church, they preach to others the leaven they have conceived in their heart, and this not in error but from love of evil. Hence God threatens the proud: I have given you dulness of teeth.
**“Come ye to”** — He speaks ironically; as if to say: till now you have sacrificed to idols of your own accord; now, with the captivity at hand, finish what you have begun, so that the more shameless you are, the more just my vengeance on you may appear.
**“and do wickedly”** — Against God, trampling on his commandments.
**“to Galgal”**
• come
• which is a place of idolatry
**“and multiply transgressions”**
• there, against God, to whom you have preferred idols
• whatever you do there is transgression
**“and bring in the morning your victims”**
• quickly, before the captivity comes
• so that there be no delay in crime
**“your tithes in three days”**
• according to Symmachus, on the third day your tithes; understand: offer
• what you offered on the first day keep to the third day, so that it may be unclean
**“in three days”** — There were certain sacrifices of which, if anything was kept to the next day, both the offering and what remained were judged unclean. There were others of which, if anything remained to the third day, it became unclean. That is: offer unclean victims.
4.5:
**“And offer … with leaven”** — understand: bread, which is forbidden in the law
**“a sacrifice of praise”** — with thanksgiving
**“and call free offerings”** — And call such offerings free, which belongs to gladness; for you do this not in error but out of zeal and curiosity.
**“and proclaim it”** — So that you may seem not only to have done it but to have taught others.
**“for so you would do”** — I command it so because so you would have it.
**“the children of Israel”** — the ten tribes
4.6:
**“Whereupon I also have given you dulness of teeth”** — Famine, when the teeth grow dull from being unused to eating, and lose the strength to eat.
**“have given you”** — According to Ezekiel: “every man that shall eat the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.” So the heretics, abusing the testimonies of the Scriptures, eat them unripe and without their sweetness, and so lose the strength of their teeth, so that they cannot eat hard things and send them into the belly to profit the whole body. And this dulness, and the want of the bread “which came down from heaven,” he says, is to be sent in all their places, so that they may suffer want of the word of God.
**“in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places”** — This great famine, which wore down the land of the ten tribes, happened in the times of Elijah.
**“yet you have not”** — And though I did all these things, not out of cruelty but for your correction, yet you were not corrected; according to that saying: “In vain have I struck your children, they have not received correction.”
4.7:
**“I also”**
• so that you should suffer the danger not only of hunger but also of thirst
• I gave not only dulness and want of bread, but also:
• God withholds the dew of divine wisdom from the heretics, and commands the clouds not to rain on them the rain three months before the harvest, so that they may not come to the mystical fruit of the mystery of the Trinity; and he rains on the one Church, not on the gatherings of the heretics. And if one of them, driven by want, comes back to the city of God to draw water, he is not filled, because he has come not by will but by necessity.
**“have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and … upon one city”** — the Church
**“I caused it to rain …, and … upon another city”** — of the heretics
**“caused it not to rain. One piece”** — the unity of the Church, which is the Lord’s portion
**“was rained upon”** — and brought forth fruit
**“the rain”** — Which is called the latter rain in the fields of Palestine, which must water the grass, so that it may yield wheat, at the time when there are three months to harvest, that is, May, June and July: at this time rain is needed. And lest it be thought to happen by the law of nature and the course of the stars, he added: and I caused it to rain upon one city. This want of water too happened under Elijah.
4.8:
**“And you”** — driven by thirst
**“two and three cities went”**
• on which I did not rain, and in which the cisterns were dry
• divers heretics
**“to one city”**
• the Church, from which they went out
• On which I rained, and which had water
**“to drink water”**
• living water
• from its wells and cisterns
**“and were not filled”** — as the water failed
**“yet you returned not to me”**
• though I did this for your correction, like a physician
• because they return not by will but by necessity
4.9:
**“I struck you”**
• I afflicted
• For this; as if to say: what was left over from the drought I consumed with a burning wind.
• The heretics are struck with the burning of lust; hence the Apostle: “it is better to marry than to burn.” They are struck also with anger and envy, by which the redness of the blood is changed into paleness, because they take away the true understanding, and so corrupt everything that even sweet honey seems bitter: for whatever pleased them before in the Church seems bitter to them now they have become heretics. They multiply gardens, that is, doctrines, into which Naboth would not have his vineyard changed. The heretics also do good things, so as to mix poisons with honey; so they boast that they have vineyards and olive groves and fig groves. But “their vines are of the vineyard of Sodom.”
**“with a burning wind, and with mildew”** — Aurugo, that is, rubigo or erugo, which in Joel is called the palmer-worm. Others have it thus: aurugo, that is, rubigo, which in Joel is called erugo; which comes about when, at night, dew or rain falls on the tender ears, and as the sun grows hot they turn red, and the still tender grains become empty. Aurugo is also the name of a disease that arises in man from an abundance of corrupt gall, which corrupts the blood and turns it pale, and turns all sweet things to bitterness.
**“your many gardens”** — the ten tribes were zealous in multiplying these, and the Jews stirred up God’s anger against themselves
**“and your vineyards”** — not God’s
**“your olive groves”** — which are not of good olives
**“and fig groves”** — this is the fig tree that Jesus cursed and withered
**“the palmerworm hath eaten up”** — the more harmful one, which does not fly away, but consumes everything
**“yet you returned not to me, saith the Lord”** — Though you suffered all these things, yet you did not return.
4.10:
**“I sent death upon you in the way of Egypt”** — While you sought help from the Egyptians, I killed your young men with the sword of the Syrians; and when they had been killed, their horses, which they had multiplied against God’s commands, were led away captive by the victors, and the stench of the dying offended the nostrils of the living.
**“I sent … upon”** — Jerome: Daily God sends death on those who walk in the way of Egypt, that is, through the evils of the world, so that, their members “which are upon the earth” being mortified, Christ may live in them. God also strikes in the wicked whatever is proud and perverse in youth, so that it may not reach old age; and he hands the horses over to captivity, so that they may not slide down the precipices into hell; and he makes the stench come up, so that they may know their sins. But not even so do they return.
**“I slew your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses: and I made the stench of your camp to come up”** — or of the horses
4.11:
**“I destroyed some of you, as God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrha”** — In those of you who perished by the sword of the Assyrians.
**“I destroyed some of you”** — The Sodomites died in body and soul, and these likewise for the same sin. Lot alone was set free with his daughters, like a half-burnt brand, having lost part of his body, that is, his wife, with whom he was one flesh. So, compared with those who perished by famine and sword, few remained; and they too lost part of their body, that is, the temporal things by which the body is sustained and in which they delighted.
**“and you were”** — In those of you who remained.
**“as a firebrand plucked out of the burning”** — that is, a brand
**“yet you returned not to me, saith the Lord”** — It is the last medicine, for the ten tribes and the heretics and all sinners: that when, struck in many ways, they have not come to their senses, at last the divine fire should overthrow their buildings, and they themselves be set free like a firebrand plucked out of the burning and escape naked; according to that saying: “If any man's work burn, he shall suffer loss.” For he who has the works of Sodom and is saved by fire is plucked like a brand out of the burning, the works of Sodom being first destroyed by fire. Hence we read in the prophet: Sodom shall be restored to its ancient state; for he who by his vice was joined to the Sodomites, if the works of Sodom have burnt in him, will be restored to his ancient state.
4.12:
**“Therefore I will do these things to thee, O Israel: and after … these things”** — which I think on and threaten
**“Therefore”** — Since you despised what is past, at least be corrected by what is to be brought on you. And he does not say what he will do, but leaves them in suspense, so that they may think whatever worse things could be brought on them, and at least through this fear return.
**“I shall have done … to thee”** — therefore
**“be prepared to meet thy God, O Israel”** — Be prepared to meet, so that thou mayest eagerly receive the deliverer who comes to thee through the mystery of the Incarnation; or be prepared to call upon the Lord thy God, that he may set thee free from the present tribulation, for “every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
4.13:
**“For behold he that formeth the mountains”** — who is he? he it is that formeth the mountains
**“and createth the wind”** — every creature, or the saints in faith
**“createth the wind”** — The breath of this air, or the soul of man; and he declares his word to those he has created; according to what he says: “For the Lord God doth nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets.”
**“and declareth”** — through the prophets
**“to man”** — to the chosen man
**“his word …, he that maketh the morning mist, and walketh”**
• The work he himself is about to do; or he declares himself to the elect.
• Mist is the richness of the air, and signifies the richness of faith, which is conceived in the morning, that is, at the time of baptism. The high places of the earth are the virtues, or the saints set on the summit of the virtues; but God surpasses the virtues of all, and walks in the hearts of his own.
**“that maketh the morning”** — According to the letter, in the morning he makes mist come over the earth, and he walks upon the high places of the earth, who is within all things and outside all things.
**“upon the high places of the earth”** — That is, the minds of those whose “conversation is in heaven,” who “walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.”

5.1:
**“Hear ye this word, which I take up concerning you for a lamentation”**
• Amos, out of the affection of love, like David and Samuel mourning Saul.
• Mystically, he weeps for those who see God with the mind, and afterwards cease to serve him and do not return to the true light of God.
**“Hear this word”** — As to the letter, the prophet laments the ten tribes, who for their sins are to be taken captive beyond the mountains of the Persians, so that they will never again return to their own place. They are called a virgin because in the patriarchs and prophets they were joined with a chaste mind to one bridegroom; which virginity they had already corrupted, committing adultery with idols.
**“The house of Israel”**
• of the ten tribes
• The house of Israel; Septuagint: is fallen; no more shall the virgin of Israel rise again in her land.
5.2:
**“is fallen”**
• into perpetual captivity
• by sinning
**“and it shall rise no more”**
• being so, because corrupted
• a spirit that goes of itself and does not return; it falls of itself, and rises again through God
• He does not deny that she can rise again; but the virgin of Israel will not rise again, because, having once strayed, even if she is carried back on the shoulders of the loving shepherd, she has not the same glory as he who never strayed from God. Hence by the prophet: I would rather the penance of the sinner than his death. He does not compare penance with the holiness of the Church, but it becomes better when compared with death and hell.
**“The virgin of Israel”** — who once was joined to the Lord as a virgin
**“is cast down”**
• laid low
• or killed by the sword of the Assyrians
**“upon her land”** — through idolatry
**“there is none to raise her up”** — There is no one to bring her back to life by his intercession, as Moses appeased God’s anger. And why? Because she will not turn to God by penance. And this is what he says: For thus saith the Lord God: because you would not be converted, O ten tribes, when the Assyrians come, a tenth part of you will remain in the first captivity, the rest will be taken captive; and if that tenth, remaining in the land of promise, does not repent, it too will be wholly taken captive when the Assyrians come. And so it was done.
5.3:
**“For thus saith the Lord God: The city, out of which came forth”** — in time of peace
**“The city, out of which”** — Jerome: The unit holds the mystery of the one God, and to be in this number is the first blessedness, for God is one and true. The second is in the second number, that is, in ten; the third in the third, that is, in a hundred. For as ten is completed by ten units, so a hundred by ten tens, and so a thousand by ten hundreds; by which the fourth and highest or firmest blessedness is marked. If anyone, having lost it, does penance, from that fourth, the thousand, he hardly returns to the third, the hundred; and if he is in the hundred, he hardly returns to the second, that is, the ten.
