And so it comes about that the virgin of Israel, who had strayed, has no one to raise her up: for he who has once departed from the unit, and lost the virginity he had with the one husband, will not be able to recover his first state and the blessedness of the unit; and it is hardly granted him to return from a thousand to a hundred, and from a hundred to ten.
**“a thousand”** — men
**“there shall be left in it a hundred”** — when the Assyrians come
**“and out of which there came a hundred, there shall be left in it ten, in the house of Israel”** — of the ten tribes
5.4:
**“For thus saith the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek ye me, and you shall live”**
• having threatened most harshly, the loving father gently calls them back to penance
• by living well, believing, persevering, and conquering in the works of justice, you who were dead in idolatry
5.5:
**“But seek not Bethel”** — so as to worship the calf there
**“and go not into Galgal”** — Which is a city at the edge of the possession of two of the ten tribes, a place to which the ten tribes went out to worship idols
**“to Bersabee”** — by this place it is noted that some of the two tribes too worshipped idols
**“neither shall you pass over”** — otherwise: you shall pass over
**“for Galgal shall go into captivity”** — and I forbid this because the inhabitants of these two cities will be taken captive by the Assyrians; and by them the ten tribes, which are to be taken captive, are understood
**“and Bethel shall be unprofitable”** — Of Beersheba he says nothing, because when the ten tribes were conquered, Beersheba, which was in the tribe of Judah, was not destroyed at that time.
**“seek not”** — Mystically, Bethel means “the house of God.” He seeks it who says: “The temple of the Lord,” and trusts in buildings that are to be destroyed; he seeks it too who follows the letter that kills, not the spirit that gives life. Galgal is the place where the people was circumcised the second time; he goes into it who, after the coming of Christ, wishes to be circumcised again. Galgal also means “revelation”: he goes into it who strives after things above him and promises himself the knowledge of revelations and of higher things. He passes over also to Beersheba, or, according to the Septuagint, to the well of the oath, from which the Samaritan woman longs to draw the water that does not drive out thirst, not knowing him out of whose belly “shall flow rivers of living water.” For Galgal, that is, the circumcision of the flesh, will be led captive by the circumcision of the heart, and Bethel, which you think the house of God, will not be at all, or will be unprofitable.
5.6:
**“Seek ye”** — He who seeks by faith begins to live by the works of justice.
**“the Lord”** — who is life
**“Seek ye the Lord”** — After the words of the Lord, the prophet adds his own warning, urging them to return to the Lord.
**“and live”**
• through him
• you who are now dead
**“lest the house of Joseph be burnt”** — the ten tribes
**“with fire”** — of the devil
**“and it shall devour”** — the fire of captivity
**“and there shall be none to quench”** — who can set it free from captivity
**“Bethel”**
• those who worship the calf in Bethel
• Jeroboam, who made the calves and separated the people from the house of David, signifies the heretics, who by crafted speech fashion, as it were, golden images, and worship what they have fashioned. To them it is said: Seek ye the Lord, and live. Unless they do this, they are burnt with the burnings of the devil; and this fire none of their masters can put out, for they too are heretics, who falsely call themselves the house of God.
5.7:
**“You that turn … into wormwood”** — into the bitterness of idolatry
**“judgment”** — by which you ought to discern between the Creator and the creature
**“and … justice”** — the just Lord; taking up iniquity, or clinging to earthly things, you forsake him who “shall judge the world in equity”
**“forsake … in the land”**
• set in your land
• and
5.8:
**“Seek him that maketh Arcturus”** — Boötes
**“him that maketh Arcturus”** — Hearing these things, let us not run back to the fables of the poets, but understand the Creator of all, the Almighty.
**“and Orion”**
• The saints, shining with divers brightness
• as others the splendour, namely the shining stars
• By Arcturus, which is made of seven stars, is signified the Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit; by Orion, which rises in winter and by its rising stirs up storms, are signified the martyrs, who in a time of unbelief preach to the unbelieving and stir up against themselves the storm of persecution.
• Speaking of Arcturus and Orion, he preferred to call them by the names the Gentiles devised rather than by Hebrew names, lest they seem barbarous to us. By this he also marks that this prophecy was to be read by the Gentiles.
**“and that turneth”** — for his elect
**“into morning”** — into clear light, or prosperity
**“darkness”** — of ignorance, or of tribulation
**“and that changeth day”**
• of happiness
• those who were thought day are changed into the night of sins
• And … day into: From the sixth hour, as a figure of the blindness of the Jews, day was turned into night for the crucifiers; the light too which rose in the law and the prophets was turned into darkness for those of whom it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened.”
**“into night”** — of tribulation
**“that calleth the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The Lord is his name”** — he lifts the bitter waters by the heat of the sky, and, turned into the sweet taste of rain, pours them out to water the earth
**“that calleth”** — The waters of the sea are sinners, whom he pours out so that, turned to sweetness, they may preach to others; in whom whatever there was of earth and bitterness is boiled away by the heat of the true sun.
5.9:
**“He that with a smile”** — he threatens with a smile
**“destruction”** — of captivity
**“upon the strong”** — so that he who is strong for evil may be made weak for good
**“and waste”** — The plundering of goods
**“bringeth … upon the mighty”**
• the people of the ten tribes, and all who trust in worldly power or in heresy
• He that with a smile: he returns to the present time; as if to say: he who is the Creator of all threatens Samaria with captivity, he smiles as one who is angry, and, opening his lips a little, pretends to laugh, so as to show the greatness of his anger.
5.10:
**“They have hated”**
• yet they
• The ancients sat in the gates to give judgment, so that the countryman coming to a lawsuit might not be frightened by the unfamiliar sight of the citizens, or so that the citizen might not go far from the city.
**“have”** — which is a grave sin
**“in the gate”**
• in judgment, or in the virtues
• The gates of death are the vices, the gates of life the virtues. The just man, standing in the gate of the virtues, is hated if he rebukes the wicked man standing in the gate of death.
**“him that rebuketh”** — some prophet sent by God for their correction
**“and have abhorred him that speaketh perfectly”** — who rebukes, not out of hatred, but out of love, as God commanded
5.11:
**“Therefore”**
• for the things said before
• and also
**“because you robbed the poor”**
• who has not what is needed to live
• Therefore because: lest Israel think it was to be punished for idolatry alone, he adds the other evils.
**“and the choice prey”** — namely whatever he had that pleased you
**“took … from him”** — for your own use
**“houses”** — where you may stay secure
**“you shall build … with square stone”** — having stripped the poor, you have faced your walls with marble
**“and shall not dwell in them”**
• because you build them from the plunder of the poor
• carried off by sudden captivity or death
• also
**“you shall plant most delightful vineyards”** — providing for the delight of drinking
**“and shall not drink the wine of them”** — Heretics plunder the understanding of the poor, who do not know how to answer back, and whatever good work they had prepared. They also build houses out of the arrangement of words, but they are overthrown by the men of the Church. They plant most delightful vineyards too, when they falsely claim to possess the mysteries of Christ. But they drink no wine except that which is “the gall of dragons,” a fury past healing.
5.12:
**“Because”** — therefore you shall not dwell, you shall not drink
**“I know”** — from whom nothing is hidden
**“your manifold crimes, and your grievous sins”**
• not only many, but also grievous enough to provoke the wrath of God
• because
**“enemies”** — O princes of the ten tribes, you are the enemies
**“of the just”** — of the just man, or of justice
**“taking bribes, and oppressing the poor”**
• from the powerful, so that the poor man is condemned in judgement
• “their right hand is filled with gifts”
**“taking bribes”** — Against the truth of judgement; hence: “gifts blind the eyes of the wise.” Heretics accept these so as to turn the severity of the Scriptures, which promise torments to sinners, into blessedness, and promise prosperity to the rich; yet to the poor they are harsh and stern. A man of the Church, seeing them incorrigible, withholds correction, lest he seem to “give that which is holy to dogs.”
**“in the gate”** — in judgement
5.13:
**“Therefore the prudent shall keep silence at that time”** — understanding the many impieties in that which is called the house of God
**“at that time”** — when he sees that his correction does no good, since the captivity is already at hand, from which they will not be able to be set free.
**“for it is an evil time”** — because there is no one who will listen to him who judges rightly
5.14:
**“Seek ye good, and not evil”**
• that is, the world, which “is seated in wickedness”
• Seek good: God, who is the good shepherd, and not an idol or the devil; or good, that is, judge right judgement, and not falsehood or oppression.
**“that you may live: and”** — thus
**“the Lord the God … will be”** — who is able to save
**“of hosts … with you, as you have said”** — As you are wont to boast that God is with you because you are of the race of Abraham; but “if you be the children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham,” that is, hate evil.
5.15:
**“Hate evil, and love good”** — it is not enough to have warned once
**“And you”** — after these things
**“establish judgment in the gate: it may be the Lord the God of hosts may have mercy”** — as if to say: if you do these things, perhaps
**“on the remnant of Joseph”**
• so that the ten tribes may escape captivity
• Allegorically. God commands heretics to leave their error and return to the Church, and, hating their former teachings, to love the truth in the Church, and to do true judgement in the gates, whether of the vices by leaving them, or of the virtues by following them; and so they will be sure of mercy.
**“Hate evil”** — He hates evil who is not only not overcome by pleasure, but hates the works of pleasure; he loves good who does what is good not unwillingly and for fear of the laws, but out of love of the good itself. Hence: “God loveth a cheerful giver.”
5.16:
**“Therefore”** — I have often warned you about the good, but because you would not do my commandments, therefore you shall be afflicted.
**“thus saith the Lord the God of hosts the sovereign Lord: In every street”** — there shall be
**“street”** — of the cities of the ten tribes; or the streets through which the captives will be led; or the streets, that is, the flowing out of the desires, which streets signify.
**“wailing: and in all places that are without”** — in the hamlets or forts that are outside the city “alas” shall be said: that is, to those remaining in their own land or to those going into captivity; or in body and soul; or in the present and in the future
**“they shall say: Alas, alas!”** — when the Assyrians come
**“and they shall call the husbandman to mourning, and such as are skilful in lamentation to lament”**
• He speaks after the custom of the province, that those who know how to lead the singing that stirs up tears may rouse others to wailing, so that together they may weep for their misery, and that in every place where there was gladness before, there may be the spring of tears.
• Heretics and Gentiles have, in their fictions and fables, broad streets which lead to death; and it follows fittingly: “and in all places that are without, they shall say: Alas.” For those who are in the Church will not hear the “alas” of eternal damnation; but if they sin, a lamentation will be taken up over them. Heretics too have husbandmen in whose fields thorns spring up, who are called to mourning, because they were willing to mourn their own sins or those of others. Otherwise: a man of the Church, able to call to penance, mourns with the affection of pity over those who have not done penance.
5.17:
**“And in all vineyards there shall be wailing”** — they have many ways, not that one which “leadeth to life”
**“because”** — all these things shall come to pass, because
**“I will pass through in the midst of thee”** — angered at remaining with you, I will punish you
5.18:
**“Woe to them that desire”**
• to the two tribes
• Lest this prophet seem to have wholly neglected the two tribes, he now directs his prophecy to them. For it had been prophesied that they would be taken captive, and would return after seventy years and have greater happiness; so they were wont to wish that the captivity would come, so that, once it was over, the happiness would come too. The prophet meets this, saying that that prosperity would not be given them as soon as they returned, but that afterwards they would suffer much: from Nabuchodonosor, the lion; or from Assuerus, as it were the bear; or from Antiochus Epiphanes, who like a serpent will bite them in Judea. But the prophecy of that prosperity was to be fulfilled in the time of Christ.
• Allegorically. Many, so as to seem just, say that they desire the day of judgement, or of their death, so that they may begin to be with Christ. But to these he says there is woe, because no one is without sin, and by the very fact that they do not fear for themselves they deserve punishment. If they were truly just, they ought not to desire the judgement in which the sins of the reprobate will be gravely punished; they ought rather to be anxious for them. But these are like a man who, put in some strait, wants his whole country overthrown so that he alone may be set free, without compassion for the calamity of others. Such a man is handed over to the lion, that is, the devil; to the bear, that is, the devil's ministers; to the serpent, that is, his own conscience accusing him of having trusted in his own strength. Or by the lion, the bear and the serpent can be understood different kinds of torment, with which this proud and merciless man will be punished in the life to come.
**“the day of the Lord”** — of the captivity
**“to what end”** — do you desire it to come
**“is it for you? the day of the Lord is darkness”** — tribulation
5.19:
**“As if”** — so shall it come upon you
**“a man should flee from the face of a lion”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“and a bear should meet him”** — Assuerus, who, as we read in Esther, commanded that all the Jews be killed in one day in Susan
**“or enter into the house, and lean with his hand upon the wall, and a serpent should bite him”** — When you have returned, and, secure, have begun to build the temple at Darius's command, so that you may rest your weary hands upon the walls, then Alexander of Macedon will come, or Antiochus Epiphanes, who, dwelling not in Babylon or in Susan, but in the temple and within the borders of the holy land, will bite you like a serpent. So where they thought there was a remedy, there they will find a greater punishment.
5.20:
**“Shall not the day of the Lord be darkness”** — of the captivity, or of the judgement
**“and not light: and obscurity, and no brightness in it?”**
• Darkness and obscurity are the contraries of light and brightness; so are grief and sadness of gladness and happiness. These befell those going into captivity, or will befall heretics on the day of judgement.
• All these things fit the heretics, who flee the lion and run into the bear, and, entering the house which they think the Church of God, lean upon walls they made themselves, and are bitten by the serpent. Darkness snatches away their day; God hates their sacrifices; and as often as they gather in the name of the Lord, God turns his nostrils from their stench; and if they offer holocausts of fasting and of many such things, God does not look on them.
5.21:
**“I hate, and have rejected your festivities”** — the Pasch, Pentecost and the like
**“I hate, and have rejected”** — Properly this is said against Juda and against those of Israel who kept the ceremonies for God, who offered to God with the hand but to demons with the heart; and therefore the odour of their sacrifice was turned into a stench rather than a sweet savour. He is not speaking here of the offerings of calves which they made in Dan and Bethel, but of those that were offered in the temple.
**“and I will not receive the odour of your assemblies”**
• These things are plainly said to the Jews, who, though the temple is destroyed, believe that they offer to God; but God casts them off and cares nothing for the assemblies of those who say: Crucify.
• Morally. At any time, sins are not redeemed by alms made out of plunder.
5.22:
**“And if you offer me holocausts, and your gifts”** — not mine; because even if you offer to me with your hands, you offer to demons with your heart
**“I will not receive them: neither will I regard the vows of your fat beasts”** — for their fat
5.23:
**“Take away from me the tumult of thy songs”** — That people was wont to use the lyre and the organ and other such things as a figure of things to come.
**“Take away from me the tumult”** — A tumult is a confused sound, such as is commonly heard in the market place. The canticles which David composed, and which the Levites used in praising God, he scornfully calls a tumult, because they had been wont to offer the same to idols. The tradition of the Jews too, and the psalms they sing in the synagogues, and the praise that heretics compose, are reckoned a confused sound by the Lord, because “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.”
5.24:
**“But … shall be revealed”**
• to the eyes of all
• Because you have offered to idols the sacrifices that were owed to me, I will make my judgement and my justice manifest to all, when, you having been led into captivity, the land will be left bare of its inhabitants; as water running down passes on where it finds a sloping place, and leaves bare the places it covered before. This water is also called a torrent, because no one can withstand it.
**“judgment … as water”** — vengeance
**“and justice”** — understand: shall sweep all things away
5.25:
**“Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me in the desert for forty years, O house of Israel?”**
• no, but rather you carried
• From the time when the head of the calf was made in the desert, all that the children of Israel did or offered is shown to have been done for idols and not for God. And if we read that afterwards they offered some things to God, they offered them not willingly but out of fear of punishment, and so they did not please God; and not only in the desert, but in the land of promise too, whenever there was occasion, in their hearts they went back into Egypt. Moloch is the idol of the Ammonites, and means “king”; and it signifies Lucifer, whom the Saracens worship still.
5.26:
**“But you carried a tabernacle”**
• which had been made for me by Moses
• for the honour
**“for your Moloch”** — elsewhere: god
**“and the image”** — understand: you carried
**“of your idols”** — for they did not worship only one idol, nor do heretics hold only one heresy
**“the star of your god”** — that is, you carried the image of a star, namely of Lucifer
**“which you made to yourselves”**
• for you did not receive them from God, but invented them in your own mind
• Mystically, he carries the tabernacle of Moloch who makes himself the dwelling of a demon, when he ought to be the temple of God; and under the name of Christ invents false doctrines, and worships the star of him who “transformeth himself into an angel of light.”
5.27:
**“And I will cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus”**
• to the Assyrians, and beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians
• Damascus means “drinking blood,” or “the blood of sackcloth,” so that by penance we may be called to drink the blood of the Lord. But heretics are carried beyond Damascus, so that they do not drink the blood of Christ, but are made drunk with the golden cup from the hand of Babylon.

6.1:
**“Woe to you that are wealthy in Sion”** — who give yourselves up to riches in the two tribes
**“and to you that have confidence in the mountain of Samaria”** — in the strength of the people of the ten tribes
**“ye great men, heads of the people”** — who are the great men and heads, that is, the princes among the people
**“that go in with state into the house of Israel”** — showing the swelling of the mind in the body, so that you may be honoured by men
**“Woe to you that”** — These things refer to the two tribes and to the ten, but most of all to the great men of both peoples. Mystically, woe is proclaimed to heretics, who think themselves wealthy while they call the Church of God poor and abject, and who are proud as though they were the keepers of God's commandments. They are also bidden to consider the philosophies of the various nations, and they will find them narrower than the bounds of Holy Scripture, which has filled the whole world. Then he sets out from what evils he bids them pass over: namely, you who come to the day of damnation, a hardship to those who suffer it; who rejoice in this world to be raised up by iniquity; who, heedless of your salvation, grow sluggish in fleshly uncleanness; who eat no solid food to strengthen your powers, but soft and tender food, such as a lamb or a calf fattened on milk alone. You who also, so that all things may serve your pleasure, clap your hands to the sound of the organ, not to the praise of God as David did. You who drink the wine of error from the bowls of divine Scripture. You who too, though without knowledge of God, claim for yourselves the dignity of the priesthood, calling yourselves the anointed of God. These men too are moved by no pain over the death of those whom they have deceived.
6.2:
**“Pass ye over”** — you who are the great men and heads of the people
**“to Chalane”** — which is a city of the faithless
**“and see, and go from thence into Emath the great: and go down”** — you who dwell in mount Sion and in the mountain of Samaria
**“into Geth”** — the city
**“of the Philistines”** — who live in the plains
**“And you”** — understand: go down
**“to all the best kingdoms of these”** — such as Azotus and Gaza
**“if their border be larger than your border”**
• consider whether their kingdom is better or larger than yours
• Pass ye over to Chalane. The Septuagint: House of Israel, pass over and see, and go on to the many walls, and go down to the winepress of those who fall as they drink.
**“into Emath”** — This is a city of Syria, and is called Antioch; he calls it “the great” to distinguish it from the other Emath, which by another name is called Epiphania. In Emath Nabuchodonosor killed the sons of Sedecias, and blinded Sedecias himself.
6.3:
**“You that”** — you, I say, of the people of Israel
**“are separated”** — from your land
**“unto the evil day”** — of the captivity, which brings hard evils to those who bear it
**“and that approach to the throne of iniquity”** — you who are soon to be made subject to the rule of Sennacherib, or of Nabuchodonosor, or of the Romans, under whom you are to suffer many evils; and yet now I say:
6.4:
**“You that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton”** — so as to join sleep to lust
**“on your couches”** — soft
**“that eat the lambs out of the flock”** — not to sustain nature but for luxury, since whatever is best or fat in the flocks they give up to your gluttony
**“and the calves out of the midst of the herd”**
• fattened ones, while you offer me the sickly and weak
• You that sleep. They abounded in such riches that they would satisfy their lust even on beds of ivory, or of gold.
6.5:
**“You that sing to the sound of the psaltery: they have thought themselves to have instruments of music like David”**
• that is, you think you are heard because of your singing
• As David had vessels, that is, instruments of the art of music, with which he pleased God, so these think they please God merely by the clashing of sounds, while “their heart is far from” God; but David pleased him with his voice too, and above all with his heart.
**“You that sing”** — For them luxury and gluttony are not enough unless you soothe your ears with the songs of pipes and psaltery and lyre; so that the many instruments David devised for the worship of God, you turn to pleasure and luxury.
6.6:
**“That drink wine in bowls”** — not to quench thirst, but to overwhelm the mind
**“and anoint themselves with the best ointments: and they are not concerned for the affliction of Joseph”** — not with pure oil to relieve the pains of the body, but with costly ointments
**“and they are not concerned”** — And while the princes abound so in riches, they do not care if any of the people of the ten tribes perish, but despise them as though brute beasts were dying.
6.7:
**“Wherefore”** — because the princes do this
**“now”** — in the present; the punishment will not be put off to the future
**“they shall go captive”** — the princes will be led away captive first, because “the mighty shall be mightily tormented”
**“at the head of them that go into captivity”** — in the forefront
**“and the faction of the luxurious ones shall be taken away”** — then the assembly of the wanton people will be taken captive, so that those who were of one mind in their pleasures may be punished together.
6.8:
**“The Lord God hath sworn by his own soul, saith the Lord the God of hosts: I detest”** — I cast off and abhor; either the ten tribes in particular, or the twelve in general
**“the pride”** — against God and against Christ
**“of Jacob, and I hate his houses, and I will deliver up”** — to the Assyrians or to the Romans
**“the city with the inhabitants thereof”**
• Samaria, or Jerusalem, or any cities of that land
• The Lord has sworn that he hates the insults of the heretics, because whatever they say deserves hatred, and that he will destroy the city and its inhabitants, that is, the people and the teachers. And if there are some who seem to differ from their wickedness, yet are deceived by living and talking with them, they die the death that leads to hell; for their neighbours bury their bones, that is, their strength, of whom it is said: “Let the dead bury their dead.” But he who stays wholly outside, not entering the dead man's house but rather casting out the dead and calling them to penance, commands him who burns the dead to hold his peace, because he must not name the good name of God with a defiled mouth. Hence it is said: “But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices,” etc.
**“The Lord God hath sworn”** — Every word of his ought to be taken as an oath; and he speaks after our manner, not that he has a soul as we do, but by the name of “soul” the affection of the divine will is shown. So he swore by his own will.
6.9:
**“And if there remain ten men in one house”** — if they remain from the captivity
**“they also shall die”** — by famine and pestilence
6.10:
**“And … shall take him up”** — him who has died
**“a man's kinsman”** — the neighbour who remains
**“and shall burn him, that he may carry the bones out of the house”** — for burial, because for the multitude of the dead the bodies cannot be carried out whole, nor a grave be given to each body
**“and he shall say to him that is in the inner rooms of the house”** — he who has been called, when he is now tired of carrying
**“to him”** — to him who has stayed in the inner room of the house, and who called him to burn the bones of the dead.
**“Is there yet any with thee?”** — understand: some body for me to burn
**“And he shall answer”** — from within, he who was carrying out the bodies
**“There is an end”** — I have no one left to hand over to you
**“And he shall say to him: Hold thy peace, and mention not the name of the Lord”**
• who brings so many evils upon you
• He who burns the bodies outside, before the other can swear that he has no one to hand over, commands him to hold his peace and not to mention the name of the Lord. For among Israel the name of the Lord had come into such forgetfulness that, neither pressed by evils nor driven by tribulations, would they deign to hear an oath by the name of the Lord.
6.11:
**“For behold the Lord hath commanded”** — he will give command to his ministers the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and through them he will strike the house, because he will give them the strength to strike
**“and he will strike the greater house with breaches”** — of the ten tribes, which sinned more, will be struck with everlasting captivity
**“and the lesser house with clefts”** — Juda, in which was the temple, will indeed be torn, but after seventy years will be mended
**“For behold”** — By the two houses is signified the Church gathered to God from the Jews, as from the greater house, because of the law and the prophets, and from the Gentiles, as from the lesser house, because they were strangers to the covenant of God. This Church, if it does not keep discipline and observe the commandments of God, feels the hand of God striking it, when it is weighed down by persecutions and heresies and schisms. If we wish to escape that hand, let us take an example from the comparisons of the animals: the rock is Christ, or the highest teachers; the horses are demons. The devil cannot reach him who is in Christ, but is dashed against the solidity of the rock.
6.12:
**“Can horses run upon the rocks”** — on rocky ground
**“or can any one plough with buffles?”**
• no
• the wild ox cannot be tamed to take the plough
**“for you have turned … into bitterness”** — Though horses and buffles cannot change their nature, you have changed the nature of God, because you have provoked the gentle one to anger.
**“for you have turned”** — He makes clear why he spoke of the horse and the buffle: “for you have turned”: while these animals keep their nature, the children of Israel do not keep theirs.
**“judgment”** — him who judges justly
**“and the fruit of justice”** — that is, its good working
**“into wormwood”**
• into bitterness
• He turns judgement into fury who judges in anger; and such a man gets no fruit, or a bitter fruit, from justice.
6.13:
**“You that rejoice in a thing of nought”** — in the calves, which are nothing, because “an idol is nothing”; or in no good word
**“you that say: Have we not … by our own strength”** — the heretic, or any wicked man, glories in his own strength; but the just man pushes down his enemies in God
**“Have we not”** — The ten tribes said that by their own strength they had chosen Jeroboam and his sons against the will of God.
**“taken unto us horns”** — kings with whom to push down our enemies
6.14:
**“But behold, I”**
• because of these evils
• Because the wicked are lifted up into pride even against God, so that “they have set their mouth against heaven,” God raises up a savage nation to destroy them, and does not let them enter Emath or the torrent. Emath means “wall” or “walled,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. Into it no one lifted up in pride can enter or be saved, nor into the torrent of which it is said: “thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure.”
**“will raise up … against you”** — [a nation] which seems to be asleep
**“The house of Israel”** — O greater house and lesser house
**“saith the Lord the God of hosts; … a nation”** — of the Assyrians and Chaldeans
**“and they shall destroy you from the entrance of Emath, even to the torrent of the desert”**
• that is, from the beginning of the land of promise to its end.
• Emath, that is, Antioch, is at the beginning of the land of promise; on the other side it is bounded by the torrent of the desert, which runs down between the cities of Pelusium and Rhinocorura.

7.1:
**“These things the Lord God shewed to me”** — Not only what was foretold, but also what I am about to say.
**“These things … shewed”** — The prophetic word foretells not only what will come to pass after many ages, but also what will come to pass in times near at hand. For we are commonly more frightened by the evils of our own time than of the future. So he says that Sennacherib will soon come with a countless multitude, and after him Nabuchodonosor.
**“and behold the locust was formed”** — the creator of the Assyrians, who are signified by the locusts
**“in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter rain, and lo”** — understand: was coming
**“it was the latter rain”** — or: the bruchus
**“after the king's mowing”**
• or: the king's shearing
• As locusts, if they come at the beginning of the latter rain, that is, in springtime, when everything is green and every field is bringing forth, eat up nearly everything; so Sennacherib, coming while the kingdom of the ten tribes flourished, laid everything waste and took it captive. And as a razor drawn over plucks out the hairs left by the shearer, so Nabuchodonosor, coming after Sennacherib, who in Isaias is called a razor and here is signified by the bruchus, took captive the two tribes that were left in that land. The shearer, or the king's shearing, is the name for the army of the Chaldeans, which left no green grass in the land.
• Allegorically. When someone commits grave sins after works of justice, a brood of locusts is brought upon him, coming in the morning, when he begins to recognise his sins; and because he does not do penance, the bruchus is brought on, that is, a certain proud and arrogant strength which consumes everything. But the saints pray for such a man, saying: “Spare, O Lord,” for which of the physicians can heal this issue of blood but thou alone? He is a little one, because there are no traces of the virtues in him, or few. By this prayer God is appeased.
7.2:
**“And it came to pass, that when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land”** — the bruchus, which had come after the locust; and as I understood with the eye of the mind what was signified by the bruchus, fearing that the whole nation would be rooted out, I turned to prayer
**“I said: O Lord God, be merciful, I beseech thee: who shall raise up Jacob”** — from captivity, if not thou
**“for he is very little?”**
• O Lord God, be merciful. I do not wish to have been chosen from among the herdsmen to proclaim the ruin of the ten tribes.
• Little in the number of its people, or of its saints, or in strength; often wiped out by enemies.
7.3:
**“The Lord had pity upon this”** — appeased by the tears of him who prays
**“The Lord had pity”** — When the ten tribes were taken captive beyond the mountain of the Persians, many of them remained; the two tribes too were released after seventy years, when they repented.
**“It shall not be”** — I will not destroy the whole race of Israel, but I will save a remnant
7.4:
**“These things the Lord God shewed to me”** — also what I am about to say
**“and behold the Lord called for judgment”**
• God sends Nabuchodonosor for vengeance
• Nabuchodonosor is called judgement, because through him God judged the people that would not distinguish between the Creator and the creature.
**“and behold the Lord called”** — By the destruction that Sennacherib wrought in the ten tribes is signified the irreparable destruction of heretics. By the two tribes that Nabuchodonosor took captive are signified the sinners in the Church who believe rightly but are foul with vices. To cleanse these, God calls for judgement unto fire, so that it may “try every man's work, of what sort it is.” This fire first devours the deep, that is, every kind of sin, and afterwards comes upon those who are in God's part, so that “judgment should begin at the house of God,” so that “if any man's work burn, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved.” And so God has mercy on the humbled; and because they are little ones and humble, they are raised up now by the virtues, and at last in glory.
**“unto fire”** — to set fire to the city and the temple
**“and it devoured the great deep”** — He will destroy the people, which is compared to water because of its flowing.
**“and ate up a part at the same time”** — understand: God's part, that is, the temple and the altar.
7.5:
**“And I said”** — praying for the people
**“O Lord God, cease, I beseech thee”** — from the vengeance thou hast begun to carry out
**“who shall raise up Jacob, for he is a little one?”** — Because there is no other who can lift up the humbled, but thou, who canst bring the captives back to the land of Juda.
7.6: **“The Lord had pity upon this. Yea this also shall not be”** — Having said in the passage above, “It shall not be,” he adds: this too, which he feared, shall not come to pass
7.7:
**“These things the Lord shewed to me: and behold the Lord was standing upon a plastered wall”** — plastered, and adorned and smooth, made proof against the damage of the rains
**“and behold the Lord was standing”** — By the plastered wall, the Jewish people, plastered by circumcision and the knowledge of God. By the trowel, which adorns the wall, the help of God, who protects those who hope in him.
7.8:
**“And the Lord said to me: What seest thou, Amos? And I said: A mason's trowel. And the Lord said: Behold, I will lay down”** — I will lay it down: I will take away my help
**“the trowel in the midst of my people Israel. I will plaster … over no more”** — to adorn and protect
**“them”** — the wall
7.9:
**“And … shall be thrown down”** — and when I cease from helping, they will be destroyed
**“the high places of the idol”** — in Dan and in Bethel and on all the hills
**“and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste”**
• that is, the calves, by which they thought they were sanctified
• And the sanctuaries: for the Assyrians not only took captive the princes and the people, but also broke up the golden calves and turned them into money.
**“and I will rise up against the house”** — that is, his household and his sons; for he himself was not killed by the sword
**“of Jeroboam”** — who was a descendant of Jehu
7.10:
**“And Amasias the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos hath rebelled against thee in the midst of the house of Israel”** — in this, the insult is to you, not to me
**“And Amasias … sent”** — As though he were the high priest he dares to send to the king, fearing that if the people turn to the worship of God, he himself will lose the glory of the priesthood.
**“the land is not able to bear all his words”**
• He says so much against you and yours that the inhabitants of the land cannot bear it.
• These things refer to the heretics, whose priest Amasias is wont to send to the king and patron of the heretics, accusing the just, and ordering them not to preach against the king's will; because Bethel, that is, their false church, is the king's sanctuary. For they say: The king agrees with us, and whoever preaches otherwise offends God.
7.11:
**“For thus saith Amos”** — the words that God spoke through Amos he ascribes not to God but to the prophet, so as to stir up the king's anger against him
**“Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be carried away captive”** — in this he lies; for Amos did not say “Jeroboam shall die,” but “I will rise up against his house,” unless he does penance
**“Jeroboam shall die by the sword”** — If he had said “Jeroboam shall die,” he would have seemed not to accept penance. But he says “the Lord will rise up,” as it were threatening punishment, so that they may do penance.
**“out of their own land”** — unless he repents
7.12:
**“And Amasias said to Amos”**
• When Jeroboam rejected Amasias's words as idle, Amasias takes up the authority of a priest, saying to Amos
• O prophet Amos
**“And Amasias said”** — He calls him a seer either in mockery, as if a liar, or because he sees that the people gladly listen to him, and he dares not do him open injury, lest he offend his hearers.
**“Thou seer, go, flee away into the land of Juda”** — in which you were born, where madmen are gladly listened to
**“and eat bread there”** — practise your art there, by which you may get your food.
**“and prophesy there”**
• so that you may live by prophecy
• because there you have many whom you are used to leading astray
7.13:
**“in Bethel”** — where I am priest
**“But prophesy not again any more … because it is the king's sanctuary”** — the king has sanctified this place; here the people is sanctified
**“and it is the house of the kingdom”** — here the king has a royal house
**“it is the king's sanctuary”** — He does not say “it is the sanctuary of our God,” but “of the king,” flattering the royal majesty; for it is the custom of those who worship false gods to ascribe what they do to their kings.
7.14:
**“And Amos answered and said to Amasias: I am not”** — or: I was not
**“a prophet”** — this is said in humility
**“I am not a prophet”** — The Spirit does not always minister prophecy to the prophets, but for a time; and they are rightly called prophets when they are enlightened. So he who says “I am not a prophet” meant: at this moment.
**“nor am I the son of a prophet”** — this is said in truth
**“but I am a herdsman”** — a cowherd, or a keeper of other cattle
**“plucking wild figs”**
• stripping the leaves of sycamores and other trees for the cattle's feed
• The sycamore is the same as the bramble, bearing mulberries, which drive off the shepherds' hunger, and leaves, which drive off the hunger of the cattle.
7.15:
**“And the Lord took me when I followed the flock, and the Lord said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel”**
• He notes that he was taken up by grace from a lowly state to the height of a worthy office, so that in this office he ought to obey God who commands rather than the priest who forbids.
• Go, prophesy. Because he humbled himself, saying “I am not a prophet,” he at once deserved to receive the spirit of prophecy.
7.16:
**“And now hear thou the word of the Lord”** — since you forbid me to prophesy
**“Thou sayest, thou shalt not prophesy against Israel”** — the ten tribes
**“and thou shalt not drop thy word upon the house of the idol”**
• you shall not proclaim the wrath of God to the worshippers of idols
• Thou shalt not drop. The prophets are said to drop, that is, to proclaim some small things of the wrath of God, as though letting fall some drops. For no creature could bear the wrath of almighty God as great as it is.
7.17:
**“Therefore”** — see, a fitting requital
**“thus saith the Lord: Thy wife … in the city”** — Bethel
**“shall play the harlot”** — She will be defiled by the enemy before your eyes
**“and thy sons and thy daughters … by the sword”** — of the enemy
**“shall fall …, and thy land”** — which you possess
**“shall be measured by a line”** — it will be measured out by the Assyrians, who will give it to their menservants and maidservants
**“and thou”** — who now glory in the dignity or power of the priesthood
**“in a … land”** — of the Assyrians
**“polluted”** — with idolatries.
**“Thy wife”** — Amasias means “strong and cold,” because the fierce and rebellious heretic forbids the man of the Church to bring forth God's teaching and correct the erring people. His wife, that is, the false church, will be laid open to all; the sons he has begotten in error will be struck by the sword of God; his land and all he has will be the possession of a demon; and he himself dies in a polluted land, which has not God for its inhabitant but is defiled by many errors; and the people that takes to itself the false name of Israel is taken captive out of the land, to serve not God but demons and heretics.
**“shalt die …, and Israel shall go into captivity out of their land”** — There is not such grief over a daughter ravished as over a wife defiled, nor so much over a wife slain as over sons butchered. A husband would rather his wife were killed than defiled.
**“and Israel shall go into captivity”** — At length the captivity will come, after these evils have first been seen; for you will not die before you see those you had deceived taken captive.

8.1:
**“These things”** — also what I am about to say.
**“a hook to draw down the fruit”** — As the branches of trees are drawn down with a hook to pick the fruit, so he brings near the time of the captivity; and to show openly what is signified by the hook, he adds: “The end is come upon.”
**“the Lord shewed to me: and behold a hook to draw down the fruit”** — By the hook is understood the shortened time before the captivity.
8.2:
**“And he said: What seest thou, Amos? And I said: A hook to draw down fruit. And the Lord said to me: The end is come”** — of captivity and slaughter
**“upon my people Israel”** — upon the twelve tribes in general
**“I will not again pass by them any more”** — I will not overlook them, nor leave their crimes unpunished, as I used to
**“The end is come”** — These things can also be referred to the time of the captivity brought about by the Romans in vengeance for the blood of Christ; and this is the end and the last captivity, beyond which God does not spare them. And the hinges of the temple howl, falling upon the slain people; and in every place silence is cast upon the Jews, who read the letter of Moses and the prophets, but, because they have lost the spirit, have no spiritual understanding. Wherever the Jews may be, they mutter rather than speak, and every interpretation of the Scriptures is dumb and silent to them, because they do not set their ears to hear.
8.3:
**“And the hinges of the temple shall screak in that day”** — when the Assyrians come
**“And the hinges … shall screak”** — They will howl because of the great misery of the inhabitants. It is said by hyperbole, that the hinges of the gates, feeling the weight of the misery, howl. And because he mentions the temple, which was at Jerusalem, this seems to concern the two tribes.
**“saith the Lord God: many shall die”** — not all, because many will be led beyond the mountains of the Medes
**“shall be cast in every place”** — of their land
**“silence”** — That is, it will come about when the inhabitants are taken away, who were wont to make their banquets ring with the various instruments of the art of music.
8.4: **“Hear this”** — Lest the threat of captivity seem to be made without cause, he recalls the people's offences: O Juda and O Israel, hear what crimes you have committed: you crush the poor man in judgement, so that, worn out by hunger and want, he is taken away from the land.
8.5:
**“Saying: When will the month be over”** — That is, the time of harvest; when it is over we shall be able to sell more dearly the wares we gathered in the harvest.
**“and we shall sell our wares: and the sabbath, and we shall open the corn”** — When will it be over, so that we may open the granaries and be free to sell the corn?
**“that we may lessen the measure”** — Because they make the measure smaller in selling wares, and larger in receiving them.
**“and increase the sicle, and may convey in deceitful balances”**
• let us sell at a higher price than we buy
• Perverse princes and teachers, “supposing gain to be piety,” sitting in the temple like money changers, set out doves, not in the clefts but in the chairs; like masters they sell the gifts of the Holy Spirit. They make a smaller measure and a larger, so as to give the poor nothing or little, while to the rich they speak at length. And for want of food they trample on the heads of the poor; and it is not God's corn, which “may strengthen man's heart,” but the vilest dust that they cram into greedy throats; selling even this, though the Lord says: “gratis you have received, gratis give.”
8.6:
**“and increase the sicle, and may convey in deceitful balances”** — and this for the purpose
**“That we may possess … for money”** — that is, by usury
**“the needy …, and the poor for a pair of shoes”** — you hold men so cheap, that what I said above is fulfilled in you: you have sold the just man for silver, and the poor man for a pair of shoes
**“and … the refuse of the corn”** — You have leapt into such a frenzy of gain that you sell not only corn to sustain bodies, but even the sweepings of the corn, mixing dust and chaff with the wheat.
8.7:
**“The Lord hath sworn”** — because of this
**“hath sworn”** — Let him who does not believe God when he threatens, believe him at least when he swears.
**“against”** — against
**“the pride of Jacob”** — “God resisteth the proud”
**“surely I will never forget”** — that is, I will not forget, but will keep in memory their sins until the end and the time of judgement
**“never”** — or: to
8.8:
**“Shall not … for this”** — the evil they do
**“tremble”** — against them, from gladness to sadness
**“The land”** — the inhabitants of the land
**“and every one mourn that dwelleth therein”** — not the tenant farmer and the stranger, but the one who dwells there.
**“and rise up … as a river”** — That inhabitant will come up from captivity if he does penance; as the Nile by God's ordering waters all Egypt once a year, heaps of sand closing its mouths so that it does not flow into the sea; and as, after the watering, the heaps are broken and it returns to its channels and, entering the sea, is swallowed up; so this people, if it persists in its offences, will go down into captivity, or even into eternal damnation.
8.9:
**“And it shall come to pass in that day”**
• of the captivity of the ten tribes and of the two
• These things can be referred to the time of Christ's passion, when at the sixth hour the sun, not bearing to see the Lord on the cross, drew back its rays; and when, the hearts of the Jews being blinded, the true Sun set in the day of light. And when the Romans came, their feasts and songs were turned into mourning, and from that day everything was filled with tears and regret and sackcloth; and they were made bald, because they have not Christ, who is the covering of all the elect. Then the people of Israel, once God's firstborn, was handed over to everlasting mourning.
**“saith the Lord God, that the sun shall go down at midday”** — All gladness will pass from them in open captivity.
**“and I will make the earth dark in the day of light”** — I will fill the inhabitants of this land with sadness by making this captivity plain.
8.10:
**“And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation”** — because you were wont to sing songs of gladness
**“and I will bring up sackcloth upon every back of yours, and baldness upon every head: and I will make it”** — the land
**“upon every head”** — He speaks according to the custom of the ancients, who in sorrow shaved their heads, or whose heads were shaved by the enemy in captivity.
**“as the mourning of an only son”** — And the mourning and sadness will be so great that it will surpass a mother's grief over the death of her only son.
**“and the latter end thereof as a bitter day”** — the last captivity as a day of judgement; elsewhere: of death.
8.11:
**“Behold the days”** — of the resurrection
**“come, saith the Lord, and I will send forth a famine into the land”** — of the Jews
**“not a famine of bread”** — for the sustenance of the body, a famine that sometimes forces men to eat human flesh; but a famine of the divine word for the refreshment of the soul, which was sent upon the Jews after the Lord's resurrection. This famine presses harder than that of the body.
**“Behold the days come”** — God sends upon those who mind earthly things a famine of hearing the word of God, when for the people's sins teaching fails in the churches. And from the sea, that is, from salty and bitter waves, they come back again to the sea, that is, to bitter things, because the sweetest springs do not meet them. And from the north to the east: they long to leave the north, the harshest wind, and to reach the east; but they cannot find it, because they do not go by the straight road, but wander round by winding byways.
**“nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord”** — Holy Scripture is water in some places, where it is easily taken in; in some it is bread, where the understanding is harder and it must be broken.
8.12:
**“And they shall move”** — pressed by this famine
**“from sea”** — the British
**“to sea”** — the Atlantic
**“and from the north to the east: they shall go about”** — wanderers through the whole world
**“seeking the word of the Lord, and shall not find it”** — Reading and meditating on the sayings of the prophets; and they shall not find it, because they deny the Word of God, which came by the hands of all the prophets: that which was with the Father, and “was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
8.13:
**“In that day”**
• when I have sent the famine
• When God takes away from the Church the understanding of the divine word, the virgins die, that is, the souls of those under authority, who have chastity by abstaining from evils but are foolish, because they have not the light of truth. When the life-giving word is withdrawn, modesty perishes, chastity dies, the virtues cease. And when the virgins faint, the young men too, that is, those who have bravely overcome the world, faint; because they swear by the idol of Samaria, that is, they are made firm in the doctrines of the heretics, who are understood by Samaria. These heretics also long for the way of Bersabee, which is in the tribe of Juda, because many heretics long to imitate the sacraments of the Church.
**“the fair virgins … shall faint”** — the synagogues, which were once virgins in the fathers
**“And you”** — shall faint
**“the young men”** — that is, the teachers of the synagogues
**“for thirst”** — for the word of God
8.14:
**“You that”** — now
**“swear by the sin of Samaria”** — that is, by the idol, or by the sin
**“and say: Thy God, O Dan, liveth: and the way of Bersabee liveth”** — As the oath of God was said, “As I live, saith the Lord,” so they on the contrary say: Thy God, O Dan, liveth.
**“and they shall fall”** — Those who swear so will fall into captivity.
**“and shall rise no more”**
• They will not return from captivity to their former happiness.
• And the way of Bersabee liveth, by which they went to worship its gods. The ten tribes went so far astray that they not only worshipped the calf in Dan, a city in their farthest borders, but went a long journey to Bersabee, a city at the border of the tribe of Juda, to worship the idols that the two tribes once worshipped.

9.1:
**“I saw”** — Because the veil had been taken from his eyes
**“the Lord standing upon the altar”** — which was in Jerusalem
**“and he said”** — to the prophet, or to an angel
**“Strike the hinges”** — proclaim that it is to be struck by Nabuchodonosor
**“and let the lintels be shook”** — why?
**“for there is covetousness”** — that is, the desire of temporal things
**“in the head of them all”** — in the princes, or in the mind
**“and … the last of them”** — understand: the last man of them
**“I will slay … with the sword”** — of Nabuchodonosor and the Chaldeans
**“there shall be no flight for them”** — Sedecias wanted to flee into Egypt and could not
**“and he that shall flee of them shall not be delivered”** — Those who reached Egypt were not saved there.
9.2:
**“Though they go down even to hell”**
• as happened to Dathan and Abiron, who were buried before they were dead
• by hyperbole: even if they did these things, they could not escape
**“thence shall my hand bring them out”** — not that anyone is drawn back before the resurrection, but that even those in hell are in the power of God
**“and though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down”**
• as Enoch and Elias, caught up into heaven with their bodies, are ruled by the will of God.
• Though they go down. When the soul, loosed from the bonds of the body, has freedom to fly because of the fineness of its substance, it is either led to the lower world, of which it is written: “The wicked shall be turned into hell,” and again: “who shall confess to thee in hell?”; or it is lifted up to the heavenly places, for there are “spirits of wickedness in the high places.” And if they have claimed for themselves the knowledge of the true circumcision (for that is what Carmel means), and if, scorning humility, a man dwells on the mountains, there he does not escape the searching hand of God. And if, despairing of salvation, he wants to avoid the eyes of God and to reach the farthest bounds of the waves of falsehood, there too God commands the crooked serpent, and that avenger bites. The soul taken captive by vices too is punished by the sword of God, and he sets his eyes upon it for evil and not for good, so that through torments and punishments it may return to God.
• One goes down into the hell of the vices by despairing, but the power of God brings him out from there; one goes up to heaven by pride, but he pulls him down from there.
9.3:
**“And though they be hid in the top of Carmel”** — which has a very thick forest
**“I will search”** — more thoroughly
**“and take them away from thence: and though they hide themselves from my eyes in the depth of the sea”** — If they want to hide from my eyes, as Jonas wanted to.
**“there”** — to receive them
**“will I command”** — as he had commanded concerning Jonas
**“the serpent”** — Leviathan, or the whale
**“and he shall bite them”**
• It will devour them in its jaws, like an enemy.
• There are two Carmels: one between Phenicia and the land of promise, where Elias prayed; the other in the tribe of Juda, to the south, where Nabal the Carmelite lived.
9.4:
**“And if they go into captivity before their enemies”** — what he had said in a riddle he puts more plainly
**“there will I command the sword”** — to the ministers of Sennacherib and Nabuchodonosor
**“and it shall kill them”** — nor will slavery set them free from death
**“And I will set my eyes”** — as one angered
**“upon them”** — those who are able to escape death
**“for evil, and not for good”** — so that through torments they may be driven to penance
9.5:
**“And you”** — will do this
**“who toucheth the earth”**
• who is of such power: do not think him unequal to this
• Who toucheth the earth. If the senseless earth feels its Creator and is shaken at his nod, how much more frail man, whose soul is in the earthen vessel of the body.
**“and it shall melt”** — that is, shall fail
**“and all that dwell therein shall mourn”** — of the twelve tribes
**“and it shall rise up as a river, and shall run down as the river of Egypt”**
• That whole people will come up from captivity if it does penance, as the Nile rises to water the land; and if it does not repent, it will run down out of its land, as the Nile rushes down into the sea.
• Allegorically. When God shakes someone's earth, the man so shaken, understanding his crimes, turns it to gain; and so the Lord rises up like a river of consummation to consume earthly works, and comes down upon the sinner like the river of Egypt, so that he is thrust by the onrush of God into the bitterness of torments.
9.6:
**“He that”** — understand: will do this:
**“buildeth his ascension in heaven, and hath founded his bundle upon the earth”**
• by faith and religion
• He that buildeth. Daily the Lord builds his ascension in heaven, when he draws his saints from the depths to the heavenly places over which he presides, and in them he ascends. He also calls any unbeliever to his faith, and tames him and heats him with the fire of the Holy Spirit, and afterwards pours him out, when far and wide he preaches the wonderful works of God, so that “where sin abounded, grace hath abounded more.”
**“and … his bundle”** — That is, the flock of believers. This bundle is bound together by the one religion of God; hence religion itself took its name from binding again (religare) and tying into the Lord's bundle.
**“who calleth the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth, the Lord is his name”** — sweetened in the air and by the heat of the sun, and pours them out upon the face of the earth
9.7:
**“Are not you as the children”** — The Jews gloried that they were of the stock of the fathers to whom God spoke, and that they had been brought out of Egypt. Against this the Lord says: As I created you, so I created the Ethiopians too. As I brought you out of Egypt, so I brought these others too from various parts. So do not be proud, because those made in equal condition will be subject to equal sentence.
**“did not I bring up Israel, out of the land of Egypt: and the Philistines”** — or the Philistines
**“out of Cappadocia”** — I brought
**“and the Syrians”** — who now live in Damascus
**“out of Cyrene”**
• which is a city of Libya beyond Egypt.
• Allegorically. The black Ethiopians, if they repent, can be turned into children of God. The Cappadocians, who lay under the cold north wind, are turned into Philistines, so that, laying aside their pride, they may fall as they drink, that is, as they feel the judgement of God. The Syrians, that is, the lofty, are brought over from Cyrene, that is, from a weak wall, who were neighbours to the bitter sea and the Syrtes, and begin to be lofty in good. On the other hand the children of God, if they go astray, are turned into Ethiopians; for the eyes of the Lord are upon all the sinful kingdoms which the devil showed to the Lord. Hence the Apostle: “Let not sin, therefore, reign in your mortal body.”
9.8:
**“Behold the eyes of the Lord God”** — who is “no respecter of persons”
**“are upon the … kingdom”** — of any nation whatever
**“sinful …, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth: but yet … utterly destroy”** — punishing all the kingdoms of the earth
**“but yet … utterly destroy”** — Though he destroys those who persist in evil, he will not kill those who trip up the vices and conquer in the struggle.
**“I will not … destroy the house of Jacob”**
• The merciful Lord speaks mercifully of his people.
• so as to wipe it out altogether; but a remnant will be saved.
9.9:
**“For behold I will command”**
• to my ministers Antiochus Epiphanes and the successors of Alexander
• I will command, or I will cleanse: that is, for cleansing I will chastise in the present, and I will shake in the day of judgement the house of Jacob, that is, the Church scattered everywhere.
**“and I will sift”**
• I will scatter
• It is shaken in a sieve, that is, the shaking is done so that the corn may be stored in the granaries and the chaff burnt in the fire.
**“among all nations”** — among which it will be scattered
**“the house of Israel …, as … is sifted”** — wheat
**“in a sieve”** — in the vengeance of judgement
**“and there shall not a little stone fall to the ground”**
• that is, every just man, firm with the weight of faith
• As in a sieve, I will cleanse and choose out those who are tossed and shaken, so that he who has become a stone through penance does not fall out of the sieve. He who falls to the ground like dust, let him be struck by the sword and die.
• God, who in his greatness holds all things in the hollow of his hand, as it were holding the edges of the earth with both hands, will shake it to and fro like a sieve, so that, the chaff and dirt falling to the ground, only the corn remains; and this because they do not believe the oracles of the prophets, which threaten punishment to sinners.
9.10:
**“All the sinners of my people shall fall by the sword”** — persisting in their sins until death
**“who say: The evils shall not approach”** — trusting in the dignity of their race, they promise themselves exemption from evils; therefore they will suffer evils
**“and shall not come upon us”** — which the prophets threaten
9.11:
**“In that day”**
• of my resurrection
• of confusion; elsewhere: of shaking.
• Having brought in the terror of punishments, he promises prosperous and glad things, after the manner of the prophets' writings, namely:
**“I will raise up the tabernacle of David”** — the Jewish people
**“that is fallen”**
• in the synagogue by denying [Christ], or earlier through idolatry
• That which has fallen and lies on the ground is said to be raised up, because they lay among earthly things.
**“and I will close up”** — in the Church, through the apostles
**“the breaches of the walls thereof”** — that is, those who had torn it apart by idolatry
**“and what”** — the places
**“was fallen”** — in them
**“repair”** — in the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles
**“and I will rebuild it”**
• the tabernacle
• I will rebuild it, so that as the Church among the Jews, made up of the fathers, was pleasing, so the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles may be pleasing.
**“as in the days of old”**
• that is, in the times of Solomon and David, the holy fathers
• The Jews, understanding everything carnally, interpret this of the time of their Christ, whom they await, by whom they think Jerusalem is to be rebuilt and the kingdom of David restored.
9.12:
**“That they may possess”** — the apostles and preachers
**“the remnant of Edom”** — the Gentile people, which was earthly and bloodthirsty, so that earth may be changed into heavenly things
**“and all nations, because my name is invoked upon them”**
• Christians, from Christ
• of which: “I have manifested thy name to the men”
9.13:
**“Behold the days come, saith the Lord, when the ploughman shall overtake the reaper”** — By all these is signified the order of preachers.
**“Behold the days come”** — According to the letter, all these things befell the Jews after the return from Babylon: because reaping followed on ploughing, and the sowing of seed on the vintage. In this is shown that such happiness was given them that every abundance befell them at once, and there was no day without corn, wine and oil; elsewhere: gladness.
**“and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed: and … shall drop”** — by wise ordering
**“the mountains”** — the apostles, high in virtues
**“sweetness”** — of the words of the Old and New Testaments
**“and every hill”** — the lesser ones, to be tilled
**“shall be tilled”**
• by faith and confession, so that they lack no fruit
• Allegorically. The days will come, namely after the Lord's ascension, in which the ploughman, that is, he who furrows his own heart and others' with faith and love, driving out the hardness of unbelief so that it bears the fruit of good works, overtakes the reaper, that is, him who by preaching the word of God plucks men out of the cares of the world, to store them in the Church of God. The treader of grapes is the martyr, who, treading on death and on the devil himself, suffering for the name of Christ rather than fall away from the faith, pours out the new wine of his blood, to give an example to others. All these God sends into the Church to sow the seed in the hearts of the elect, to separate them from the cares of the world, and themselves to lay down their lives for those entrusted to them; and one overtakes another, because one succeeds another.
9.14:
**“And I will bring back the captivity of my people Israel”** — Because the remnant will be saved, which was held captive under the devil, so that they may see God with the mind.
**“and they shall build”** — the mountains and hills
**“the abandoned cities”** — the multitude of the nations forsaken by God, so that they may be the Church of God
**“and inhabit them”** — so as to stand firm against all assaults
**“and they shall plant vineyards”** — throughout the whole world; elsewhere: congregations
**“and drink the wine of them”** — they will delight in the faith and love of those they have built up
**“and shall make gardens, and eat the fruits of them”** — For he who plants and waters, himself eats.
**“and shall make gardens”** — Not content with this happiness of things, so as to abound in fuller delights, they will fulfil every kind of virtue in themselves, so that, adorned with the various flowers of the virtues, they may go on to the heavenly paradise.
9.15: **“And I will plant them”** — And after this I will plant both the planters and the planted upon “the land of the living,” and so make their root firm that they can no longer be plucked out, either in the present or in the future; for I will be with them against all temptations, “even to the consummation of the world.”

1.1:
**“The vision”** — The understanding of the words that flow from God.
**“of Abdias”**
• The vision of Obadiah. Obadiah, the shorter, the deeper, means “servant of God,” as Moses is called the servant of God and the Apostle the servant of Christ; and he saw and heard things worthy of a prophet's service. This, then, is the vision of Obadiah, which he sees among the nations to which the Lord sent an ambassador; for the destruction of Edom is a vision of the nations. And though “vision” is put in the title, he does not go on to say that he saw anything, only that he heard. So “vision” is put here for understanding, after the manner of the prophets, who understand what they see and hear; from this vision the prophets are called seers. A great part of this prophecy is contained in the book of Jeremiah, with some words changed.
• Esau, son of Isaac, brother of Jacob, was also called Edom, that is, “red,” and Seir, that is, “hairy.” He possessed the region that is now called Gebalena, where the Horites lived before, whose name means “free men.” The city that is called Edom in Hebrew and Idumea in Greek, from the name of its founder, is a small town of Palestine, to which it is said through Amos: “For three crimes of Edom, and for four I will not convert him.” So as the same man is called by three names, so his land too is called Edom, Idumea and Seir. This region is not counted among the foreign nations, because it was possessed by the son of Isaac, the brother of Jacob; nor was it given to the children of Israel as a possession, but the children of Israel were forbidden to take up arms against their brother. But as Esau out of hatred persecuted his brother Jacob, so the Edomites were always enemies to the Israelites. So it is against the Edomites that this prophet speaks.
• According to the history: O Edom, though you are the least compared with the other nations round about, you are lifted up in pride; and though you are contemptible and poor, having no roofed buildings but living in caves, you are raised on high like an eagle, and so swollen in heart that you believe you dwell among the stars and bring all nations under your rule.
• According to the moral sense, the word is spoken against the carnal Jews, who envy the Christians and persecute Jacob their brother, that is, the people of the supplanter, who snatched the birthright from them. Or it is spoken against the heretics, who, while they seem to be our neighbours, are our opponents, and strive to drive the simple dweller out of his father's inheritance. Or against the world, which is earthly and bloody; hence Isaias: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?” Some understand by Edom the flesh, against whose assault they think the soul is called out, so that, having mortified our “members which are upon the earth,” we may attain eternal glory in Christ. The Jews dream in vain that this prophecy is aimed at the Roman empire.
**“Thus saith the Lord God to Edom”** — He joins himself to the other prophets who heard in the spirit the divine sentence against the Edomites.
**“We have heard a rumour from the Lord, and he hath sent an ambassador to the nations: Arise, and let us rise up to battle against him”** — Edom, or that Idumea
**“Arise”** — The ambassador says to the nations to which he was sent: Arise, you who are asleep, and do not be afraid to enter a heavy and unaccustomed battle; you have me in the front line, I who appeared to Joshua holding a sword, and overcame Amalec under the banner of my cross while Moses fought. I will be with you.
1.2:
**“Behold I have made thee small”**
• in the number of its men
• Allegorically. O heretic, though you seem great to yourself and despise the small numbers of the Church, yet among the men of the Church you are contemptible; and still the pride of your heart lifts you up, though you are cut off from the rock, Christ, and from his Church, and, trusting in your mysteries and secrets, you promise yourself the kingdom of heaven. These things can also be said against the flesh, whose strength was diminished at the coming of Christ, and which became contemptible and subject to the rule of the soul. In vain it lifts itself up, since it dwells in caves, that is, in the senses or thoughts, and wants to rule the soul, exalting its throne, and does not believe that its works can be overcome.
1.3:
**“The pride of thy heart hath lifted thee up, who dwellest in the clefts of the rocks”** — The land of the Edomites lies under very great heat of the sun, and so they live in caves and in the clefts of the rocks.
**“and settest up thy throne on high”** — David says something of the kind: “They have set their mouth against heaven: and their tongue hath passed through the earth.”
**“who sayest in thy heart”** — a parenthesis on the presumptuous
**“Who shall bring me down to the ground?”** — as if to say: no one
1.4:
**“Though thou be exalted”** — The eagle flies higher than other birds, and has such sharp sight that, flying on high, it sees little fish swimming in the sea, and comes down like a missile to seize them.
**“Though thou be exalted as an eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars: thence will I bring thee down, saith the Lord”** — Heretics promise themselves the likeness of the eagles, which are wont to gather at the Lord's body. They are wont too to set their nest among the stars of the Church while the master of the house sleeps, trusting in the size of their bodies and the long sweep of their wings; but God pulls them down from there. This too can be said against the flesh, which, though it lift itself up and imitate the heights of the eagle and deceive many of the saints, is yet overcome and cast down by the Lord.
1.5:
**“If thieves had gone in to thee”**
• hidden by the darkness, when they had gone round the corners of your house, how silent you would then be! Understand: so you will be silent when Nabuchodonosor comes, not daring to resist.
• If thieves had gone in. The thieves and robbers are the heretics, children of night and darkness, who preach perverse things and steal from the Church of God what is enough for themselves. These go into the Lord's vineyard, which he brought out of Egypt, and want to lay everything waste so that they scarcely leave a cluster. But God first overcomes them in this, that through the men of the Church he lays open the hidden things of the earlier heresiarchs, who are signified by Esau, and uncovers their lies. He says it with wonder: “How,” that is, how keenly, the holy men have searched out the hidden things of Esau, so that his folly may appear.
**“if robbers by night”** — who are wont to dig through houses by night and carry off what is in them
**“would they not have stolen till they had enough?”** — what they thought enough for themselves; and they would have left something in the houses, either from being sated or from not knowing. So too grapegatherers, whether with hostile mind or hired by you, if they wanted to strip your vineyard, would still leave some clusters hidden by the vines and leaves. But the Babylonians, sent against you by God, have searched out all your secret places, leaving nothing in the holes and caves.
1.6:
**“How have they searched Esau, how have they sought out his hidden things?”** — the caves, the holes
**“How have they searched”** — He says it in wonder, as if to say: they left nothing; and it is a marvel that those men, who lived in caves and holes because of the great heat, could hide nothing that was not found by the enemy.
1.7:
**“They have sent thee out even to the border: all the men of thy confederacy have deceived thee”** — The Moabites and Ammonites, once in league with you, joined the Assyrians to take you captive.
**“even to the border”**
• Not one part of the region was laid waste by the Babylonians, but, reaching to the end of your kingdom, they sent you out beyond it.
• Allegorically. When the secrets of the heretics have been made public by the saints, those who were deceived before will leave the borders of Edom and cross over to the Church, mocking their false opinions; and the believers will prevail, crushing the arguments of those who ate “the bread of mourners” with the heretics, and they will lay snares against them from the authority of the Scriptures. Then it will appear that there is no true knowledge in the heretics.
**“the men of thy peace have prevailed against thee”** — by leading them into captivity, they who had been peaceable in the garrison of their cities
**“they that eat with thee”** — Those who were joined to you so closely that they ate bread with you lie in wait for those who belong to you, so that no one escapes.
**“shall lay snares under thee”** — by this it is plain that Edom is foolish, who did not foresee that those he had as friends would be his enemies.
**“there is no wisdom in him”** — such as there ought to have been
1.8:
**“Shall not I in that day”** — when these things befall you
**“Shall not I in”** — When those deceived before return to the Church, God fighting for them, will not those appear fools who seemed wise, who savoured carnal and earthly things, who, lifting themselves up against the knowledge of God, fought for Esau with the art of dialectic? And then the masters, who thought they were at noonday, being refuted, will be afraid.
**“saith the Lord, destroy the wise”** — the philosophers
**“out of Edom”** — it is called Edom in Hebrew, Idumea in Greek
**“and understanding out of the mount of Esau?”** — so that the cunning of its folly may appear, when they can find no counsel by which to avoid the evil coming upon them.
**“out of the mount of Esau”** — The mount of Esau is the same as mount Seir, on which the city of Idumea stands. So well is wisdom said to be taken away from this mountain; or because that whole region, sloping toward the south, borders on the desert and rises in steep mountains; the same region is called Theman, that is, the south.
1.9: **“And thy valiant men of the south shall be afraid, that man may be cut off from the mount of Esau”** — When the coming of the enemy begins to be heard, and the mockery of those who were peaceable before, then the strong men of your kingdom who live in the south, who were wont to fight for the city and give counsel wisely, will be afraid.
1.10:
**“For the slaughter, and for the iniquity against thy brother Jacob, confusion shall cover thee”**
• when you are taken by the enemy
• O heretic, earthly and cruel, you will suffer the things foretold, because with the deadly teaching of your tongue and the hatred of your heart you have killed, as far as you could, Jacob, that is, the Christian people. Therefore you will suffer confusion and perish for ever; and when some violent persecutor strives to break the peace of Jerusalem, you attack it more fiercely than any Gentile.
