Otherwise: the gates of Jerusalem, that is, of the soul at rest and seeing God, are the five senses of the body, through which the enemies enter, that is, the worst thoughts, to divide the spoils of wretched Jerusalem; as when the eye is opened to covet. And when someone of the Church falls through these gates, then the Jew or the heretic rejoices, and rises against him more fiercely than a heathen.
**“For the slaughter”** — These things will be brought upon you because you killed your brother, joined with the Babylonians as they besieged Jerusalem, entered its gates and cast lots to divide the spoil; because the hatred that Esau had against Jacob over the blessing, you still carry on against his sons; because you grieve that you lost what the Jews have, and so you take the side of their enemies.
**“and thou shalt perish for ever”** — condemned to everlasting captivity
1.11:
**“In the day when thou stoodest against him”** — In the open captivity, when Joachim and Daniel and others were led into captivity by Nabuchodonosor.
**“when strangers carried away his army captive”** — from God, and from the race of the Jews
**“and foreigners entered into his gates”** — of the city of Jerusalem
**“and cast lots upon Jerusalem”** — for the spoils of the city, who should take what
1.12:
**“But thou shalt not look on in the day of thy brother, in the day of his leaving his country”**
• When the second or third captivity of the two tribes comes, you will not join the victors nor mock the captives, because you too will be a captive.
• O heretic, when you see your brother turn aside from the Church, whether by the violence of persecution or by some heresy, you shall not rejoice in their ruin, because you too will perish; nor shall you speak great things over him when, oppressed, he denies, or, drawn away by pleasure, he does not keep his firmness of mind. For the heretic, when he sees someone escaped from danger by flight or by penance, is wont to stand at the crossroads and put forward sophistries, and bring out as it were testimonies from the Scriptures to refresh the weary; so that he who had not been overcome by persecution is thrust back into the prison of errors by a depraved teaching. And since he deceives under the appearance of brotherhood, his persecution is heavier than a Gentile's.
• When someone either denies in distress or loses his former firmness through pleasure, he is then wont to slip easily into contrary teachings, which do not tend the wound but flatter and stroke the error.
**“But thou shalt not look on”** — “Now the prophetic word threatens Edom openly: because, when for the malice he showed his brother he is led captive from the mount of Esau, he will no longer look down on his brother going into captivity, as he did before.” For Edom himself will be taken captive before the Israelites are taken captive by Nabuchodonosor in the time of Joachim or the time of Sedecias.
**“and thou shalt not rejoice over the children of Juda”**
• the disciples of Christ
• the two tribes which reigned in Jerusalem, taken by the Chaldeans
**“in the day of … destruction”** — of captivity
**“their …: and thou shalt not magnify thy mouth”** — speaking great words, as if one of the victors
**“in the day of distress”** — bodily in persecutions, or spiritual in sins
1.13:
**“Neither shalt thou enter”** — rejoicing, since you too will suffer the like
**“into the gate of my people”** — because you too will be handed over into the hands of Nabuchodonosor
**“in the day of their ruin: neither shalt thou also look on”** — taken by the Babylonians, you will neither do what you did, nor what follows
**“in his evils in the day of his calamity”** — in persecution, in denial, in the day when some fall away in martyrdom
**“and thou shalt not be sent out against … army”**
• with the army of the Babylonians
• when, overcome, you flee your enemies
**“his”** — Juda's
1.14:
**“Neither shalt thou stand in the crossways to kill them that flee”** — When you begin to flee by the byways and paths you know into the wilderness, you will not stand at the crossroads to kill those who come, or keep them as captives for the enemy.
**“and thou shalt not shut up”** — those taken in prison
1.15:
**“For … is at hand”**
• therefore, O Idumea, you will cease to do these things, because vengeance is coming upon you
• All the nations, as Herodotus witnesses, as far as the Propontis and the Scythian sea and the Ionian or Aegean, the Assyrians and Babylonians brought under their rule. Hence he says: If other nations that did not sin against God drank of the cup of God's wrath, how will you, who have sinned more, remain unpunished?
**“the day of the Lord”** — judgement and vengeance
**“upon all nations: as thou hast done, so shall it be done to thee”** — As you killed the Jews, so you will be killed by the enemy.
**“as thou hast done, so shall it be done”** — The like is read in the Psalms: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom, in the day of Jerusalem: Who say: Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.” Hence the prophet also prays against Babylon: “O daughter of Babylon, miserable: blessed shall he be who shall repay thee thy payment which thou hast paid us. Blessed be he that shall take and dash thy little ones against the rock.”
**“he will turn thy reward upon thy own head”**
• the day of the Lord
• “His sorrow shall be turned on his own head: and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown.”
1.16:
**“For as you have drunk”**
• the devil's cup
• As you rejoiced with the Babylonians over the destruction of Jerusalem, where my temple and altar were, so the nations which the Babylonian then had with you in his garrison will delight in the shedding of your blood.
**“upon my holy mountain”** — the Church.
**“so all nations shall drink continually”** — turned against you
**“all nations shall drink”** — The opposing powers appointed for punishments, or whatever hostile powers.
**“and sup up”** — Not only will they rejoice in your ruin, but they will also sup you up by slaughter, so that the Edomites will be as though they were not; or those nations will be as though they were not, because those who sup you up will be supped up by the Medes. For as the Babylonians conquered other nations, so the Medes conquered the Babylonians, the Macedonians the Medes, the Romans the Macedonians, and Christ the Romans.
**“and they shall be as though they were not”** — Whoever does not cleave to him who says “I am” is nothing. So the heretics, who are not with him, will perish, and in the day of judgement it will be repaid them as it is to those who sinned against the Church.
1.17:
**“And in mount Sion shall be salvation”** — When Idumea has been destroyed, under Zorobabel the two tribes will return to Jerusalem in their freedom.
**“And in mount Sion”** — Allegorically. When the works of the flesh have been destroyed and the earthly empire laid waste, in the Church will be the salvation of those who have not gone out from their mother, and in her the Holy of holies will dwell. And the house of those who supplant the vices will possess, made Christians, those who had possessed them before. And the house of Esau, that is, of the earthly, will not be able to withstand the fiery disputation of the Catholics, but will be devoured for its own salvation; and there will be no remains of Esau, when to Christ “every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” And since God is “a consuming fire,” his own are turned into the nature of fire, so as to consume the stubble of sins.
**“and it shall be holy”** — The Lord having returned to the temple, which he had abandoned for their sins. Or mount Sion itself will be holy because of the worship of God that will be celebrated there; and then those who have returned, whether of the two tribes or of the ten, will fight together against the Edomites, whom the Edomites will not be able to withstand, as stubble cannot withstand fire.
1.18:
**“And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau”**
• Idumea
• And the house of Jacob shall be. By Jacob the two tribes; by Joseph the ten, because Jeroboam, who reigned first among them, was of Joseph.
• The Jews interpret all these things of the time of Antichrist, whom they will receive as Christ. And whatever is said against Idumea, they dream was said of the Roman empire. But we understand that it has already happened under Zorobabel, or we see it fulfilled daily in the Church, and in the kingdom of the soul against the flesh in each one.
**“stubble”** — which is quickly burnt up
**“and they shall be kindled in them”** — the house of Esau, by them
**“and shall devour them”** — not one will escape the overthrow
**“and there shall be no remains of the house of Esau, for the Lord”** — who is truth
**“hath spoken it”** — whose speaking is doing
1.19:
**“shall inherit”** — When Juda has returned to his kingdom, those who lived in the south and had narrow borders will occupy the mountain country of the Edomites; and those of the two tribes who were in the plains before, at Lydda, Emmaus, Diospolis, Nicopolis, will possess the five cities of the Philistines: Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, Accaron, Geth. Juda will also spread as far as Ephraim, where Neapolis now is, and to the region, namely, where Sebaste now is. And Benjamin, whose border runs from Jerusalem toward the north, will possess all Arabia, which was once called Galaad and is now called Gerasa.
**“And they that are toward the south, shall inherit the mount of Esau, and they that are in the plains, the Philistines: and they shall possess the country of Ephraim, and the country of Samaria: and Benjamin shall possess Galaad”** — Mystically, those who are in the true light, and those who hold the plains of humility, will possess the masters of the Gentiles, who are compared to mountains because of their philosophy and eloquence, and also the Philistines, their disciples, who are called foreigners. They will also possess the heretics of the Church, who promise fruitfulness and the keeping of God's commandments. Further, Benjamin, that is, the sons of the right hand, namely the Christian people, possessed Galaad, that is, the Jews, from whom the testimony passed over to the Christians.
1.20:
**“And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel, all the places of the Chanaanites even to Sarepta”** — that is, those of the ten tribes who have returned from captivity will possess all the kingdoms of the Chanaanites as far as Sarepta, where once a widow fed Elias.
**“and the captivity of Jerusalem that is in Bosphorus”** — those who were carried away from Jerusalem, the mother city, to the Bosphorus
**“shall possess the cities of the south”**
• which are in the tribe of Juda; for, having returned, they will hold their city and the places near the city
• And the captivity of this host. Allegorically. Sarepta means “narrowness of bread,” or “burning”; Chanaan, “movement,” or “merchant,” or “humble.” When the captivity of the children of Israel, leaving the letter that killeth, comes to the spirit that quickeneth, it will set in motion all that belongs to the law, and, made humble, will trade many pearls for one; and where there was once a scarcity of bread, it will give food, and will burn up the vices. And the captivity of Jerusalem, where once was the vision of peace, now spread through the whole world, will possess the churches of the true light. And then the saviours, the apostles, chosen from the remnant of the Jews, will go up to the watchtower of the mountain of the Church, and, putting down the pride of the Jews and of all the mountains that lift themselves up against the knowledge of God, will prepare the kingdom for the Lord.
1.21:
**“And … shall come up”** — when these things are fulfilled
**“saviours”**
• such as Zorobabel was
• As we read in the book of Judges that the Lord sent saviours to set his people free.
**“into mount Sion”** — shall come
**“to judge”** — to judge and deal with the Edomites as subjects and servants
**“the mount of Esau: and”** — all having been subdued
**“… shall be for the Lord”** — alone
**“the kingdom”**
• prepared through the apostles
• “God is wonderful in his saints.”

1.1:
**“And it came to pass”**
• The conjunction “and” joins this to what was already turning over, by the Spirit, in the prophet’s mind.
• As prophets do: seeing many things in the Spirit, out of the many he breaks into these words.
**“the word of the Lord”** — Christ, on whom the Spirit came in the form of a dove, and who grieved for us too.
**“to Jonas the son of Amathi”** — of truth: God is truth.
**“saying”** — The Father to the Son:
1.2:
**“the city”** — The world, so that the whole world might receive him whom the Jew despised. God made it like a beautiful house for man, who was to serve him; and because man strayed through pride, he is called back to repentance.
**“Arise, and go to Ninive the great”**
• Jonah, whose name means “dove,” is sent to Nineveh, which means “spacious.” So Christ, full of the Holy Spirit, is sent to the world, which in Greek, from its Maker’s craftsmanship, is called kosmos, that is, adorned and beautiful; hence “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.” So the whole world hears him whom Israel despised, that, laying aside the pride by which it fell, it may rise humbled into heaven through the Son of God who came down.
• Though Jonah, by the meaning of his name, bears the figure of Christ himself, we need not strain to refer the whole course of the story to Christ by allegory, but only what can soundly be understood so without danger in the interpreting. For although, as the Apostle says, the mystery of Christ and the Church was foreshadowed in our first parents, not everything said of those parents can be referred to that mystery.
**“for… is come up”** — Like this in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrha is multiplied”; and to Cain: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth to me from the earth.”
1.3:
**“And Jonas rose up”** — thinking he could escape God’s anger in a foreign place if he left Judea, where alone he thought God was known; and in this he imitated Cain.
**“And he rose up”** — The prophet knew, by the Spirit’s revealing, that the repentance of the Gentiles would be the ruin of the Jews. And so, loving his country, he does not so much begrudge Nineveh as long that his own people should not perish. For he knew that when Moses prayed, the Lord had found occasion to deliver the Israelites. He had seen prophets sent to the Jews to call them to repentance, and even the soothsayer Balaam prophesying the salvation of the Jews. So he grieves that he alone is chosen to be sent to the gate of a city where idols are worshipped and God despised. He knew too that one day the Gentiles would believe and Judea be blinded. So he fears that in his own time, by occasion of his preaching, with the Gentiles converted, the Jews would be utterly abandoned; and therefore he flees.
**“to flee into Tharsis from the face of the Lord”**
• Tarshish, according to Josephus, is a city of Cilicia; according to what is read in Chronicles, a place in India. But the Hebrews think the sea in general is called Tarshish; hence “With a vehement wind thou shalt break in pieces the ships of Tharsis,” that is, of the sea. This suits a fugitive and fearful man better: not to choose a fixed place to flee to, but to be content wherever the sea might carry him. Or, since Tarshish means “contemplation of joy,” the prophet hastens to the joy of rest, wishing rather to give himself wholly to contemplation and to enjoy the beauty and variety of knowledge, which is signified by Joppa, which means “beautiful,” than that, through the salvation of the Gentiles, the people should perish of whom Christ was to be born according to the flesh.
• Mystically: Christ, taking flesh, in a manner flees his homeland, that is, heaven, and comes to Tarshish, that is, the sea of this world, where he cried, “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me,” lest, the people of the Jews being condemned, the multitude of the Gentiles should believe. And he so loved that people, for love of their fathers and for the promise to Abraham, that on the cross he said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” With this love, on the farthest shore, which was called most beautiful because it was in Judea, he will not take the bread of the children and give it to the dogs. But because he had come to the sheep of Israel, he pays the fare to the sailors, so that he who had first come to save his own people might save the dwellers by the sea; and, plunged into hell amid the storms, that is, his passion and the insults of the cross, he saves those whom he seemed to neglect, as if asleep in the ship.
• The prophet’s flight can signify the human race, when, despising God’s commands, it withdrew from his face and gave itself to the world; and afterwards, as the shipwreck of the world rages against it, it is forced to return to him from whom it fled. What it thought would save it turns to its ruin; and not only is men’s help of no use to those who receive it, but those who give it are crushed with them, as we read that Egypt was laid waste by the Assyrians because, against God’s will, it gave help to the Israelites.
**“And he went down”** — as the lie of the land goes
**“to Joppe”** — the port of Judea, where to this day are shown the rocks to which Andromeda was bound, and freed by Perseus’s help.
**“and found a ship going to Tharsis: and he paid”** — the price of submission
**“the fare thereof, and went down into it”** — like a fugitive, anxiously seeking hiding-places
1.4:
**“But the Lord sent a great wind into the sea”** — when God is against us, nothing is safe
**“and a great tempest was raised in the sea”** — when before all had been calm
**“and the ship was in danger to be broken”**
• because it had taken on one who was himself in danger
• it was shaken almost to breaking
1.5:
**“And they cried”** — Not knowing the truth, they are yet not ignorant of God’s providence, and under the error of their religion they know that there is something to be revered. Israel, by contrast, perceives God in neither good things nor bad, and while Christ weeps, that people’s eyes are dry.
**“And the mariners were afraid, and the men cried to their god”**
• That we took him on board, that the sea rages, that he is found out by lot, that he himself tells what must be done with him: this is the work of thy will. Hence the Saviour in the Psalm: “O Lord, that I should do thy will, I have desired it.”
• Before Christ’s passion, errors and divers teachings, like opposing waves, troubled the little ship of the Church and the whole human race; but after the passion comes the calm of faith, peace in the world, conversion to God, all things safe. So, after Jonah is cast down, the sea grows still from its raging.
**“and they cast forth the wares that were in the ship, into the sea”** — thinking the ship was weighed down by its usual load. They do not know that the whole weight is the fugitive prophet.
**“to lighten it of them”** — that the lighter cargo might leap the waves
**“And he was fast asleep”** — While the others are troubled, the prophet is described as safe and calm, enjoying a peaceful sleep in the inner part of the ship. Or it can be said that, knowing his flight and his sin while the others did not know the cause of the storm, he dares not look at the waves swelling against him, and he sleeps, not from security but from sorrow, as the apostles did at the Lord’s passion.
**“And Jonas went down into the inner part of the ship, and fell into a deep sleep”** — The prophet’s heavy sleep signifies a man sunk in the stupor of error, for whom it is not enough to have risen up from the face of the Lord; overwhelmed besides by a kind of madness, he does not know God’s anger, and sleeps secure, and the deep sleep snores through his nose.
*In the moral sense:* Many there are who, sailing with Jonah and having their own gods, hasten to the contemplation of joy. But once Jonah has been found out by lot, and by his death the world’s storm has been stilled and calm restored to the sea, then one God will be worshipped, and spiritual victims offered, which, by the letter, they did not have in the midst of the waves.
1.6:
**“And came to him”** — it is natural for each man in his own danger to hope more from another than from himself
**“the shipmaster”** — he who ought to have comforted the others, troubled by so great a danger
**“and said to him: Why art thou fast asleep?”** — he rebukes his foolish security
**“rise up, call upon thy God”** — against a common danger let there be common prayer
1.7:
**“And they said every one to”** — Often having known the nature of winds and storms, they see that these waves are not rising from the usual causes. If it were by chance, they would not seek the author of the shipwreck, nor wish to escape a certain danger by an uncertain means.
**“Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know why this evil is upon us”** — that is, this affliction
1.8:
**“And they said to him”**
• the man the lot had pointed out, they make confess with his own voice
• That Matthias is chosen by lot, and that this fugitive is found out by lot, is done not by the power of lots but by the will of God, who governed the uncertain lots. So we must not, by this example, believe in lots or use them, for the privileges of individuals cannot make a common law. By God’s will Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar learned the future by judging dreams; but not for that reason are dreams to be believed everywhere.
**“Tell us”** — With wonderful brevity they ask his person, his country, his city, so that from these the cause of the danger may be known.
**“what is thy business”** — what work you do
**“what is thy country, and whither goest thou? or of what people art thou?”** — from what region, or from the people of what city
1.9:
**“And he said to them: I am a Hebrew”** — a passer-by, like Abraham and the other fathers, who were pilgrims in this world
**“I am a Hebrew”** — He did not say “I am a Jew,” a name given the people when the ten tribes split from the two, but “a Hebrew,” a name common to the two tribes and the ten alike.
**“and the Lord the God of heaven”** — not the gods you worship, but him who made all things and is mighty in all
**“I fear”**
• that is, I worship him whom you do not know; or, I fear him as a servant, though I do not love him as a son
• When he had declared that he feared the Lord, he declared too that he had fled from the face of that Lord and had not done his commands. So the men are afraid, because they understand that he is holy, a man of a holy nation, and that he who flees is great, but he who seeks him greater: they dare not give him up, and they cannot hide him.
**“who made the sea”** — on which I flee
**“and the dry land”**
• from which I flee
• to set it against the sea, he elegantly calls it not “the earth” but “the dry land”
• Since he confesses the Creator of the sea and of the dry land, why does he think, leaving the dry land, that he can escape the Maker of the sea at sea?
1.11:
**“and they said”** — AND THEY SAID to him, rebuking him, as if to say: if you fear God, whom you proclaim so mighty, how do you think you can escape him? Or they say it asking, wishing to know the cause of his flight: why, leaving his own land, does he seek safety at sea?
**“What shall we do to thee”** — WHAT SHALL WE DO UNTO THEE? They ask that the one who was the author of the sin be its remedy too, as if to say: you have shown the cause of the sickness; show also its cure. From the swelling of the sea we understand God’s anger against us, because we took a fugitive aboard. But shall we kill you to appease this anger? Since you are a worshipper of God, it is for you to command what must be done; it is for us to lend our hands, that so, God’s anger turned away, the sea may cease.
**“and”** — that being done
**“the sea may be calm to us?”** — see the reason why they asked this:
**“for the sea grew”** — at God’s bidding, pursuing the fugitive
**“and swelled upon them”** — while the sailors delay it grew rougher, showing it could not put off its Creator’s vengeance
1.12:
**“And he said to them”** — The fugitive, found out, does not dissemble or deny, but, confessing his fault, gladly takes the punishment, preferring to perish alone for his own sin rather than that others should sin with him and perish. By the salvation and conversion of the sailors he is taught besides that the great multitude of Nineveh can be saved by a like confession.
*Allegorically:* Allegorically: these winds, these waves are referred to Christ and the Church in danger, or to the Apostles, who rouse him and, bearing him in his passion, are troubled in the waves. So Christ says: the world sees me sailing with you to the contemplation of joy, so that “where I am, you also may be.” Therefore it rages and longs to devour me, so as to kill you with me; nor does it understand that it takes me like bait on a hook, so that it dies by my death. Take me up and cast me into the sea. The storm that rages against you because of me will be stilled when I die. It is not for you to seize death, but gladly to accept it when another brings it on you, except where charity is in danger.
**“Take me up, and cast me into the sea, and the sea shall be calm to you”** — The storm seeks me; destroy me, that by my death you may live
**“for I know that for my sake this great tempest is”** — I know well that the elements are troubled for my punishment; if I suffer the storm, you will have calm
**“upon you”** — who took me in
1.13: **“And the men rowed hard”** — Though he has pronounced the sentence against himself, they dare not lay hands on a worshipper of God. So they labour to get back to land, preferring to perish rather than shed blood. They row because they think the ship can be freed from danger without the mystery of him who was to suffer, when Jonah’s sinking is the ship’s relief.
1.14:
**“And they cried”** — They call God to witness, that what they are about to do may not be counted against them as a fault. As if to say: we do not want to kill your prophet; but he himself has confessed your anger, and your storm convicts him: your will is fulfilled by our hands. Pilate does and says something like this, washing his hands and saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this just man.” The Gentiles do not want Christ to perish and bear witness that he is innocent, and the Jews say, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
**“and they said”** — knowing that the death of sin is worse than that of life; and with great faith they pray for another’s soul when they themselves are in danger of their bodies
1.15:
**“And they took”** — they do not snatch him, but carry him with deference and honour
**“Jonas”**
• Christ
• not resisting, but offering his hands by the will of God
**“and cast him into the sea, and the sea ceased from raging”** — the sea, angry while Jonah was away, now takes and holds him whom it longed for; it rejoices and cherishes him, and for joy the calm returns
1.16:
**“And the men feared the Lord exceedingly”** — with all their soul, all their heart, all their strength
**“And they feared”** — Before the passion, in their fear they cried to their own gods; after the passion they fear God, venerating and worshipping him, and they offer sacrifices, not those which by the letter they did not have among the waves, but “the sacrifice of an afflicted spirit”; and they vow vows never again to depart from God, seeing from the flight of the storm that the prophet’s words were true.
1.17:
**“Now the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonas”** — He commands death and hell to receive the prophet; but as much as they rejoice in the swallowing, so much do they mourn in the casting up.
**“And he prepared”** — Either he made it from the beginning, when he created it, or he made it come alongside the ship, to receive him as he fell headlong and give him a dwelling in place of death; so that he who in the ship had felt God angry might in death feel him gracious.
**“And Jonas was”** — As Jonah, by being three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, points to the passion, so his prayer too is a figure of Christ’s prayer.
**“three days and three nights”**
• As Jonas was in the whale’s belly three days and three nights, so shall the Son of man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.
• Whoever believes that the three young men were so delivered from the fire that not even the smell of fire touched their garments ought not to doubt Jonah’s safety in the whale’s belly.
• Some say that on the day of Preparation, when the sun fled from the sixth hour to the ninth and night came upon the day, two nights and days are to be counted there up to the morning of the Sabbath; and with the Sabbath and the night after it added, three days and nights are counted. Others understand it by synecdoche, that is, the whole for the part.

2.1: **“And Jonas prayed to the Lord out of the belly of the fish”** — Once he felt himself safe in the whale’s belly, he turns to pray for God’s mercy
2.2:
**“And he said”** — Christ, free among the dead, living in hell, cries out: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption.
**“I cried out of my affliction”** — When I saw the huge beast with its open jaws, I remembered God and cried out. Either aloud, the waters giving way and the cry finding room, or by the heart’s longing alone.
**“I cried out of my affliction to the Lord, and he heard me”**
• As for Jonah, it is plain that he was shut in the belly in the middle of the sea. But the Saviour, appearing in the flesh, fully knew the storms of this earthly dwelling, which, compared with the heavenly dwelling, is called a sea and a storm. Hence: “I stick fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no sure standing”; and again: “I am come into the depth of the sea, and a tempest hath overwhelmed me.”
• By anagogy he records that he was in the heart of the sea, that is, in the midst of the storms; and yet, tempted in all things among bitter waters, without sin, he felt no bitterness from the waters, but was surrounded and refreshed by the sweetness of the river that maketh the city of God joyful.
• In the person of Jonah it is plain that all this happened by the letter. In Christ, every temptation, without sin, that came about by God’s will did not crush him but passed by, because in him it lost its strength, so that those who used to be endangered by it might be freed through him who overcame.
**“out of the belly of hell”** — that is, from the belly of the whale, which for its size is like hell
**“I cried, and thou hast heard”** — thou who triest the reins and the hearts
2.3: **“thou hast cast me forth into the deep in the heart of the sea”** — that is, in hell, for which the Gospel says “in the heart of the earth”: for as an animal’s heart is in the middle, so hell is held to be in the middle of the earth.
2.4:
**“I am cast away”** — I who had taken the form of a servant, sharing man’s frailty, said this before I cried out and was heard. I who in thee, the Light, was light, made man was cast out, so that by this I might lead the human race back to thee.
**“out of the sight of thy eyes: but yet again”** — though cast out for a time
**“I shall see thy holy temple”** — set in the depth of the sea, by the spirit of prophecy he is elsewhere
**“I shall see thy temple”** — This suits Jonah, either wishing or trusting, who by the prophetic spirit saw this as yet to come. It suits Christ, as we read: “Father, glorify thou me with thyself, with the glory which I had before the world was.” As the Son is the Father’s temple, so the Father is the Son’s temple, of whom he said, “I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world.”
2.5:
**“The waters compassed me about even to the soul”** — the waters of the world, which drag mud with them, cherish the body but kill the soul; yet they could not harm Christ, because he had taken them on not by necessity but by will
**“the deep hath closed me round about”** — The deep here means the opposing powers, or the powers given over to torments, to which, in the Gospel, the demons beg not to be made to go to be tormented.
2.6:
**“the sea hath covered”** — By the history, it is plain that Jonah came down to the depths of the earth, by which, as if by bars and pillars, the globe of the earth is upheld by the will of God.
**“I went down to the lowest parts of the mountains”** — Allegorically: in Christ the man, the chief part, as it were the head, was the soul, which went down to the lower places where the souls of men were held under the devil’s power. These are the bars that keep souls from leaving hell; these bars the Lord breaks, and frees those who were held shut in.
**“the bars of the earth have shut me up for ever”**
• another reading: have shut me in
• in men’s opinion
**“and”**
• and yet
• “Thou wilt not give thy holy one to see corruption”
**“thou wilt bring up from corruption”** — lest, corrupted in death, we pass into the food of beasts
**“my life, O Lord my God”** — This with the tenderness of one who coaxes, because by the greatness of his kindness he makes the God of all his own
2.7:
**“When … was in distress”** — This suits Christ when he says, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”; and again, “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.”
**“I remembered the Lord”** — When in the whale’s belly, by the frailty of the flesh, no hope was left, by remembering the Lord I overcame the impossible
**“that … may come to”** — So in tribulation I remembered God, that from the depth of the sea my prayer might climb to heaven: that it might come to thy holy temple, in which thou enjoyest eternal blessedness. He asks, as a high priest, that his prayer may go up to God, that in his body the people may be freed.
**“that my prayer may come to thee, unto thy holy temple”** — I so; but they who
2.8:
**“They that keep”** — Since all things are vanity, all of necessity do vanity; but not all keep it as a treasure, nor love what they do. So he does not deny mercy to the whole human race.
**“They that in vain observe vanities”**
• God, merciful by nature, is ready to save by clemency those he cannot save by justice; but by our fault we forsake the mercy that offers itself. And note that the prophet in the whale’s belly, forgetting his own danger, philosophises on the nature of things in a general maxim.
• The Jews, while they keep the traditions of men, forsake the commands of God, who had always had mercy on them.
**“forsake their own mercy”**
• that was prepared for them
• which does not leave a man in vanity, but waits for him to return
2.9:
**“But I”** — who was swallowed for the salvation of many
**“But I with the voice”** — Before the passion Christ had in a manner fled from obeying God, when he says, “It is not good to take the bread of the children, and to cast it to the dogs”; and again, “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me.” But after the resurrection, leaving the faithless, he willingly preaches to the world what had been commanded him before the passion.
**“will sacrifice to thee”** — myself, who am victim and high priest
**“whatsoever I have vowed”** — In his passion he vowed us all to the Father, that none of those given him should perish. He promised for the salvation of all; let us not make him a liar: let us be clean, that he may offer us to the Father.
2.10:
**“And the Lord spoke to the fish”** — The whale, the deeps and hell are commanded to give the Saviour back to the earth, that he may lead out with him the many dead who were held in the bonds of death
**“and it vomited out Jonas upon the dry land”** — out of the inmost parts of death came forth life, death’s conqueror

3.1: **“And it came to pass”** — All of this, that he is commanded, that he obeys, that he is unwilling, that he is made to will again, that a second time he carries out the Father’s will, suits Christ in the form of a servant.
3.2:
**“Arise, and go to Ninive”** — the world
**“the great city: and preach in it the preaching that I”**
• the Father
• I speak not of myself;
**“bid thee”** — the Son
3.3:
**“And … rose”**
• from death
• obeying without delay
**“And he rose up”** — Allegorically: Christ, after hell, is properly said to rise and to preach when he sends the apostles to baptise men in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is the journey of three days. Yet this mystery of man’s salvation is accomplished in a day’s journey, that is, by the confession of one God, with Jonah, that is, Christ, preaching in the apostles, who said, “I am with you, even to the consummation of the world.”
**“Jonas”** — Christ
**“and went”** — through the apostles
**“to Ninive, according to the word”** — the command
**“Now Ninive was”** — Nineveh was so large that it could scarcely be gone round in three days’ journey. But he, mindful of the command and of his shipwreck, made haste and covered in one day what took three. Some say that he preached only in a third part of the city, and at once the word of his preaching reached the rest.
**“of the Lord. Now Ninive was”** — He did not say three days and nights, or one day and night, but simply “days” and “day,” to show that in the mystery of the Trinity and the confession of one God there is nothing dark.
3.4:
**“And Jonas began to enter into the city one day’s journey: and he cried”** — Christ, standing in the temple, cries out: “If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.” Every word of Christ is called a cry, because it treats of great things.
**“Yet forty days”** — “Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” according to the Septuagint. Whether by forty days or by three, the same Christ is signified: by forty, because he spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection and ascended into heaven; by three, because he rose on the third day.
**“and said: Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed”**
• This is not prophecy coming down from God’s foreknowledge, where all things remain just as they are, but a threat meant to correct, setting out a just vengeance for the Ninevites’ present sins.
• The number forty suits sinners for penance, fasting, prayer, sackcloth, tears and perseverance in entreaty. Moses, Elijah and Christ himself fasted for this number of days. This number is set for us to prepare our souls for eating the body of Christ.
• A fine order: God commands the prophet; the prophet preaches to the city. The men believe first; when they proclaim a fast, every age puts on sackcloth. The men proclaim only the fast, not the sackcloth; but those to whom penance is commanded add sackcloth to the fast, so that with an empty belly and the garb of mourning they may entreat God the more strongly.
• Those who had offended God by luxury and ambition appease him by condemning the very things by which they had first offended. First the fast, which is offered to God in secret; then the sackcloth, which is shown to men outwardly.
*Jerome:* Jerome: Nineveh, that is: overthrown was the Nineveh that was evil, and the good Nineveh that was not was built. With its walls and houses standing, the city was overthrown in its lost ways. And though what those men feared, when Jonah prophesied, did not come about, yet what had been foretold at God’s command did.
3.5:
**“And … believed”** — the uncircumcision believes; the circumcision remains unbelieving
**“the men of Ninive”** — who come “unto a perfect man, unto the age of Christ.”
**“in God: and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth”** — sackcloth and fasting are the weapons of penitents
**“from the greatest to the least”** — because no one is without sin, not even an infant of one day
3.6:
**“And the word came”** — After the weak and base things of the world had been chosen, the word of Christ came at last to the philosophers and the mighty, who seemed to rule the world. First Peter the fisherman enters, then Cyprian. Once an idolater, at last he believes and becomes a defender of the truth; after hearing the word of Jonah he calls the Carthaginians to repentance and preaches Christ openly. See, the king of Nineveh rises from his throne, changes purple for sackcloth, ointments for mud, finery for filth. It is hard for the mighty and the eloquent of the world to be turned to the humility of Christ.
**“and he rose up out of his throne”** — he humbled himself, laying aside the height of power and eloquence
**“and cast away his robe from him, and was clothed with sackcloth”** — of penance for past evils
**“and sat in ashes”** — in the plainness not of thought but of words
3.7:
**“And he caused it to be proclaimed”** — He cried, saying in Nineveh what had been decreed by the mouth of the king and his princes; hence the Septuagint: “And it was proclaimed in Nineveh by the king and by all his great men.”
**“and published in Ninive from the mouth of the king and of his princes, saying: Let neither men”** — the reasonable
**“nor beasts”**
• the foolish
• “Men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord.”
**“oxen”** — the prudent
**“nor sheep”** — the simple
3.8:
**“And let men and beasts be covered with sackcloth”** — in the garb of mourning, in grief and sorrow, which is called sackcloth by metaphor
**“men and beasts, and cry to the Lord with all their strength, and let them turn”** — to the Lord
**“every one from his evil way”** — which is of himself
**“and from the iniquity that is in their hands”** — not only in thought but in deed
3.9:
**“Who can tell”** — He speaks doubtfully so that, while men are unsure of their salvation, they may do penance more strongly and move God more to mercy.
**“if God will turn”** — to those who turn
**“and forgive”** — so
**“and will turn away from his fierce anger”** — which he had all but begun to pour out
**“and”** — when he has turned
3.10:
The prophet is not asked, “Why did you not do what I commanded?” Being swallowed is correction enough for the shipwreck, so that he who had not felt the Lord commanding might feel him delivering.
**“And God saw”** — Now to the Ninevites, and daily to the peoples of the world, God threatens, that they may do penance. If they turn, he too turns his sentence, and is changed by the people’s turning.
**“And God saw their works, that they were turned from their evil way: and God had mercy”** — He did not hear the words Israel was often wont to promise, “All that the Lord shall say to us, we will do,” but he looked at their works, because he would rather the sinner’s life than his death. Seeing their works changed, he gladly changes his sentence. Rather let us say that he held to his purpose, willing from the beginning to have mercy. For he did not wish to punish, nor was he going to punish what he threatened.
**“with regard to the evil”** — affliction

4.1:
**“And … was exceedingly troubled”** — He is not saddened that the multitude of the Gentiles is saved, but that he sees his own nation perish, and himself chosen out of so great a number of prophets to announce, through the salvation of others, the ruin of his own people, already in a way despairing of Israel’s salvation. So the Lord wept over Jerusalem and would not cast the bread of the children to the dogs. The apostles too preached first to Israel. Paul even wished himself accursed for his brethren.
**“And Jonas was exceedingly troubled, and was angry”** — Fittingly Jonah, that is, “grieving,” is sorrowful even unto death, because, so far as in him lay, he suffered much that the people of the Jews might not perish: a toiling prophet, weighed down by exile and shipwreck.
4.2:
**“And he prayed to the Lord, and said”** — About to say that he was right to want to flee, he in a way accuses God of injustice; so he tempers his complaints with the opening of an entreaty. For “I pray thee” is to be read with the tenderness of one who coaxes; for which the Hebrew has Anna, which is an interjection of coaxing.
**“for I know that”** — I knew you were merciful and would do this. I did not want to announce a harsh God, but wanted to flee to Tarshish, that is, to be free for contemplation, and to enjoy rest and leisure on the sea of this world; I left my house, going out from your bosom. If I said you were forgiving and merciful, no one would do penance. If a cruel judge, I knew that is not your nature. In this uncertainty I chose to flee rather than either deceive the impenitent by gentleness or preach of you what you were not. So take my soul.
**“I beseech thee, O Lord, is not this what I said, when I was yet in my own country? therefore I went before to flee into Tharsis: for I know that thou art a gracious and merciful God, patient, and of much compassion, and easy to forgive evil”** — The prophet, saddened, wants to die, lest, with the multitude of the Gentiles converted, Israel perish for ever.
4.3:
**“And now, O Lord”** — My soul is sorrowful even unto death. And again: “Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”
**“I beseech thee take my life from me: for”** — living, I could not save the one nation of Israel; let me die, and the whole world will be saved.
4.4: **“Dost thou think”** — He does not say “you are wrong to be angry,” lest he seem to rebuke the one who grieves; nor “you are right to be angry,” lest he go against his own sentence. But he questions the angry man himself, so that either he answers with the causes of his anger, or, if he is silent, God’s true judgment is proved by his silence.
4.5:
**“Then Jonas went out”** — Jonah, that is, “dove” or “grieving,” goes out of the city that Cain built and dwells toward the east, where the sun rises; and there he is in his tent, waiting for the passing times, watching what will befall the city of the world. Before Nineveh was saved through the gospel of Christ, and both the gourd and the east were made plain, Jonah was under a shelter, because the truth was not yet revealed.
**“of the city”** — of the world
**“and sat toward the east side of the city”** — because then none of the Ninevites could dwell with him
**“and he made himself a booth there, and he sat”** — he sits as a judge, or as one withdrawn from his majesty
**“under it in the shadow, till”** — in the manner of Scripture it ascribes human feelings to God
4.6:
**“And he prepared”** — In the Hebrew, ciceion is read for “gourd,” which springs up quickly and quickly withers. It is compared to Israel, putting down small roots into the earth and striving to lift itself on high, but not equalling the height of God’s cedars or firs.
**“And the Lord God prepared an ivy”** — A gourd or ivy: a kind of shrub or small tree with broad leaves, giving very thick shade, which creeps along the ground and does not reach higher without props to lean on. But God prepared this one so that, rising suddenly on high without any supports, it might give the prophet a shelter; and in this the power of God was shown. To this ivy or gourd is compared Israel, which once sheltered Jonah under its shade, Jonah awaiting in Christ the conversion of the Gentiles; and it gave him no small joy, making him a shelter rather than a house, having the look of a roof but no foundations.
**“and it came up”** — suddenly, by God’s wonderful power
4.7:
**“And he prepared”** — Some understand the worm and the burning wind as the Romans, who destroyed Israel after the resurrection of Christ.
**“a worm”** — Christ, who says, “I am a worm, and no man.”
**“when the morning arose on the following day: and it struck the ivy”** — which flourished before the Sun of righteousness rose; but when Christ rose, the shelter was left without God’s help and lost all its green
4.8:
**“And when the sun was risen”** — by whose light the darkness of the Ninevites was scattered
**“the Lord commanded a hot”** — Hence in Hosea: “The Lord will bring a burning wind that shall rise from the desert, and it shall dry up his springs, and shall make his fountains desolate.”
**“and burning wind: and the sun beat upon the head of Jonas, and he broiled with the heat”** — with Israel
**“and he desired for his soul that he might die”** — In baptism, as in a bath, that he may receive back the moisture he had lost by denying. Hence Peter says to the parched Jews: “Do penance, and be baptized every one of you, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.”
4.9:
**“And the Lord said”** — the Father
**“to Jonas”** — the Son
**“Dost thou think thou hast reason”** — Above, when the Ninevites repented and were saved, the prophet, asked the same, answered nothing, but approved God’s question by his silence; for, knowing God to be merciful and forgiving of evils, he did not grieve at the salvation of the Gentiles. But here, because the gourd has dried up and Israel withers, and he is asked pointedly, “Dost thou think thou hast reason to be angry, for the ivy?”, he says boldly: “I have reason to be sorrowful, even unto death; for I did not wish to save others in such a way that others perished, nor to win strangers in such a way that I lost my own.” So Christ mourns for Jerusalem even unto death, not his own death but the Jews’, that they may die denying and rise confessing the Son of God.
4.10:
**“And the Lord said: Thou”** — Son
**“art grieved for the ivy”** — for the Jews condemned
**“thou hast not laboured”** — As regards the people of the Gentiles. Hence Israel says plainly: “Behold, for so many years do I serve thee, and thou hast never given me a kid; but for this one, who hath devoured his substance with harlots, thou hast killed the fatted calf.” He is not refuted in this, but hears: “All I have is thine.” Yet it was meet to make merry for the brother’s return. For it was for the Gentiles that Christ’s precious blood was shed, and he went down to hell that that people might go up to heaven. No such toil was spent for the sons of Israel; and so he envies the younger brother.
**“in one night”** — that is, the time before the coming of Christ
**“came up, and in one night perished”** — when the Sun of righteousness set for it
4.11:
**“And shall not I spare Ninive, that great city”** — by which is signified the Church, in which the number is greater than the twelve tribes of Israel
**“in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons that know not how to distinguish between their right hand and their left, and many beasts?”** — a great number of creatures without reason
**“more than a hundred and twenty”** — This can be understood of the age of infants, which is innocent and simple; and since the number of little ones is so great, it is plain that the multitude of older age was great. Or, since Nineveh is a great city, and in a great house there are vessels not only of gold but also of earthenware, it can be said that there was a great multitude which, before it did penance, did not know the difference between good and evil.

1.1:
**“The word”**
• that is,
• that which “was in the beginning with God”
**“of the Lord”** — the Father
**“that came to Micheas”**
• whose name means “humility”
• Micheas is the sixth according to the Hebrew truth; so, placed as it were in the heart of the volume, he ought to contain deep mysteries.
**“the Morasthite”** — that is, inheritance
**“in the days of Joathan, Achaz, and Ezechias, kings of Juda: which he saw”** — spiritually
**“concerning Samaria and Jerusalem”**
• The word of the Lord that. The title of the prophecy is set first. Revelation is made to the humble man, the co-heir of Christ, both about perverse teachings and about the Church, if she has committed any sins.
• The word of God, which always comes down to the prophets, comes also to Micheas, whose name means “humility”; to Micheas of Morasthi, which to this day is a small village near Eleutheropolis, a city of Palestine, and whose name means “heir.” And beautifully humility, which is foremost among the virtues, is born of the hope of God's inheritance. Here is not meant the humility that comes from the consciousness of sins, but that which is counted among the virtues. Hence it is said: “Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God”; and: “he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted”; and the Lord: “learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart.” So as among us names are given as a wish and as it were an omen of virtue, for example Victor, Castus, Pius, Probus, and common nouns are turned into proper names, so among the Hebrews too Micheas and Abdias and Zacharias and the like were given to children by their parents from the names of virtues.
• Under Ozias, Osee, Amos and Isaias began to prophesy. Under Joathan, the son of Ozias, Micheas begins to prophesy; he prophesied also under Achaz and under Ezechias, under whom the ten tribes were taken captive by the Assyrians. And because Samaria, the chief city of the ten tribes, was taken captive first, and then Jerusalem, the prophet's title is set down first concerning Samaria, second concerning Jerusalem.
• Mystically, by Samaria the heresies are signified, by Jerusalem the Church. For Samaria made for herself, out of her own understanding, golden calves, beautiful on the surface but having no living spirit; and this in the house of God, which is what Bethel means. For Israel will receive no gods but those fashioned from the Scriptures and in the house of God. And though they call their conventicles Bethel, yet after the idols are fashioned they are rightly called not Bethel but the house of the idol.
1.2:
**“Hear”** — this
**“all ye people”** — all that are in it
**“and let the earth give ear”** — with the heart
**“and all that is therein: and let the Lord God be a witness to you”** — or: testifying
**“the Lord from his holy temple”**
• of the Church of the whole world
• that is, earthly men, in whom the heretics' teachings have been built up

• If one of the faithful, caught in adultery, is beheaded, it seems that he is not to be punished further, “lest he be judged twice for the same thing.” But it must be known that “God, as he knows the measure of all things, so knows also the measure of punishments; and the sentence of the judge is not forestalled, nor is the power taken from him of exercising punishment on the sinner hereafter; and a great sin is atoned for by long torments, but a light fault is paid for by a light punishment.”
• The Hebrews' explanation: O Assyrians, why do you think evil against God, that he will destroy the twelve tribes entirely? There shall not rise a double affliction: he will not hand over Juda and Jerusalem to you as he handed over the ten tribes and Samaria.
1.10:
**“For as thorns embrace one another: so while they are feasting and drinking together, they shall be consumed as stubble that is fully dry”**
• The two tribes will not be taken by the Assyrians as the ten were, because, while the Assyrians are still in the land of Juda, and embrace one another like thorns, rejoicing and glad, they will be consumed by the angel, when in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain; a multitude well compared to a feast of drunkards, and to thorns embracing one another, which are wont to be given to the fire, and to stubble, which is burnt up by a light flame.
• The covenants and alliances of the heretics embrace one another like thorns; and their feast, that is, the mysteries of the altar (for they too say that they have the Lord's table), is a covenant of thorns, eating together and drinking alike. For when, drunk on the vineyard of Sodom, they blaspheme against God, is it not a feast of thorns? Yet it will be consumed with its authors like stubble that is fully dry, since from them goes out the hostile thought against God.
1.11:
**“Out of thee shall come forth one that imagineth evil against the Lord”** — heresies, zealously
**“contriving treachery in his mind”** — so as to carry on the lie with inventions
**“Out of thee”** — This is said of Rabsaces, who went out from the Assyrians and blasphemed God, persuading the Israelites to despair of God's help and give themselves up to the Assyrians, to serve not God but idols.
1.12:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Though they were perfect”**
• in strength
• As if to say: though the Assyrians are strong and many, they will not prevail against you.
**“they were”** — the Assyrians
**“and many of them so”** — having joined many nations to themselves
**“yet thus shall they be cut off”**
• the angel laying waste
• that is, the Assyrians
• As many hairs by the shears, so their multitude will easily be cut down.
**“and he shall pass”** — Assur will either cease to be, or, his army laid waste, will return to his own country, leaving you safe
**“Though they were perfect”**
• Again the word is directed to Juda and Jerusalem, to whom God promises security, not for ever, but for that time and from those enemies by whom they were besieged.
• God's kindly threat against the heretics: though they are strong and many, they will be worn down, and their onset will pass. There follows also a promise: I have let you be afflicted by the power of the devil, at whose prompting you had invented so much and had woven bonds to bind the souls of sinners; but all these I will now break, saying to those who were held in bonds: Come out.
1.13:
**“And now I will break in pieces his rod”**
• the power
• with which he tried to strike you
**“his”** — of the Assyrian
**“with which he struck thy back, and I will burst thy bonds asunder”** — which the captor was preparing; although the siege can also be taken for the bonds of the shut-in multitude
1.14:
**“And the Lord will give a commandment concerning thee”**
• against you, Assur
• having made the promise of deliverance to the Israelites, he turns his words to the Assyrians, threatening them with punishment.
**“that no more … shall be sown”** — that is, there will be no sowing
**“of thy name”** — because Sennacherib, having returned to Ninive, was at once killed by his sons in the house of his god while worshipping; punished there whence he hoped for help
**“I will destroy … out of the house of thy God”** — you
**“the graven and molten thing … I will make it thy grave”** — among the altars and couches of the one worshipping idols, wicked blood will be shed.
**“for thou art disgraced”**
• And the Lord will give a commandment concerning thee. O Assur, what you are to suffer, do not think it happens by chance and without a judge, because all things will be done at God's command.
• O heretic, the souls deceived by you will not take up the names they had called upon over their lands before, but the sects of the heretics will cease, so that others are not named after them. So the doctrines of errors will die to you; and you too, who seemed to yourself to live, will die to error, and, dead to your own good, you will have the idols you worshipped as your grave; and errors will be taken from your breast, in which before was the temple of your God, whom you feigned. Because you are disgraced, while you worship vain idols, you who are rational.
1.15:
**“Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, and that preacheth peace: O Juda, keep thy festivals, and pay thy vows”** — singing to the Lord with the angels
**“for Belial shall no more pass through thee again”**
• the transgressor
• Hence the Apostle: “What concord hath Christ with Belial?”
**“he is utterly cut off”**
• because
• Ninive being overthrown
• Behold upon the mountains. We read in Paralipomenon that, while Sennacherib was besieging Jerusalem, the pasch could not be kept in the first month; but when his army had been slain and the death of Sennacherib announced, the pasch was celebrated in the second month. Hence he says: O Juda, do not be anxious; your enemy has been killed in the temple of his god; behold, a messenger comes to you running over the mountains and hills, and, as if from a watchtower, announces to you that by Sennacherib's death the city is set free. Keep, then, your festivals, and pay to God the vows you promised, for the death of the enemy; because Belial, that is, that transgressor, will not pass through you, for he has wholly perished: the army and the king and the empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen.
• If at any time there has been a heavy persecution, and God's vengeance has appeared on its adversaries, let us say to the Church: O Juda, keep thy festivals, and pay thy vows.
• Allegorically. The heresies destroyed, the voice of the Church's preacher is brought in, urging to joy the souls that confess God, for the devil destroyed in the idols and with the idols.

2.1:
**“He is come up that”** — Having announced the destruction of Ninive, he adds by whom it is to be carried out, directing his words to Ninive herself.
**“He is come up that shall destroy before thy face”** — Nabuchodonosor, who will besiege you, lay waste the fields before your face, hunt down the farmers, and hold you shut in.
**“that shall keep the siege: watch the way”** — O Ninive, the things I foretell will come upon you
**“watch”** — The prophet, seeing war hanging over Ninive, already mocks her with joy as she is about to fall.
**“fortify”** — gird yourself
**“thy loins”** — mockery
**“strengthen thy power exceedingly”**
• gather armies
• Allegorically. Three things are commanded to Juda: first, that he look to the way by which he may walk to him who says: “I am the way”; then, that he hold his loins, that is, mortify the flesh; third, that he take up power, so as not to fail in the war against the enemies. And so that he may not fail in this war, he adds in what he can have hope: namely, that God has rendered the pride of Jacob; the wrongs which in his pride he used to do to others he now, humbled by God's grace, bears patiently from the Assyrians. Jacob means “supplanter,” Israel “seeing God.” As, then, seeing God and always thinking of God, he does not know how to do wrong to others, so, supplanting his enemies in the wrestling, he ceases to do wrong to others, because the spoilers, that is, the angels of each one, “who see the face of the Father,” have scattered in Jacob and Israel whatever dust had clung to them, and have turned away from the true Jacob and Israel the mind that before was quick to insult, and have put out whatever evil was spreading in their thoughts.
2.2:
**“For the Lord hath rendered”** — as God avenged Juda on the pride of Sennacherib, so he avenged the ten tribes, who will be held by Ninive
**“the pride of Jacob”** — which he used against Juda
**“as the pride of Israel: because the spoilers”** — the Assyrians
**“have laid them waste”** — Juda and Israel
**“because the spoilers”** — According to the history, he speaks against Ninive, and the army of the Babylonians coming against her is described.
**“and … vine branches”** — metaphorically
**“their”** — of Juda and Israel
**“have marred”**
• For … hath rendered. The Septuagint: For the Lord hath turned away the captivity of Jacob, as the insult of Israel.
• The Assyrians laid waste both Juda and Israel.
2.3:
**“The shield of his mighty men is like fire”**
• because the Ninivites laid waste Israel, therefore the shield, that is, the strength of the Babylonians, will blaze against Ninive
• Allegorically. The shield, that is, the arms of the devil and his members, are kindled with the fire of envy, of anger and fury; and the men of his army are red in scarlet with the blood of the martyrs. The flaming reins of the chariot that carries the devil through the world are set on fire with the fire of hell; the drivers, who hunt prey for the devil, are stupefied and take their pleasure, and as it were sleep when the prey is taken. But all these, for their evil ways, will be thrown into confusion in the day of judgement, and the chariots are jostled in the streets. Though broad is the way that leads to death, yet, in the pressure of the shortened time, they will not be able to find the right road, but will dash against one another; yet there they will breathe their old fury, and run to and fro like lightning. And the devil and his members will remember, to their own punishment, those who acted mightily and violently against the Church; and they will stumble in their ways, unable to carry out their attempts, and will swiftly go up on her walls. Weakened by terror at the coming judge, they will flee to the ends of the world, by which, as by walls, the world is shut in and surrounded; and, unable to go further, they will be forced as if by necessity to fight against him who presses on them. But while they think this, all that they had gained will be scattered, and the gates that had been shut will be opened, that is, the consciences of each will be revealed; and the kingdoms of the wicked will fall, and the soldier, the devil, and his bondwomen, that is, the soft who are under him, will be led into Tartarus, groaning and indignant against themselves for the evils they have done, and yet murmuring and indignant against God for the punishments they suffer; for they would not have God as their punisher.
**“the men of the army are clad in scarlet”** — ready for the shedding of blood
**“are flaming”** — were
**“the reins … are flaming”** — In the burning reins is signified the swiftness of those hastening, and the pomp of those preparing for war is told; and the Scripture is woven together, mixing now what Israel once suffered, now what the Assyrian did, now what the Babylonians carry out against the Assyrians.
**“the reins of the chariot … in the day”** — elsewhere: in the day
**“of his preparation, and the drivers are stupefied”** — No wonder the Babylonians come so swiftly to lay waste, since the Israelites, or the Ninivites, once the drivers of others, were now useless.
2.4:
**“They are in confusion in the ways”** — they are mingled together
**“the chariots jostle one against another in the streets”** — dashed against one another
**“their looks”**
• of the Babylonians
• namely, so that they may terrify with their face the enemy before they strike him with the sword
**“in the ways”** — Again he returns to the order of the description: so great is the multitude of those coming that the column on the road is mixed and cannot be told apart. The chariots too, for the multitude, will dash against one another in the streets.
2.5:
**“He will muster up”** — he will look for those who fell in the flight
**“his valiant men”** — before
**“they shall stumble in their march: they shall quickly get upon the walls thereof”** — Not withstanding the force of the enemy, they will enter the walls of Ninive
**“and a covering shall be prepared”** — because of the long siege, to keep off the heat, the enemy will make shelters
2.6: **“The gates of the rivers”** — Though the Ninivites shut the gates, the Lord unbars them, and they are opened to the Babylonians; the gates held a multitude of citizens like a river; and the temple, that is, the kingdom, is destroyed.
2.7:
**“And the soldier is led away captive”** — all were led to Babylon
**“and her bondwomen”**
• the lesser towns and strongholds
• captive women
• Under the figure of a woman taken captive the laying waste of Ninive is described.
**“were led away”** — by the victors
**“mourning as doves, murmuring in their hearts”** — So great will be the terror that not even a sob will break out, but, like softly cooing doves, they will swallow their tears with a dim murmur
2.8:
**“And as for Ninive”**
• the world
• When the daughters, that is, the lesser towns, have been destroyed, the people of Ninive itself, which for its multitude is compared to pools of water, will be so useless that, unable to resist the enemy, it will flee.
**“Stand, stand”** — To the peoples fleeing with their goods Ninive cries out like a mother: Stand, stand; shut the gates; at least resist the enemy on the walls. But no one turns back out of love for his mother; they abandon her as prey to the enemy. Hence the voice is directed to the Babylonians: Take the spoil of the gold.
**“but there is none that will return back”**
• to the mother who cries out
• Allegorically. The waters of Ninive, that is, of the world, are those who, leaving the height of heaven, have slipped to the depths; for all the teachings of the world which are outside the garden enclosed, though they seem great, are yet confined within a narrow bound.
• Allegorically. The first thing is that the dwellers in the world should not flee from God by sinning; but if they have fled, at the voice of God, or of mother Church calling them back and saying, You have sinned, be still, one ought to cease from the flight, that is, from the fault; but the obstinate man will not return. To him it is said by the devil: Take with you the silver of worldly eloquence and the gold of worldly wisdom; adorn your teachings with the flower of every meaning and word. But the vessels, that is, their hearts, are so deep in desire that no multitude of riches, however great, can fill them.
2.9:
**“Take ye the spoil”**
• O Babylonians
• because the Ninivites have fled
**“of the silver, take the spoil of the gold”** — seize suddenly what was gathered over so long a time
**“for there is no end of the riches of all the precious furniture”** — you cannot seize as much as she offers to be seized
2.10:
**“She is destroyed”**
• Ninive
• This is of those who are converted to God, who, frozen before by unbelief, are scattered by the warmth of faith; and they rend their hearts by confessing, and tear them by repenting; and the heart, hard before, melts with the warmth of the Holy Spirit; and the knees, stiff before, are bent to God; and all the pleasures of the flesh fail. But what follows, and the faces of them all are as the blackness of a kettle, belongs to those who will not return, whose faces will be covered with confusion like a sooty pot.
**“and rent, and torn: the heart”** — her
**“melteth, and … fail”** — and in her is
**“the knees … and … lose their strength”** — the breaking
**“all the loins … and the faces of them all are as the blackness of a kettle”** — from the greatness of their fear the faces of the inhabitants will look like pots, burnt and disfigured
2.11:
**“Where is now the dwelling”**
• the dwelling
• Allegorically. When Ninive, that is, the world, has passed away, then the saints, wondering and rejoicing, will say: Where is the dwelling of the lions, to which went the devil, and also the whelp, that is, Antichrist, and every word of perverse teaching, which before the coming of Christ no one frightened away? But it killed very many by its demons, and filled its caves, that is, its churches, with corpses and the blood of the dead.
**“of the lions, and the feeding place of the young lions?”** — O Ninive, you were the dwelling of kings and the refreshment of nobles; but now you are no more, because the king of Babylon has invaded you.
**“to which”** — to storm it
**“the lion went”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“to”** — with none resisting
**“enter in thither, the young lion”** — his under-kings
2.12: **“The lion caught enough”** — Nabuchodonosor by right of victory possesses all things, and handed over the captives into servitude to his cities or his wives, and filled his treasuries and his cities with the plunder and the ornaments of Ninive.
2.13:
**“Behold I come against thee”**
• no other
• O Ninive, you will suffer all that has been said, by my doing
• Behold I come against thee: I send the Babylonians.
• Allegorically. God threatens the world that he will burn up the multitude that goes by the broad way to death, and stifle it with the smoke of its malice; and in his goodness the sword, that is, the word of God, will devour even the lions, so that from then on no one is taken to death by them; and he will put down all the din of evil works, which used to announce death to men.
**“saith the Lord”** — for whom to say is to do
**“of hosts, and I will burn … even to smoke”** — to the end
**“thy chariots”** — chariots
**“and … thy young lions”** — I will kill the nobles and under-kings with the sword
**“the sword shall devour: and I will cut off thy prey out of the land”** — you will no longer lay waste the land or exact tribute
**“and the voice of thy messengers shall be heard no more”**
• nor will your emissaries be heard through the provinces; or: I will not hear the angels who are set over you, praying for you.
• Allegorically, all these things can be understood of the confusion to come of those who are to be damned.

3.1:
**“Woe”** — to thee
**“O city of blood, all full of lies and violence”** — in which there is no truth but all lies; you, I say, full of rapine and the tearing of prey
**“Woe to thee, O city”**
• The power of Ninive is described, and under a lament her cruelty is rebuked.
• Allegorically. The world, which “is seated in wickedness” and kills men with its tongues, is called the city of blood; it is lying in the perversity of the teachings by which it tears and carries off many. In the world too is the noise of the whip, that is, of the tribulations under which the just cry out when they are afflicted: when one is tormented by anger, another by lust, another by hatred or envy, the whip of the Assyrian king sounds in them. Sometimes the devil's whip is felt in bodily diseases; for sometimes, not from the nature of the elements but from the devil striking, jaundice is sent, or dropsy, or the pain of the stone, and the like. In the world there is also the rattling of the wheel, when men, not knowing where safety is and where danger, run to and fro. There is also the neighing horse, that is, the devil, who fiercely pursues those who flee, tramples them and mocks them. There is also the running chariot, which is drowned with Pharao; it is drawn by four horses, that is, by the four passions of the mind. Hence: “Hence they desire and fear, grieve and rejoice.” In Ninive there sounds also the horseman coming up, that is, the devil, whose sword shines with the art of dialectic and rhetoric, and his spear glitters while he “transformeth himself into an angel of light”; and by these arms many are killed; and unless they are at once healed by grace, there is a grievous destruction, in which there is no end, because malice has no end. These evils fall, that is, they befall, on the bodies of the dead, which are laid low by the multiplying of fornication. And in Ninive there is a harlot, beautiful and agreeable, who draws almost everyone to love of her by various witchcrafts. She sells the nations in fornications, namely when, through love of temporal things and weariness of good things, those who had been members of Christ become “the members of an harlot,” and draw others with them.
3.2:
**“The noise of the whip”**
• of a savage empire
• O Ninive, is in you
• The army of Ninive preparing for war is described.
**“and the noise”** — the sound
**“of the rattling of the wheels”** — running about in all directions
**“and”** — the noise
**“of the neighing horse, and of the running chariot, and of the horsemen coming up”** — As many as are the kinds of sins, so many are the nations of Ninive.
3.3:
**“And of the shining sword, and”** — the noise
**“of the glittering spear, and of a multitude slain”** — the noise of the adversaries slain by the Ninivites
**“and”** — the noise
**“of a grievous destruction: and there is no end of carcasses, and they shall fall down on their dead bodies”** — either they will fall in their own multitude while they are crowded against one another, or they will fall over the corpses of the slain
**“and they shall fall down”** — The wanton both perish in soul and are weakened even now in the body they serve.
3.4:
**“Because of”** — see the cause
**“the multitude of the fornications of the harlot that was beautiful and agreeable”** — because she committed fornication with many nations, and worshipped the idols of the whole world which she had made subject to herself
**“and that made use of witchcraft”** — it signifies magicians
**“that sold nations through her fornications, and families through her witchcrafts”** — that is, she had power over all nations
3.5:
**“Behold”**
• I will come
• O Ninive, because you have made yourself ready for all fornications like a public brothel
**“I come against thee”** — to overthrow you
**“saith the Lord of hosts: and I will discover thy shame”** — I will not entrust your judgement to angels or to anyone else, but I myself will uncover your shame
**“to thy face”** — so that what you did not see before may be set before your eyes
**“and will shew thy nakedness to the nations, and thy shame to kingdoms”** — so that those who committed fornication with you may themselves despise you and mock you and heap insults on you, as an example to others, with all looking on
**“Behold I come against thee”** — He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman who, caught, is brought out into the midst and stripped of her finery before the eyes of all.
3.6: **“And I will cast abominations upon thee, and will disgrace thee, and will make an example of thee”** — The physician speaks, who comes from heaven to heal the world and can cure all diseases. I will discover, that is, I will make you understand your errors, which before you thought were virtues; and to the nations which you sold in your fornication I will shew your nakedness, so that, seeing your foul body, by whose surface they were led before, they may cease to commit fornication with you; and to kingdoms, which are greater than nations, the shame you brought on yourself. And I will cast abominations upon thee, that is, I will show how abominable you ought to be to those who before were made one body with you; and I will make an example of thee, so that the likeness of the punishment may frighten men away from the likeness of the fault.
3.7:
**“And it shall come to pass that every one that shall see thee, shall flee from thee, and shall say: Ninive is laid waste: who shall bemoan thee?”** — Who will grieve over you?
**“whence shall I seek a comforter for thee?”**
• Whoever sees Ninive set as an example will be afraid and wonder.
• Whence could anyone be your comforter, when in your power you had mercy on no one, nor prepared anyone to share your mourning, you who would not have a partner in reigning?
**“And it shall come to pass”** — Mystically. He who is not ensnared by the false beauty of the world, and sees its foulness within, flees from it, and, judging all earthly goods worthy of lament, will say: Wretched is the world, which binds and holds so many men in vices. But who that understands this misery grieves with the world? As if to say: few there are who, even in their death, can be torn from the embraces of the beautiful harlot. Whence shall I seek a comforter? Who, discussing your unstable way of life, in which all things are wavering, can find anything in you from which he could bring you comfort?
3.8:
**“Art thou better than the populous Alexandria, that dwelleth among the rivers? waters are round about it”** — for it is girt on one side by the stream of the Nile, on another by the lake Mareotis, on the other side by the sea
**“the sea is its riches”** — is
**“the waters”** — are
**“Art thou better”**
• Art thou better than Alexandria, or more populous, or more powerful? She too will be taken by the king of Babylon, Nabuchodonosor, as you will. After this the site of Alexandria is described, which, set on the Nile and the sea, is surrounded on every side by waters.
• Allegorically. He rebukes the lover of the world.
